abstract: In this paper, we will describe several extensions to our earlier work, utiliz(cid:173) ing a segment-based approach. We will formulate our segmental framework and report our study on the use of multi-layer perceptrons for detection and classification of phonemes. We will also examine the outputs of the network, and compare the network performance with other classifiers. Our investigation is performed within a set of experiments that attempts to recognize 38 vowels and consonants in American English independent of speaker. When evaluated on the TIMIT database, our system achieves an accuracy of 56%.

paragraphs: This paper investigates multilayer perceptrons for detecting and classifying phonemes within a segment-based speech recognition framework. The task concerns identifying individual speech sounds, including vowels and consonants. Its speaker-independent setting asks the system to recognize these categories across speakers rather than tying the recognition problem to one person's speech.

The authors formulate their segmental framework and extend earlier work using that approach. Their investigation covers both the outputs produced by the neural network and comparisons with other classifiers. Examining the outputs makes the study about how the network behaves within the recognition framework as well as how often the complete system is correct.

The experiments address 38 American English vowel and consonant categories. On the TIMIT database, the system achieves 56% accuracy. This is the stated recognition result for the speaker-independent task. The contribution combines a segment-based formulation with an evaluation of multilayer perceptrons as phoneme detectors and classifiers, providing a concrete measure of their performance in that setting.
summary.tldr: A segment-based multilayer-perceptron system achieves 56% accuracy on speaker-independent recognition of 38 phoneme categories in TIMIT.

title: Phonetic Classification and Recognition Using the Multi-Layer Perceptron

paragraphs: Inverse kinematics asks which robot configuration produces a desired position in its workspace. The difficulty addressed here is that the forward mapping from configuration to workspace need not have a unique inverse. The paper develops a bootstrap method that learns an inverse using only sampled pairs of configurations and workspace locations.

The method first uses unsupervised clustering on neighborhoods of configurations associated with workspace points. Its purpose is to partition configuration space into subsets where the forward mapping is invertible. Supervised learning then fits a separate inverse function within each subset, giving each learner a relationship with a well-defined direction back to configurations.

This combination turns an ill-posed inverse problem into a collection of better-defined learning problems. The authors demonstrate a global inverse-kinematics solution for a wristless Puma manipulator. The contribution lies in learning the partition as well as the inverse mappings: the organization of the data resolves ambiguity before supervised approximation is applied to the individual regions.
summary.tldr: Clustering separates robot configurations into invertible regions so supervised learners can build a global inverse-kinematics solution.

title: Learning Global Direct Inverse Kinematics

paragraphs: RAPTURE is a system for improving an existing probabilistic knowledge base through a combination of neural and symbolic learning. The knowledge is expressed as rules with certainty factors, so revision can involve changing confidence in an existing rule or introducing a new rule. The system provides a learning mechanism for each kind of change.

A modified backpropagation procedure refines the certainty factors in a MYCIN-style rule base. For additions to the rule set, RAPTURE uses the information gain heuristic associated with ID3. These components act on different aspects of the same knowledge base: one adjusts the strength of what is already represented, while the other expands what can be represented.

The authors evaluate the combined approach by refining two actual expert knowledge bases and report better performance than previous methods. The significance is that revising rule confidence and revising rule structure can work together within one system. Existing expert knowledge supplies the starting point, and learning changes both its numerical assessments and its collection of rules.
summary.tldr: RAPTURE improves expert rule bases by combining backpropagation for certainty factors with information gain for adding rules.

title: Combining Neural and Symbolic Learning to Revise Probabilistic Rule Bases

abstract: We describe an extension to the Mixture of Experts architecture for modelling and controlling dynamical systems which exhibit multi(cid:173) ple modes of behavior. This extension is based on a Markov process model, and suggests a recurrent network for gating a set of linear or non-linear controllers. The new architecture is demonstrated to be capable of learning effective control strategies for jump linear and non-linear plants with multiple modes of behavior.
originalAbstract: We describe an extension to the Mixture of Experts architecture for modelling and controlling dynamical systems which exhibit multi(cid:173) ple modes of behavior. This extension is based on a Markov process model, and suggests a recurrent network for gating a set of linear or non-linear controllers. The new architecture is demonstrated to be capable of learning effective control strategies for jump linear and non-linear plants with multiple modes of behavior.

paragraphs: This paper addresses dynamical systems that operate in multiple modes of behavior. Such systems create a modeling and control problem because their behavior is not described by one unchanging mode. The authors extend the mixture-of-experts architecture so that a collection of controllers can work within a model of these changing operating conditions.

The extension is based on a Markov process model, which represents transitions between modes. It leads to a recurrent gating network that manages a set of linear or nonlinear controllers. Recurrence makes the gating mechanism part of the system's temporal processing, connecting the choice of controller with a description of how modes change over time.

The authors demonstrate that the architecture can learn effective control strategies for both jump-linear and nonlinear plants with multiple behavioral modes. Here, a plant is the system being controlled. The stated result supports combining specialized controllers with a temporal model of mode changes, bringing the organization of the controller set into the learning problem.
summary.tldr: A Markov-based recurrent gating network learns to coordinate controllers for dynamical systems with multiple operating modes.

title: Mixtures of Controllers for Jump Linear and Non-Linear Plants

abstract: Previously, we had developed the concept of a Segmental Neural Net (SNN) for phonetic modeling in continuous speech recognition (CSR). This kind of neu(cid:173) ral network technology advanced the state-of-the-art of large-vocabulary CSR, which employs Hidden Marlcov Models (HMM), for the ARPA 1oo0-word Re(cid:173) source Management corpus. More Recently, we started porting the neural net system to a larger, more challenging corpus - the ARPA 20,Ooo-word Wall Street Journal (WSJ) corpus. During the porting, we explored the following research directions to refine the system: i) training context-dependent models with a reg(cid:173) ularization method; ii) training SNN with projection pursuit; and ii) combining different models into a hybrid system. When tested on both a development set and an independent test set, the resulting neural net system alone yielded a per(cid:173) fonnance at the level of the HMM system, and the hybrid SNN/HMM system achieved a consistent 10-15% word error reduction over the HMM system. This paper describes our hybrid system, with emphasis on the optimization methods employed.

paragraphs: This paper develops optimization methods for using Segmental Neural Nets in continuous speech recognition. Earlier work had applied this phonetic modeling approach to the 1,000-word Resource Management corpus. The authors then moved to the more challenging 20,000-word Wall Street Journal corpus, motivating further changes to training and the combination of recognition models.

They investigate three directions: regularized training of context-dependent models, training with projection pursuit, and combining different models into a hybrid system. These directions address both how the neural component is optimized and how its information contributes alongside a Hidden Markov Model. The paper emphasizes the optimization methods used in the resulting hybrid recognizer.

On a development set and an independent test set, the neural system alone performs at the level of the HMM system. Combining them produces a consistent 10–15% reduction in word error over the HMM. The reported gain therefore comes from the hybrid construction, showing that the two modeling approaches can contribute useful complementary information even when their standalone recognition performance is comparable.
summary.tldr: Optimized Segmental Neural Nets combined with HMMs reduce word error by 10–15% over the HMM system.

title: Segmental Neural Net Optimization for Continuous Speech Recognition

This theory hypoth(cid:173) esizes that the onset of schizophrenia is associated with reactive synaptic regeneration occurring in brain regions receiving degener(cid:173) ating temporal lobe projections. Concentrating on one such area, the frontal cortex, we model a frontal module as an associative memory neural network whose input synapses represent incoming temporal projections. We analyze how, in the face of weakened external input projections, compensatory strengthening of internal synaptic connections and increased noise levels can maintain mem(cid:173) ory capacities (which are generally preserved in schizophrenia) . paragraphs: The paper implements a proposed explanation of schizophrenia in which degeneration of temporal-lobe projections triggers compensatory synaptic changes in connected brain regions. It focuses on the frontal cortex, representing it as an associative memory network. Connections carrying input into that network stand for the projections arriving from the temporal lobe.

The authors examine what happens when these external inputs weaken while internal connections strengthen and noise increases. In the model, those compensatory changes can preserve memory capacity. They also make stored memories emerge spontaneously and unevenly, so that some memories are retrieved more readily than others even without an external trigger.

The authors interpret this biased spontaneous retrieval as a model of hallucinations and delusions, including their concentration around a few recurring themes. They also use the model to explain declining symptoms as the illness progresses and slower responses following delayed intervention. These are explanations within the modeled theory. The central result is that changes preserving memory function can simultaneously produce abnormal retrieval, linking compensation and symptoms through one computational mechanism.
summary.tldr: An associative-memory model links compensation for weakened inputs to preserved memory capacity and spontaneous, biased retrieval resembling psychotic symptoms.

title: A Neural Model of Delusions and Hallucinations in Schizophrenia

abstract: This paper presents an unsupervised learning scheme for categorizing 3D objects from their 2D projected images. The scheme exploits an auto-associative network's ability to encode each view of a single object into a representation that indicates its view direction. We propose two models that employ different classification mechanisms; the first model selects an auto-associative network whose recovered view best matches the input view, and the second model is based on a modular architecture whose additional network classifies the views by splitting the input space nonlinearly. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed classification models through simulations using 3D wire-frame objects.

We propose two models that employ different classification mechanisms; the first model selects an auto-associative network whose recovered view best matches the input view, and the second model is based on a modular architecture whose additional network classifies the views by splitting the input space nonlinearly. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed classification models through simulations using 3D wire-frame objects.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an unsupervised approach to categorizing three-dimensional objects from their two-dimensional projected views. Its starting point is an auto-associative network that encodes views of a single object into a representation indicating viewing direction. This connects the changing appearance of an object to a representation of how it is being viewed.

The authors build two classification models around this capability. The first selects the auto-associative network whose reconstructed view most closely matches the input. The second uses a modular architecture with an additional network that classifies views by dividing the input space nonlinearly. The two models therefore make category decisions through different mechanisms.

Simulations using three-dimensional wire-frame objects demonstrate the effectiveness of both proposed models. The contribution is a way to use learned view representations for object categorization, with reconstruction matching and nonlinear classification as alternative decision methods. The stated demonstration concerns projected views of wire-frame objects, grounding the results in that particular visual setting.
summary.tldr: Two unsupervised models categorize projected views of 3D objects using auto-associative representations that encode viewing direction.

title: Unsupervised Classification of 3D Objects from 2D Views

abstract: A neural network model of 3-D lightness perception is presented which builds upon the FACADE Theory Boundary Contour Sys(cid:173) tem/Feature Contour System of Grossberg and colleagues. Early ratio encoding by retinal ganglion neurons as well as psychophysi(cid:173) cal results on constancy across different backgrounds (background constancy) are used to provide functional constraints to the theory and suggest a contrast negation hypothesis which states that ratio measures between coplanar regions are given more weight in the determination of lightness of the respective regions. Simulations of the model address data on lightness perception, including the coplanar ratio hypothesis, the Benary cross, and White's illusion.

Early ratio encoding by retinal ganglion neurons as well as psychophysi(cid:173) cal results on constancy across different backgrounds (background constancy) are used to provide functional constraints to the theory and suggest a contrast negation hypothesis which states that ratio measures between coplanar regions are given more weight in the determination of lightness of the respective regions. Simulations of the model address data on lightness perception, including the coplanar ratio hypothesis, the Benary cross, and White's illusion.

paragraphs: This paper develops a neural network account of how perceived lightness depends on the spatial organization of a scene. It builds on the FACADE theory's boundary and feature contour systems, connecting the representation of visual regions with the way their lightness is determined.

Two kinds of evidence constrain the model: early encoding of intensity ratios by retinal ganglion neurons, and perceptual findings about lightness remaining stable across different backgrounds. These constraints motivate a contrast negation hypothesis. Its central proposal is that comparisons between regions on the same plane receive greater weight when the visual system determines their lightness.

The model therefore makes three-dimensional relationships relevant to interpreting local contrast. A ratio between two regions matters partly because of how those regions are arranged in the scene. Simulations address the coplanar ratio hypothesis, the Benary cross, and White's illusion. Together, these applications explore whether a shared neural account can connect background constancy with several established lightness phenomena.
summary.tldr: A neural model explains lightness judgments by giving greater weight to contrast comparisons between regions on the same plane.

title: A Neural Network Model of 3-D Lightness Perception

abstract: Initial experiments described here were directed toward using reinforce(cid:173) ment learning (RL) to develop an automated recovery system (ARS) for high-agility aircraft. An ARS is an outer-loop flight-control system de(cid:173) signed to bring an aircraft from a range of out-of-control states to straight(cid:173) and-level flight in minimum time while satisfying physical and phys(cid:173) iological constraints. Here we report on results for a simple version of the problem involving only single-axis (pitch) simulated recoveries. Through simulated control experience using a medium-fidelity aircraft simulation, the RL system approximates an optimal policy for pitch-stick inputs to produce minimum-time transitions to straight-and-Ievel flight in unconstrained cases while avoiding ground-strike. The RL system was also able to adhere to a pilot-station acceleration constraint while execut(cid:173) ing simulated recoveries. Automated Aircraft Recovery via Reinforcement Learning

paragraphs: This paper explores reinforcement learning for an automated aircraft recovery system. Such a system sits above the underlying flight controls and aims to return an aircraft from an out-of-control condition to straight-and-level flight as quickly as possible. The broader objective includes physical constraints on the aircraft and physiological constraints affecting the pilot.

The reported experiments address a simplified version involving simulated recoveries around a single axis: pitch. Using experience from a medium-fidelity aircraft simulation, the learning system develops a policy for pitch-stick inputs. In unconstrained cases, it approximates a minimum-time policy for returning to straight-and-level flight while avoiding a collision with the ground.

The system also performs simulated recoveries while respecting an acceleration constraint at the pilot station. This shows that the learning approach can incorporate a restriction relevant to the person flying the aircraft. The evidence concerns initial, single-axis simulation experiments, establishing a result for that restricted recovery task within the larger aircraft-control objective.
summary.tldr: Reinforcement learning produces rapid simulated pitch recoveries while avoiding ground strikes and can respect a pilot-station acceleration constraint.

title: Automated Aircraft Recovery via Reinforcement Learning: Initial Experiments

abstract: There are many applications in which it is desirable to order rather than classify instances. Here we consider the problem of learning how to order, given feedback in the form of preference judgments, i.e., statements to the effect that one instance should be ranked ahead of another. We outline a two-stage approach in which one first learns by conventional means a preference Junction, of the form PREF( u, v), which indicates whether it is advisable to rank u before v. New instances are then ordered so as to maximize agreements with the learned preference func(cid:173) tion. We show that the problem of finding the ordering that agrees best with a preference function is NP-complete, even under very restrictive assumptions. Nevertheless, we describe a simple greedy algorithm that is guaranteed to find a good approximation. We then discuss an on-line learning algorithm, based on the "Hedge" algorithm, for finding a good linear combination of ranking "experts." We use the ordering algorithm combined with the on-line learning algorithm to find a combination of "search experts," each of which is a domain-specific query expansion strategy for a WWW search engine, and present experimental results that demonstrate the merits of our approach.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning to rank from judgments that one item should appear before another. Its approach separates the task into two stages. First, a learner constructs a preference function for pairs of items. Then an ordering procedure arranges new items to agree with as many learned preferences as possible.

Turning pairwise preferences into the best overall ordering is itself difficult. The authors prove that finding the ordering with maximum agreement is NP-complete, even under restrictive assumptions. They therefore provide a simple greedy algorithm with an approximation guarantee, making the second stage usable without requiring an exact solution.

The paper also develops an online method based on Hedge for learning a linear combination of ranking experts. It combines this learning method with the ordering algorithm in a web-search application, where experts are domain-specific query-expansion strategies. Reported experiments support the approach. The contribution joins preference learning, approximate ordering, and adaptive expert combination into one ranking workflow.
summary.tldr: The paper learns pairwise preferences and combines ranking experts, then efficiently approximates an ordering that agrees with those preferences.

title: Learning to Order Things

paragraphs: Sequential recognition problems require models of how observations depend on their context. A useful model may need to allow several plausible values for an observation, rather than concentrating probability around a single possibility. This paper introduces bidirectional recurrent mixture density networks to represent such multimodal conditional distributions.

The distributions considered describe an observation at a particular time conditioned on a sequence, and can also include preceding observations as conditions. The authors emphasize that the models do not require explicit assumptions about how context should be used. This matters for sequential pattern recognition, including speech recognition, where those conditional relationships arise naturally.

In the reported experiments, the proposed models assign higher likelihood to test data than a traditional modeling approach. Higher test likelihood means that the fitted distributions give greater probability to observations outside the training data. The authors interpret this as evidence that their models summarize the data's statistical properties better. That finding concerns the quality of the generative model; the abstract does not report a corresponding recognition-accuracy result.
summary.tldr: Bidirectional recurrent mixture density networks model multimodal sequential distributions and achieve higher test likelihood than a traditional approach.

title: Better Generative Models for Sequential Data Problems: Bidirectional Recurrent Mixture Density Networks

abstract: A key question in neuroscience is how to encode sensory stimuli such as images and sounds. Motivated by studies of response prop- erties of neurons in the early cortical areas, we propose an encoding scheme that dispenses with absolute measures of signal intensity or contrast and uses, instead, only local ordinal measures. In this scheme, the structure of a signal is represented by a set of equalities and inequalities across adjacent regions. In this paper, we focus on characterizing the (cid:12)delity of this representation strategy. We develop a regularization approach for image reconstruction from ordinal measures and thereby demonstrate that the ordinal repre- sentation scheme can faithfully encode signal structure. We also present a neurally plausible implementation of this computation that uses only local update rules. The results highlight the robust- ness and generalization ability of local ordinal encodings for the task of pattern classi(cid:12)cation.

paragraphs: A sensory representation need not preserve exact intensity values to retain useful structure. This paper studies local ordinal encoding, which records whether neighboring regions are equal, brighter, or darker instead of storing absolute contrast. The question is how much information survives that deliberately restricted description.

The authors reconstruct images from local equalities and inequalities through regularization. Successful reconstruction demonstrates that those comparisons retain substantial signal structure. They also present a neurally plausible implementation based only on local update rules, connecting the computational procedure to a possible distributed mechanism.

The results emphasize robustness and generalization in pattern classification. The contribution shows that relative local order can be a powerful representational primitive, even when absolute measurements are discarded. It offers a way to understand how a sensory system might retain shape and organization while being less tied to the precise intensity scale of the input.
summary.tldr: Local intensity-order relations preserve enough structure for image reconstruction and robust pattern classification without absolute signal measurements.

title: The Fidelity of Local Ordinal Encoding

abstract: Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI) are an interesting emerging technology that is driven by the motivation to develop an effective communication in- terface translating human intentions into a control signal for devices like computers or neuroprostheses. If this can be done bypassing the usual hu- man output pathways like peripheral nerves and muscles it can ultimately become a valuable tool for paralyzed patients. Most activity in BCI re- search is devoted to ﬁnding suitable features and algorithms to increase information transfer rates (ITRs). The present paper studies the implica- tions of using more classes, e.g., left vs. right hand vs. foot, for operating a BCI. We contribute by (1) a theoretical study showing under some mild assumptions that it is practically not useful to employ more than three or four classes, (2) two extensions of the common spatial pattern (CSP) algorithm, one interestingly based on simultaneous diagonalization, and (3) controlled EEG experiments that underline our theoretical ﬁndings and show excellent improved ITRs.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether adding more classes of intended movement improves communication through a brain-computer interface. Such interfaces aim to translate intentions into device commands while bypassing ordinary muscular output. The examples considered include distinguishing left-hand, right-hand, and foot-related classes, with information transfer rate as the central performance concern.

The authors analyze the practical value of increasing the number of classes. Under assumptions described as mild, their theoretical study finds that using more than three or four classes is not practically useful. This is a conditional conclusion about useful class counts, connecting the number of available choices with the interface’s overall communication performance.

The paper also develops two multiclass extensions of the common spatial pattern algorithm, including one based on simultaneous diagonalization. Controlled EEG experiments support the theoretical findings and show improved information transfer rates. Together, the analysis and experiments address both how many classes to use and how to extract features for distinguishing those classes effectively.
summary.tldr: Multiclass CSP methods improve BCI information transfer, while a conditional analysis favors no more than three or four classes.

title: Increase Information Transfer Rates in BCI by CSP Extension to Multi-class

abstract: A typical neuron in visual cortex receives most inputs from other cortical neurons with a roughly similar stimulus preference. Does this arrangement of inputs allow efficient readout of sensory information by the target cortical neuron? We address this issue by using simple modelling of neuronal population activity and information theoretic tools. We find that efficient synaptic information transmission requires that the tuning curve of the afferent neurons is approximately as wide as the spread of stimulus preferences of the afferent neurons reaching the target neuron. By meta analysis of neurophysiological data we found that this is the case for cortico-cortical inputs to neurons in visual cortex. We suggest that the organization of V1 cortico-cortical synaptic inputs allows optimal information transmission.

paragraphs: A visual cortical neuron receives many inputs from neurons with roughly similar stimulus preferences. These are distinct quantities. One describes how broadly an individual neuron responds, while the other describes how diverse the input population's preferences are.

The authors therefore suggest that the organization of these inputs in V1 allows optimal information transmission. The biological conclusion is a suggestion supported by agreement between the model's requirement and the analyzed measurements; it is not presented as proof that every cortical input arrangement is optimal.
summary.tldr: Modeling and a neurophysiological meta-analysis suggest that matching individual tuning widths to population preference spread supports efficient information transmission in V1.

title: Optimal Information Decoding from Neuronal Populations with Specific Stimulus Selectivity

abstract: We present a theory of compositionality in stochastic optimal control, showing how task-optimal controllers can be constructed from certain primitives. The primitives are themselves feedback controllers pursuing their own agendas. They are mixed in proportion to how much progress they are making towards their agendas and how compatible their agendas are with the present task. The resulting composite control law is provably optimal when the problem belongs to a certain class. This class is rather general and yet has a number of unique properties - one of which is that the Bellman equation can be made linear even for non-linear or discrete dynamics. This gives rise to the compositionality developed here. In the special case of linear dynamics and Gaussian noise our framework yields analytical solutions (i.e. non-linear mixtures of linear-quadratic regulators) without requiring the final cost to be quadratic. More generally, a natural set of control primitives can be constructed by applying SVD to Greens function of the Bellman equation. We illustrate the theory in the context of human arm movements. The ideas of optimality and compositionality are both very prominent in the field of motor control, yet they are hard to reconcile. Our work makes this possible.

The proposed composition weights these primitives according to their progress toward their objectives and the compatibility of those objectives with the current task.

The resulting controller is provably optimal for a particular class of stochastic control problems. A defining feature of that class is that its Bellman equation can be transformed into a linear equation, even with nonlinear or discrete dynamics. This mathematical structure makes the composition possible; the optimality claim is conditional on belonging to that class.

For linear dynamics with Gaussian noise, the framework provides analytical solutions formed from nonlinear mixtures of linear-quadratic regulators, without requiring a quadratic final cost. More generally, it constructs primitives using singular value decomposition of the Bellman equation's Green's function. An illustration involving human arm movements shows how the framework can connect two prominent motor-control ideas: combining primitives and achieving task optimality.
summary.tldr: For a specified class of stochastic control problems, appropriately mixing feedback-controller primitives produces a provably optimal task controller.

title: Compositionality of optimal control laws

abstract: Gaussian graphical models are of great interest in statistical learning. Because the conditional independencies between different nodes correspond to zero entries in the inverse covariance matrix of the Gaussian distribution, one can learn the structure of the graph by estimating a sparse inverse covariance matrix from sample data, by solving a convex maximum likelihood problem with an $\ell_1$-regularization term. In this paper, we propose a first-order method based on an alternating linearization technique that exploits the problem's special structure; in particular, the subproblems solved in each iteration have closed-form solutions. Moreover, our algorithm obtains an $\epsilon$-optimal solution in $O(1/\epsilon)$ iterations. Numerical experiments on both synthetic and real data from gene association networks show that a practical version of this algorithm outperforms other competitive algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning the structure of a Gaussian graphical model from sample data. In this setting, zero entries in the inverse covariance matrix correspond to conditional independence between variables. Estimating a sparse inverse covariance matrix therefore identifies a graph with selected dependencies, linking a numerical estimation problem to the structure of a probabilistic model.

The authors solve a convex maximum-likelihood problem with an l1 regularization term that encourages sparsity. Their first-order algorithm uses alternating linearization and exploits the problem's structure. In particular, each iteration involves subproblems with closed-form solutions, avoiding the need for a separate iterative solver for those subproblems.

The theoretical analysis establishes that an epsilon-optimal solution can be obtained in O(1/epsilon) iterations. This specifies how the iteration requirement grows as the requested optimization accuracy becomes tighter. Experiments on synthetic data and real gene-association network data show that a practical version outperforms the compared competitive algorithms. The paper thus combines an explicit convergence guarantee with empirical evidence for an efficient implementation.
summary.tldr: An alternating-linearization method estimates sparse inverse covariance matrices using closed-form subproblems and an O(1/epsilon) iteration guarantee.

title: Sparse Inverse Covariance Selection via Alternating Linearization Methods

abstract: Multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) or neural networks are popular models used for nonlinear regression and classification tasks. As regressors, MLPs model the conditional distribution of the predictor variables Y given the input variables X. However, this predictive distribution is assumed to be unimodal (e.g. Gaussian). For tasks such as structured prediction problems, the conditional distribution should be multimodal, forming one-to-many mappings. By using stochastic hidden variables rather than deterministic ones, Sigmoid Belief Nets (SBNs) can induce a rich multimodal distribution in the output space. However, previously proposed learning algorithms for SBNs are very slow and do not work well for real-valued data. In this paper, we propose a stochastic feedforward network with hidden layers having \emph{both deterministic and stochastic} variables. A new Generalized EM training procedure using importance sampling allows us to efficiently learn complicated conditional distributions. We demonstrate the superiority of our model to conditional Restricted Boltzmann Machines and Mixture Density Networks on synthetic datasets and on modeling facial expressions. Moreover, we show that latent features of our model improves classification and provide additional qualitative results on color images.

paragraphs: Some prediction tasks admit several distinct plausible outputs for the same input. A predictive distribution with only one mode cannot adequately represent that structure. This paper develops a feedforward neural network for learning more complicated conditional distributions, motivated particularly by these one-to-many prediction problems.

Its hidden layers contain both deterministic and stochastic variables. The stochastic variables enable multiple modes in the output distribution, while the combined architecture is trained with a new Generalized EM procedure using importance sampling. The approach addresses the slow learning and difficulties with real-valued data associated with earlier training methods for Sigmoid Belief Nets, which also use stochastic hidden variables.

The authors report better performance than conditional Restricted Boltzmann Machines and Mixture Density Networks on synthetic data and facial-expression modeling. They also find that the model's latent features improve classification and present qualitative results on color images. These findings support the usefulness of the learned representation for both conditional modeling and classification, within the evaluated tasks, rather than only demonstrating that the network can express multimodal outputs.
summary.tldr: A feedforward network combining deterministic and stochastic hidden variables efficiently learns conditional distributions with multiple plausible outputs.

title: Learning Stochastic Feedforward Neural Networks

abstract: Over the past decades, Linear Programming (LP) has been widely used in different areas and considered as one of the mature technologies in numerical optimization. However, the complexity offered by state-of-the-art algorithms (i.e. interior-point method and primal, dual simplex methods) is still unsatisfactory for problems in machine learning with huge number of variables and constraints. In this paper, we investigate a general LP algorithm based on the combination of Augmented Lagrangian and Coordinate Descent (AL-CD), giving an iteration complexity of $O((\log(1/\epsilon))^2)$ with $O(nnz(A))$ cost per iteration, where $nnz(A)$ is the number of non-zeros in the $m\times n$ constraint matrix $A$, and in practice, one can further reduce cost per iteration to the order of non-zeros in columns (rows) corresponding to the active primal (dual) variables through an active-set strategy. The algorithm thus yields a tractable alternative to standard LP methods for large-scale problems of sparse solutions and $nnz(A)\ll mn$. We conduct experiments on large-scale LP instances from $\ell_1$-regularized multi-class SVM, Sparse Inverse Covariance Estimation, and Nonnegative Matrix Factorization, where the proposed approach finds solutions of $10^{-3}$ precision orders of magnitude faster than state-of-the-art implementations of interior-point and simplex methods.

paragraphs: Linear programming is widely used, but problems with very many variables and constraints can remain expensive for standard solvers. This paper proposes AL-CD, which combines an augmented Lagrangian method with coordinate descent. The approach is particularly relevant when the constraint matrix and the desired solutions are sparse.

The authors establish an iteration bound of O((log(1/ε))²), with each iteration costing O(nnz(A)), where nnz(A) counts nonzero entries in the constraint matrix. An active-set strategy can further reduce practical work to nonzero entries in columns or rows associated with active primal or dual variables. The computational benefit therefore connects directly to the sparse structure of the optimization problem.

At a precision of 10⁻³, the proposed approach reaches solutions orders of magnitude faster than the compared interior-point and simplex implementations. These results establish a practical alternative for the evaluated sparse problems, alongside a complexity analysis explaining how sparsity affects its cost.
summary.tldr: Combining augmented Lagrangian optimization with coordinate descent exploits sparsity to solve evaluated large linear programs substantially faster.

title: Sparse Linear Programming via Primal and Dual Augmented Coordinate Descent

abstract: Variational inference is an efficient, popular heuristic used in the context of latent variable models. We provide the first analysis of instances where variational inference algorithms converge to the global optimum, in the setting of topic models. Our initializations are natural, one of them being used in LDA-c, the mostpopular implementation of variational inference.In addition to providing intuition into why this heuristic might work in practice, the multiplicative, rather than additive nature of the variational inference updates forces us to usenon-standard proof arguments, which we believe might be of general theoretical interest.

We provide the first analysis of instances where variational inference algorithms converge to the global optimum, in the setting of topic models. Our initializations are natural, one of them being used in LDA-c, the mostpopular implementation of variational inference.In addition to providing intuition into why this heuristic might work in practice, the multiplicative, rather than additive nature of the variational inference updates forces us to usenon-standard proof arguments, which we believe might be of general theoretical interest.

paragraphs: Variational inference is widely used because it offers an efficient approach to inference in latent-variable models. Its practical usefulness, however, raises a theoretical question about when its updates actually reach a global optimum. This paper analyzes instances of topic models for which that convergence can be proved.

The result concerns particular cases and initializations, rather than a guarantee for every topic model. The initializations are described as natural, and one is already used in LDA-c, an implementation of variational inference. This connection gives the analysis practical relevance: it studies starting procedures that relate to established use of the method.

The proofs must account for the multiplicative form of variational updates, which calls for arguments different from those suited to additive updates. The authors view these arguments as potentially useful beyond the immediate analysis. The contribution is a set of provably correct cases that helps explain why an efficient heuristic can work, while keeping the global-convergence claim tied to the instances studied.
summary.tldr: The paper proves global convergence of variational inference for particular topic-model instances using natural initializations.

title: On some provably correct cases of variational inference for topic models

abstract: We introduce a general simple structural design called “Multiplicative Integration” (MI) to improve recurrent neural networks (RNNs). MI changes the way of how the information flow gets integrated in the computational building block of an RNN, while introducing almost no extra parameters. The new structure can be easily embedded into many popular RNN models, including LSTMs and GRUs. We empirically analyze its learning behaviour and conduct evaluations on several tasks using different RNN models. Our experimental results demonstrate that Multiplicative Integration can provide a substantial performance boost over many of the existing RNN models.

We empirically analyze its learning behaviour and conduct evaluations on several tasks using different RNN models. paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks repeatedly combine information inside a computational building block. The paper investigates whether changing that integration mechanism can improve learning without substantially increasing model size. It introduces a structural design called Multiplicative Integration, or MI, intended as a small modification to existing recurrent architectures.

MI changes how information flows are combined in the recurrent computation while adding almost no parameters. The design can be embedded in popular architectures, including LSTMs and GRUs. This makes it a reusable modification to the recurrent building block rather than an entirely separate task-specific model.

The authors analyze learning behavior empirically and evaluate multiple recurrent models across several tasks. They report substantial performance improvements over many existing recurrent-network models. The abstract does not specify the tasks, numerical gains, or detailed integration formula, so those claims should be read at the level of the evaluated comparisons. Its central contribution is a lightweight architectural change with broad reported empirical benefits.
summary.tldr: Multiplicative Integration changes recurrent-network information combination with almost no extra parameters.

title: On Multiplicative Integration with Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: There has been a resurgence of interest in multiagent reinforcement learning (MARL), due partly to the recent success of deep neural networks. The simplest form of MARL is independent reinforcement learning (InRL), where each agent treats all of its experience as part of its (non stationary) environment. In this paper, we first observe that policies learned using InRL can overfit to the other agents' policies during training, failing to sufficiently generalize during execution. We introduce a new metric, joint-policy correlation, to quantify this effect. We describe a meta-algorithm for general MARL, based on approximate best responses to mixtures of policies generated using deep reinforcement learning, and empirical game theoretic analysis to compute meta-strategies for policy selection. The meta-algorithm generalizes previous algorithms such as InRL, iterated best response, double oracle, and fictitious play. Then, we propose a scalable implementation which reduces the memory requirement using decoupled meta-solvers. Finally, we demonstrate the generality of the resulting policies in three partially observable settings: gridworld coordination problems, emergent language games, and poker.

paragraphs: When several agents learn together, each agent can become specialized to the particular partners or opponents it encounters during training. This paper identifies that problem in independent reinforcement learning, where an agent treats the behavior of others as part of its changing environment. It introduces joint-policy correlation as a metric for measuring this dependence on training partners.

The proposed framework trains approximate best responses to mixtures of policies rather than organizing learning around only one current policy per agent. Deep reinforcement learning generates these responses, while empirical game-theoretic analysis determines meta-strategies for selecting policies. The framework encompasses independent learning, iterated best response, double oracle, and fictitious play as related approaches.

A scalable implementation uses decoupled meta-solvers to reduce memory requirements. Experiments examine the generality of learned policies in partially observable gridworld coordination, emergent language games, and poker. Together, the contributions connect a measurable generalization problem with a training framework that explicitly accounts for multiple possible behaviors by other agents.
summary.tldr: A game-theoretic framework trains agents against mixtures of policies to address overfitting to their training partners.

title: A Unified Game-Theoretic Approach to Multiagent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) excel at creating realistic images with complex models for which maximum likelihood is infeasible. However, the convergence of GAN training has still not been proved. We propose a two time-scale update rule (TTUR) for training GANs with stochastic gradient descent on arbitrary GAN loss functions. TTUR has an individual learning rate for both the discriminator and the generator. Using the theory of stochastic approximation, we prove that the TTUR converges under mild assumptions to a stationary local Nash equilibrium. The convergence carries over to the popular Adam optimization, for which we prove that it follows the dynamics of a heavy ball with friction and thus prefers flat minima in the objective landscape. For the evaluation of the performance of GANs at image generation, we introduce the `Fréchet Inception Distance'' (FID) which captures the similarity of generated images to real ones better than the Inception Score. In experiments, TTUR improves learning for DCGANs and Improved Wasserstein GANs (WGAN-GP) outperforming conventional GAN training on CelebA, CIFAR-10, SVHN, LSUN Bedrooms, and the One Billion Word Benchmark.

title: GANs Trained by a Two Time-Scale Update Rule Converge to a Local Nash Equilibrium

abstract: This paper presents a margin-based multiclass generalization bound for neural networks that scales with their margin-normalized "spectral complexity": their Lipschitz constant, meaning the product of the spectral norms of the weight matrices, times a certain correction factor. This bound is empirically investigated for a standard AlexNet network trained with SGD on the MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets, with both original and random labels; the bound, the Lipschitz constants, and the excess risks are all in direct correlation, suggesting both that SGD selects predictors whose complexity scales with the difficulty of the learning task, and secondly that the presented bound is sensitive to this complexity.
originalAbstract: This paper presents a margin-based multiclass generalization bound for neural networks that scales with their margin-normalized "spectral complexity": their Lipschitz constant, meaning the product of the spectral norms of the weight matrices, times a certain correction factor. This bound is empirically investigated for a standard AlexNet network trained with SGD on the MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets, with both original and random labels; the bound, the Lipschitz constants, and the excess risks are all in direct correlation, suggesting both that SGD selects predictors whose complexity scales with the difficulty of the learning task, and secondly that the presented bound is sensitive to this complexity.

paragraphs: The paper develops a generalization bound for neural networks performing multiclass classification. The bound relates performance beyond training data to a margin-normalized measure of spectral complexity. Margins describe the separation between the correct class score and competing scores, while the complexity term characterizes properties of the network's weight matrices.

Specifically, spectral complexity combines the product of the weight matrices' spectral norms with a correction factor. The paper describes that product as the network's Lipschitz constant, connecting the bound to how strongly the network can amplify input changes. Normalizing complexity by the margin brings this sensitivity measure together with the separation achieved by the classifier.

The authors investigate the bound using AlexNet trained with stochastic gradient descent on MNIST and CIFAR10, with both original and randomized labels. They observe direct correlations among the bound, Lipschitz constants, and excess risks. These observations suggest that stochastic gradient descent selects predictors whose complexity reflects task difficulty, and that the proposed bound is sensitive to this variation.
summary.tldr: A margin-based generalization bound uses spectral complexity and empirically tracks changes in network complexity and excess risk.

title: Spectrally-normalized margin bounds for neural networks

abstract: When used as a surrogate objective for maximum likelihood estimation in latent variable models, the evidence lower bound (ELBO) produces state-of-the-art results. Inspired by this, we consider the extension of the ELBO to a family of lower bounds defined by a particle filter's estimator of the marginal likelihood, the filtering variational objectives (FIVOs). FIVOs take the same arguments as the ELBO, but can exploit a model's sequential structure to form tighter bounds. We present results that relate the tightness of FIVO's bound to the variance of the particle filter's estimator by considering the generic case of bounds defined as log-transformed likelihood estimators. Experimentally, we show that training with FIVO results in substantial improvements over training the same model architecture with the ELBO on sequential data.

Inspired by this, we consider the extension of the ELBO to a family of lower bounds defined by a particle filter's estimator of the marginal likelihood, the filtering variational objectives (FIVOs). FIVOs take the same arguments as the ELBO, but can exploit a model's sequential structure to form tighter bounds. paragraphs: Latent-variable models often use the evidence lower bound, or ELBO, as a practical substitute for directly maximizing likelihood. This paper develops a family of alternative lower bounds called filtering variational objectives, or FIVOs. Their construction uses a particle filter’s estimate of the marginal likelihood.

FIVOs take the same arguments as the ELBO but can use a model’s sequential structure to obtain tighter bounds. A tighter bound provides a closer surrogate for the likelihood being optimized. The authors analyze this connection through the broader class of bounds formed by taking logarithms of likelihood estimators, relating bound tightness to the variance of the particle filter’s estimate.

Experiments on sequential data compare training the same model architecture with FIVO and with the ELBO. The reported substantial improvements therefore demonstrate the importance of the training objective within that comparison, without requiring an architectural change. The contribution links a sequential inference procedure, the quality of its likelihood estimate, and the objective used to fit the model.
summary.tldr: Filtering variational objectives use particle-filter likelihood estimates to exploit sequential structure and improve reported training results over the ELBO.

title: Filtering Variational Objectives

abstract: Fine-Grained Visual Classification (FGVC) is an important computer vision problem that involves small diversity within the different classes, and often requires expert annotators to collect data. Utilizing this notion of small visual diversity, we revisit Maximum-Entropy learning in the context of fine-grained classification, and provide a training routine that maximizes the entropy of the output probability distribution for training convolutional neural networks on FGVC tasks. We provide a theoretical as well as empirical justification of our approach, and achieve state-of-the-art performance across a variety of classification tasks in FGVC, that can potentially be extended to any fine-tuning task. Our method is robust to different hyperparameter values, amount of training data and amount of training label noise and can hence be a valuable tool in many similar problems.

We provide a theoretical as well as empirical justification of our approach, and achieve state-of-the-art performance across a variety of classification tasks in FGVC, that can potentially be extended to any fine-tuning task. paragraphs: Fine-grained visual classification distinguishes classes with small visual differences, and collecting labels often requires expert annotators. This paper uses that similarity between classes to motivate maximum-entropy learning. It introduces a training routine for convolutional neural networks that maximizes the entropy of the output probability distribution in fine-grained classification tasks.

Higher output entropy means that the predicted probability distribution is less concentrated. The proposed routine makes this property part of training, connecting the treatment of prediction probabilities to the visual similarity of the categories. The authors provide both theoretical and empirical justification for the approach, rather than presenting the training change solely as an experimental adjustment.

The reported results reach state-of-the-art performance across a variety of fine-grained classification tasks. The method is also reported to be robust across changes in hyperparameters, training-data quantity, and training-label noise. The authors suggest that it could extend to other fine-tuning tasks; that broader extension is presented as a possibility, while the stated performance evidence concerns the evaluated classification tasks.
summary.tldr: Maximum-entropy training improves fine-grained visual classification and shows robustness to training-data, label-noise, and hyperparameter changes.

title: Maximum-Entropy Fine Grained Classification

abstract: In this paper, we study the stochastic contextual combinatorial multi-armed bandit (CC-MAB) framework that is tailored for volatile arms and submodular reward functions. CC-MAB inherits properties from both contextual bandit and combinatorial bandit: it aims to select a set of arms in each round based on the side information (a.k.a. context) associated with the arms. By ``volatile arms'', we mean that the available arms to select from in each round may change; and by ``submodular rewards'', we mean that the total reward achieved by selected arms is not a simple sum of individual rewards but demonstrates a feature of diminishing returns determined by the relations between selected arms (e.g. relevance and redundancy). Volatile arms and submodular rewards are often seen in many real-world applications, e.g. recommender systems and crowdsourcing, in which multi-armed bandit (MAB) based strategies are extensively applied. Although there exist works that investigate these issues separately based on standard MAB, jointly considering all these issues in a single MAB problem requires very different algorithm design and regret analysis. Our algorithm CC-MAB provides an online decision-making policy in a contextual and combinatorial bandit setting and effectively addresses the issues raised by volatile arms and submodular reward functions. The proposed algorithm is proved to achieve $O(cT^{\frac{2\alpha+D}{3\alpha + D}}\log(T))$ regret after a span of $T$ rounds. The performance of CC-MAB is evaluated by experiments conducted on a real-world crowdsourcing dataset, and the result shows that our algorithm outperforms the prior art.

paragraphs: The paper studies online decisions in which a learner chooses a set of options each round using contextual information about those options. Two complications occur together: the available options can change, and the reward of a selected set depends on relationships among its members. In particular, overlapping or redundant choices can produce diminishing returns.

These features arise in applications such as recommendation and crowdsourcing. An option that is useful alone may add less value when similar options have already been selected, while changing availability prevents the learner from relying on a fixed menu. The proposed CC-MAB algorithm addresses context, set selection, changing availability, and submodular rewards within one stochastic bandit framework.

The paper proves a regret bound of O(c T^((2α+D)/(3α+D)) log(T)) over T rounds. This quantifies how the algorithm's cumulative decision shortfall scales within the analyzed setting. Experiments on a real crowdsourcing dataset also show better performance than prior approaches. The contribution is both an online policy for the combined problem and a theoretical analysis that treats its interacting complications together.
summary.tldr: CC-MAB selects changing sets of contextual options while accounting for diminishing returns, with a regret guarantee and supporting crowdsourcing results.

title: Contextual Combinatorial Multi-armed Bandits with Volatile Arms and Submodular Reward

abstract: Sum-product networks have recently emerged as an attractive representation due to their dual view as a special type of deep neural network with clear semantics and a special type of probabilistic graphical model for which inference is always tractable. Those properties follow from some conditions (i.e., completeness and decomposability) that must be respected by the structure of the network. As a result, it is not easy to specify a valid sum-product network by hand and therefore structure learning techniques are typically used in practice. This paper describes a new online structure learning technique for feed-forward and recurrent SPNs. The algorithm is demonstrated on real-world datasets with continuous features for which it is not clear what network architecture might be best, including sequence datasets of varying length.

paragraphs: Sum-product networks combine characteristics of deep neural networks and probabilistic graphical models. Their appeal includes clear probabilistic meaning and tractable inference. These benefits depend on structural requirements called completeness and decomposability, so choosing the network's connections is part of ensuring that the representation works as intended.

Because constructing a valid architecture by hand is difficult, structure learning is commonly used. This paper introduces an online structure learning technique for both feed-forward and recurrent sum-product networks. It addresses the architecture itself, extending the learning problem beyond selecting numerical parameters for a network whose organization has already been fixed.

The authors demonstrate the algorithm on real-world datasets with continuous features, including sequences of different lengths. These settings are ones where the appropriate architecture is not obvious in advance. The stated contribution is a method for learning structure across both ordinary and recurrent SPNs, illustrated on practical data. The abstract reports those demonstrations without asserting a particular accuracy improvement or a universal advantage over other structure learning methods.
summary.tldr: An online algorithm learns the structure of feed-forward and recurrent sum-product networks, including for variable-length sequence data.

title: Online Structure Learning for Feed-Forward and Recurrent Sum-Product Networks

abstract: Traditional computer graphics rendering pipelines are designed for procedurally generating 2D images from 3D shapes with high performance. The nondifferentiability due to discrete operations (such as visibility computation) makes it hard to explicitly correlate rendering parameters and the resulting image, posing a significant challenge for inverse rendering tasks. Recent work on differentiable rendering achieves differentiability either by designing surrogate gradients for non-differentiable operations or via an approximate but differentiable renderer. These methods, however, are still limited when it comes to handling occlusion, and restricted to particular rendering effects. We present RenderNet, a differentiable rendering convolutional network with a novel projection unit that can render 2D images from 3D shapes. Spatial occlusion and shading calculation are automatically encoded in the network. Our experiments show that RenderNet can successfully learn to implement different shaders, and can be used in inverse rendering tasks to estimate shape, pose, lighting and texture from a single image.

paragraphs: Rendering turns a three-dimensional shape into a two-dimensional image. Working backward from an image is difficult when rendering includes discrete operations, such as deciding which surfaces are visible, that obstruct differentiation. This paper addresses that obstacle with a learned renderer designed to support gradients.

RenderNet is a convolutional network with a projection unit that converts three-dimensional shape information into an image. The network automatically encodes spatial occlusion and shading calculations. The authors position this approach against existing differentiable renderers whose handling of occlusion and range of rendering effects remain restricted.

Experiments show that RenderNet can learn different shaders and can support inverse rendering from a single image. The estimated properties include shape, pose, lighting, and texture. These findings demonstrate the usefulness of a learned rendering process for connecting image appearance to scene parameters. They establish that the network can perform the reported inverse tasks, rather than that every image uniquely determines the scene that produced it.
summary.tldr: RenderNet learns differentiable rendering with occlusion and shading, enabling single-image estimation of shape, pose, lighting, and texture.

title: RenderNet: A deep convolutional network for differentiable rendering from 3D shapes

abstract: We study the implicit regularization imposed by gradient descent for learning multi-layer homogeneous functions including feed-forward fully connected and convolutional deep neural networks with linear, ReLU or Leaky ReLU activation. We rigorously prove that gradient flow (i.e. gradient descent with infinitesimal step size) effectively enforces the differences between squared norms across different layers to remain invariant without any explicit regularization. This result implies that if the weights are initially small, gradient flow automatically balances the magnitudes of all layers. Using a discretization argument, we analyze gradient descent with positive step size for the non-convex low-rank asymmetric matrix factorization problem without any regularization. Inspired by our findings for gradient flow, we prove that gradient descent with step sizes $\eta_t=O(t^{−(1/2+\delta)}) (0<\delta\le1/2)$ automatically balances two low-rank factors and converges to a bounded global optimum. Furthermore, for rank-1 asymmetric matrix factorization we give a finer analysis showing gradient descent with constant step size converges to the global minimum at a globally linear rate. We believe that the idea of examining the invariance imposed by first order algorithms in learning homogeneous models could serve as a fundamental building block for studying optimization for learning deep models.

paragraphs: Training can impose structure on a model even when its objective contains no explicit regularization term. This paper studies that effect in multilayer homogeneous models, including fully connected and convolutional networks with linear, ReLU, or Leaky ReLU activations. Its central question is whether the optimization process itself keeps different layers balanced.

For gradient flow, the idealized version of gradient descent with infinitesimal steps, the authors prove that differences between layers’ squared weight norms stay constant. Consequently, starting with small weights automatically keeps layer magnitudes balanced. The result identifies a precise quantity preserved during training, rather than simply observing a tendency in experiments.

The authors then study finite steps in asymmetric low-rank matrix factorization. With a specified decreasing step-size schedule, gradient descent balances the two factors and converges to a bounded global optimum. For the rank-one case, a finer analysis establishes globally linear convergence with a constant step size. These matrix-factorization guarantees illustrate how the gradient-flow insight can support concrete optimization results.
summary.tldr: Gradient flow preserves differences in layer weight norms, automatically balancing small initializations and motivating convergence guarantees for matrix factorization.

title: Algorithmic Regularization in Learning Deep Homogeneous Models: Layers are Automatically Balanced

abstract: Soft robots have continuum solid bodies that can deform in an infinite number of ways. Controlling soft robots is very challenging as there are no closed form solutions. We present a learning-in-the-loop co-optimization algorithm in which a latent state representation is learned as the robot figures out how to solve the task. Our solution marries hybrid particle-grid-based simulation with deep, variational convolutional autoencoder architectures that can capture salient features of robot dynamics with high efficacy. We demonstrate our dynamics-aware feature learning algorithm on both 2D and 3D soft robots, and show that it is more robust and faster converging than the dynamics-oblivious baseline. We validate the behavior of our algorithm with visualizations of the learned representation.
originalAbstract: Soft robots have continuum solid bodies that can deform in an infinite number of ways. Controlling soft robots is very challenging as there are no closed form solutions. We present a learning-in-the-loop co-optimization algorithm in which a latent state representation is learned as the robot figures out how to solve the task. Our solution marries hybrid particle-grid-based simulation with deep, variational convolutional autoencoder architectures that can capture salient features of robot dynamics with high efficacy. We demonstrate our dynamics-aware feature learning algorithm on both 2D and 3D soft robots, and show that it is more robust and faster converging than the dynamics-oblivious baseline. We validate the behavior of our algorithm with visualizations of the learned representation.

paragraphs: Soft robots have deformable bodies with an enormous range of possible configurations, making their control difficult. The paper addresses this challenge by learning a compact latent state representation while the robot learns to solve its task. Representation learning therefore happens inside the optimization process, alongside the search for useful robot behavior.

The proposed co-optimization approach combines a hybrid particle-grid simulator with deep variational convolutional autoencoders. The simulator represents the robot's physical behavior, while the learned representation captures salient features of its dynamics. The central idea is to make the features sensitive to how the robot moves and changes, so they support the task being optimized.

The authors demonstrate the method on both two- and three-dimensional soft robots. They report greater robustness and faster convergence than a baseline whose features are learned without awareness of the dynamics. Visualizations of the learned representation are used to validate the algorithm's behavior. These results support learning task-relevant state descriptions during optimization, with the empirical advantage stated relative to the dynamics-oblivious baseline.
summary.tldr: Learning a dynamics-aware latent state during soft-robot optimization improves robustness and convergence over a dynamics-oblivious baseline.

title: Learning-In-The-Loop Optimization: End-To-End Control And Co-Design Of Soft Robots Through Learned Deep Latent Representations

abstract: We introduce a stochastic contextual bandit model where at each time step the environment chooses a distribution over a context set and samples the context from this distribution. The learner observes only the context distribution while the exact context realization remains hidden. This allows for a broad range of applications where the context is stochastic or when the learner needs to predict the context. We leverage the UCB algorithm to this setting and show that it achieves an order-optimal high-probability bound on the cumulative regret for linear and kernelized reward functions. Our results strictly generalize previous work in the sense that both our model and the algorithm reduce to the standard setting when the environment chooses only Dirac delta distributions and therefore provides the exact context to the learner. We further analyze a variant where the learner observes the realized context after choosing the action. Finally, we demonstrate the proposed method on synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: In this contextual bandit setting, the learner must choose an action without seeing the exact context that determines its reward. At each step, the environment chooses a distribution and samples a context from it; the learner sees only that distribution. This formulation accommodates situations in which context is stochastic or must itself be predicted.

The authors adapt the upper confidence bound approach to this information structure. For linear and kernelized reward functions, they prove an order-optimal, high-probability bound on cumulative regret. This gives a theoretical account of sequential decision-making when uncertainty concerns the context as well as the rewards associated with actions.

The framework includes the standard observed-context setting as a special case. If every context distribution concentrates on a single point, observing the distribution reveals the exact context, and both the model and algorithm reduce to their standard forms. The paper also analyzes a variant in which the realized context becomes visible after the action, and demonstrates the method on synthetic and real-world datasets.
summary.tldr: A contextual bandit algorithm acts on context distributions and achieves order-optimal regret guarantees for linear and kernelized rewards.

title: Stochastic Bandits with Context Distributions

abstract: Multivariate zero-inflated count data arise in a wide range of areas such as economics, social sciences, and biology. To infer causal relationships in zero-inflated count data, we propose a new zero-inflated Poisson Bayesian network (ZIPBN) model. We show that the proposed ZIPBN is identifiable with cross-sectional data. The proof is based on the well-known characterization of Markov equivalence class which is applicable to other distribution families. For causal structural learning, we introduce a fully Bayesian inference approach which exploits the parallel tempering Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm to efficiently explore the multi-modal network space. We demonstrate the utility of the proposed ZIPBN in causal discoveries for zero-inflated count data by simulation studies with comparison to alternative Bayesian network methods. Additionally, real single-cell RNA-sequencing data with known causal relationships will be used to assess the capability of ZIPBN for discovering causal relationships in real-world problems.

paragraphs: Count data often contain an unusually large number of zeros, as can happen in economics, social science, and biology. This paper introduces a zero-inflated Poisson Bayesian network, or ZIPBN, to infer causal relationships in such data. Its contribution is to make this distinctive distribution of counts part of the network model used for causal discovery.

The authors show that their proposed model is identifiable from cross-sectional observations. Within the ZIPBN model, this means the causal structure can be distinguished using data collected across observations without requiring a time series. Their proof uses a characterization of Markov equivalence classes, connecting the result to reasoning that also applies to other distribution families.

For learning the structure, the paper develops a fully Bayesian procedure using parallel tempering Markov chain Monte Carlo. This is intended to explore a network space with multiple competing peaks of plausibility. Simulation comparisons demonstrate the model's utility against alternative Bayesian network methods. The abstract also describes an assessment using single-cell RNA-sequencing data with known causal relationships, without reporting a specific outcome for that assessment.
summary.tldr: ZIPBN models excess zeros in count data and provides a Bayesian approach to learning causal networks with a stated identifiability result.

title: Bayesian Causal Structural Learning with Zero-Inflated Poisson Bayesian Networks

abstract: In this paper, we investigate how L2 normalisation affects the back-propagated descriptor gradients during training. Based on our observations, we propose HyNet, a new local descriptor that leads to state-of-the-art results in matching. HyNet introduces a hybrid similarity measure for triplet margin loss, a regularisation term constraining the descriptor norm, and a new network architecture that performs L2 normalisation of all intermediate feature maps and the output descriptors. HyNet surpasses previous methods by a significant margin on standard benchmarks that include patch matching, verification, and retrieval, as well as outperforming full end-to-end methods on 3D reconstruction tasks.

paragraphs: Local image descriptors support tasks such as matching image patches and reconstructing three-dimensional scenes. This paper studies how L2 normalization changes the gradients used to train those descriptors, then uses the resulting observations to design a new descriptor called HyNet.

HyNet combines a hybrid similarity measure in a triplet-margin loss, a regularization term that constrains descriptor norms, and an architecture that applies L2 normalization to intermediate feature maps as well as final descriptors. The changes jointly address the training signal and the representation produced by the network.

Experiments report substantial improvements over prior methods on patch matching, verification, and retrieval benchmarks. HyNet also outperforms complete end-to-end alternatives on three-dimensional reconstruction tasks. The abstract does not give benchmark scores or isolate the contribution of each component, so the evidence supports the combined descriptor design in those evaluations rather than a quantified benefit from normalization alone.
summary.tldr: HyNet improves local visual descriptors through normalization-aware similarity and training design.

title: HyNet: Learning Local Descriptor with Hybrid Similarity Measure and Triplet Loss

abstract: We consider two important aspects in understanding and editing images: modeling regular, program-like texture or patterns in 2D planes, and 3D posing of these planes in the scene. Unlike prior work on image-based program synthesis, which assumes the image contains a single visible 2D plane, we present Box Program Induction (BPI), which infers a program-like scene representation that simultaneously models repeated structure on multiple 2D planes, the 3D position and orientation of the planes, and camera parameters, all from a single image. Our model assumes a box prior, i.e., that the image captures either an inner view or an outer view of a box in 3D. It uses neural networks to infer visual cues such as vanishing points, wireframe lines to guide a search-based algorithm to find the program that best explains the image. Such a holistic, structured scene representation enables 3D-aware interactive image editing operations such as inpainting missing pixels, changing camera parameters, and extrapolate the image contents.
