paragraphs: Understanding a patterned scene requires identifying both repeated image structure and the three-dimensional arrangement of the surfaces carrying it. Box Program Induction addresses these together from a single image. It infers a program-like representation spanning multiple two-dimensional planes, including their positions, orientations, and the camera parameters used to view them.

The method assumes that the image depicts either the inside or the outside of a three-dimensional box. This box prior supplies the geometric structure within which the scene is interpreted. Neural networks estimate visual cues such as vanishing points and wireframe lines, and those cues guide a search algorithm toward a program that best explains the image.

The resulting representation combines repetition, surface geometry, and viewpoint in one structured description. This enables interactive editing operations that account for three-dimensional organization, including filling missing pixels, changing camera parameters, and extending image contents. The contribution is extending program induction beyond a single visible plane while keeping the inferred patterns connected to their spatial arrangement.
summary.tldr: Box Program Induction infers repeated patterns, multiple planes, and camera geometry from one image under a three-dimensional box assumption.

title: Multi-Plane Program Induction with 3D Box Priors

abstract: We introduce Exemplar VAEs, a family of generative models that bridge the gap between parametric and non-parametric, exemplar based generative models. Exemplar VAE is a variant of VAE with a non-parametric latent prior based on a Parzen window estimator. To sample from it, one first draws a random exemplar from a training set, then stochastically transforms that exemplar into a latent code and a new observation. We propose retrieval augmented training (RAT) as a way to speed up Exemplar VAE training by using approximate nearest neighbor search in the latent space to define a lower bound on log marginal likelihood. To enhance generalization, model parameters are learned using exemplar leave-one-out and subsampling. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of Exemplar VAEs on density estimation and representation learning. Importantly, generative data augmentation using Exemplar VAEs on permutation invariant MNIST and Fashion MNIST reduces classification error from 1.17% to 0.69% and from 8.56% to 8.16%.

paragraphs: Exemplar VAEs combine a learned generative model with a prior built from training examples. Their nonparametric latent prior uses a Parzen window estimator. Generation begins by selecting a random training exemplar, then randomly transforming it into a latent code and a new observation. This makes example-based generation part of the model's probabilistic structure.

The paper introduces retrieval augmented training to accelerate learning. Approximate nearest-neighbor search in latent space helps construct a lower bound on the log marginal likelihood used for training. Exemplar leave-one-out learning and subsampling are used to enhance generalization, connecting the choice of reference examples with how the model is fitted.

Experiments support the approach for density estimation and representation learning. Generated examples also improve classification: reported error on permutation-invariant MNIST falls from 1.17% to 0.69%, while Fashion MNIST error falls from 8.56% to 8.16%. These results demonstrate a practical connection between a generative model organized around exemplars, efficient retrieval during training, and useful data augmentation.
summary.tldr: Exemplar VAEs generate from training-example-based latent priors and use retrieval to accelerate training, with reported benefits for modeling and augmentation.

title: Exemplar VAE: Linking Generative Models, Nearest Neighbor Retrieval, and Data Augmentation

abstract: Large pre-trained language models have been shown to store factual knowledge in their parameters, and achieve state-of-the-art results when fine-tuned on downstream NLP tasks. However, their ability to access and precisely manipulate knowledge is still limited, and hence on knowledge-intensive tasks, their performance lags behind task-specific architectures. Additionally, providing provenance for their decisions and updating their world knowledge remain open research problems. Pre-trained models with a differentiable access mechanism to explicit non-parametric memory can overcome this issue, but have so far been only investigated for extractive downstream tasks. We explore a general-purpose fine-tuning recipe for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) -- models which combine pre-trained parametric and non-parametric memory for language generation. We introduce RAG models where the parametric memory is a pre-trained seq2seq model and the non-parametric memory is a dense vector index of Wikipedia, accessed with a pre-trained neural retriever. We compare two RAG formulations, one which conditions on the same retrieved passages across the whole generated sequence, the other can use different passages per token. We fine-tune and evaluate our models on a wide range of knowledge-intensive NLP tasks and set the state-of-the-art on three open domain QA tasks, outperforming parametric seq2seq models and task-specific retrieve-and-extract architectures. For language generation tasks, we find that RAG models generate more specific, diverse and factual language than a state-of-the-art parametric-only seq2seq baseline.

paragraphs: Language models store knowledge in their parameters, but retrieving precise facts, updating them, and exposing provenance remain difficult. This paper combines a pretrained sequence-to-sequence model with external nonparametric memory to support language generation grounded in retrieved material.

The external memory is a dense vector index of Wikipedia accessed by a pretrained neural retriever. The authors compare one formulation that uses the same retrieved passages throughout an output sequence with another that can use different passages for different generated tokens.

Fine-tuning and evaluation cover multiple knowledge-intensive tasks. RAG sets state-of-the-art results on three open-domain question-answering tasks, beating parametric sequence models and task-specific retrieve-and-extract systems. For generation, outputs are more specific, diverse, and factual than a strong parametric-only baseline. The abstract supports comparative improvements, not a guarantee that retrieved passages or generated answers are always correct.
summary.tldr: RAG combines a sequence generator with retrieved Wikipedia passages for knowledge-intensive language tasks.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks

abstract: Multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA) learns predictive models from task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, for distinguishing when subjects are performing different cognitive tasks — e.g., watching movies or making decisions. MVPA works best with a well-designed feature set and an adequate sample size. However, most fMRI datasets are noisy, high-dimensional, expensive to collect, and with small sample sizes. Further, training a robust, generalized predictive model that can analyze homogeneous cognitive tasks provided by multi-site fMRI datasets has additional challenges. This paper proposes the Shared Space Transfer Learning (SSTL) as a novel transfer learning (TL) approach that can functionally align homogeneous multi-site fMRI datasets, and so improve the prediction performance in every site. SSTL first extracts a set of common features for all subjects in each site. It then uses TL to map these site-specific features to a site-independent shared space in order to improve the performance of the MVPA. SSTL uses a scalable optimization procedure that works effectively for high-dimensional fMRI datasets. The optimization procedure extracts the common features for each site by using a single-iteration algorithm and maps these site-specific common features to the site-independent shared space. We evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method for transferring between various cognitive tasks. Our comprehensive experiments validate that SSTL achieves superior performance to other state-of-the-art analysis techniques.

abstract: We consider the task of generating diverse and novel videos from a single video sample. Recently, new hierarchical patch-GAN based approaches were proposed for generating diverse images, given only a single sample at training time. Moving to videos, these approaches fail to generate diverse samples, and often collapse into generating samples similar to the training video. We introduce a novel patch-based variational autoencoder (VAE) which allows for a much greater diversity in generation. Using this tool, a new hierarchical video generation scheme is constructed: at coarse scales, our patch-VAE is employed, ensuring samples are of high diversity. Subsequently, at finer scales, a patch-GAN renders the fine details, resulting in high quality videos. Our experiments show that the proposed method produces diverse samples in both the image domain, and the more challenging video domain. Our code and supplementary material (SM) with additional samples are available at https://shirgur.github.io/hp-vae-gan

paragraphs: Generating new videos from a single training video requires producing variation from very limited evidence. Existing hierarchical patch-GAN approaches had shown promise for single-image generation, but their extension to video often produced little diversity. Outputs could collapse toward samples resembling the training video, undermining the goal of generating novel examples.

The paper introduces a patch-based variational autoencoder and uses it within a hierarchical generation process. At coarse scales, this patch-VAE supplies diversity. At finer scales, a patch-GAN adds visual detail. The design assigns different roles to the two components, using one to create varied samples and the other to refine their appearance.

Experiments demonstrate diverse generation in both images and videos, with video identified as the more challenging setting. The stated result supports combining coarse-scale variation with fine-scale rendering when training from one sample. The contribution is especially relevant to the tension highlighted by the paper: a generator can reproduce a source convincingly while still failing to produce meaningfully varied outputs.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical generator combines a coarse-scale patch-VAE with a fine-scale patch-GAN to produce diverse videos from one training sample.

title: Hierarchical Patch VAE-GAN: Generating Diverse Videos from a Single Sample

abstract: Recent success of pre-trained language models crucially hinges on fine-tuning them on large amounts of labeled data for the downstream task, that are typically expensive to acquire or difficult to access for many applications. We study self-training as one of the earliest semi-supervised learning approaches to reduce the annotation bottleneck by making use of large-scale unlabeled data for the target task. Standard self-training mechanism randomly samples instances from the unlabeled pool to generate pseudo-labels and augment labeled data. We propose an approach to improve self-training by incorporating uncertainty estimates of the underlying neural network leveraging recent advances in Bayesian deep learning. Specifically, we propose (i) acquisition functions to select instances from the unlabeled pool leveraging Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout, and (ii) learning mechanism leveraging model confidence for self-training. As an application, we focus on text classification with five benchmark datasets. We show our methods leveraging only 20-30 labeled samples per class for each task for training and for validation perform within 3% of fully supervised pre-trained language models fine-tuned on thousands of labels with an aggregate accuracy of 91% and improvement of up to 12% over baselines.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning pretrained language models often requires many labeled examples. This paper uses self-training to reduce that annotation burden by drawing on unlabeled examples from the target task. The model supplies pseudo-labels, allowing those examples to contribute to learning alongside the small labeled collection.

The proposed approach incorporates uncertainty into both example selection and learning. Acquisition functions use Monte Carlo dropout to choose examples from the unlabeled pool, and the training mechanism uses model confidence. These additions address which pseudo-labeled examples enter training and how confidence informs the subsequent learning process.

Across five text-classification benchmarks, the methods use only 20–30 labeled examples per class for training and for validation. They achieve 91% aggregate accuracy, perform within 3% of fully supervised pretrained models fine-tuned on thousands of labels, and improve by up to 12% over baselines. The findings show that uncertainty-aware use of unlabeled data can substantially reduce labeled-data requirements in the evaluated tasks while retaining performance close to the larger supervised setups.
summary.tldr: Uncertainty-aware example selection and confidence-based self-training bring few-shot text classification close to fully supervised performance on five benchmarks.

title: Uncertainty-aware Self-training for Few-shot Text Classification

abstract: Most state-of-the-art Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) can be defined as a form of graph convolution which can be realized by message passing between direct neighbors or beyond. To scale such GNNs to large graphs, various neighbor-, layer-, or subgraph-sampling techniques are proposed to alleviate the "neighbor explosion" problem by considering only a small subset of messages passed to the nodes in a mini-batch. However, sampling-based methods are difficult to apply to GNNs that utilize many-hops-away or global context each layer, show unstable performance for different tasks and datasets, and do not speed up model inference. We propose a principled and fundamentally different approach, VQ-GNN, a universal framework to scale up any convolution-based GNNs using Vector Quantization (VQ) without compromising the performance. In contrast to sampling-based techniques, our approach can effectively preserve all the messages passed to a mini-batch of nodes by learning and updating a small number of quantized reference vectors of global node representations, using VQ within each GNN layer. Our framework avoids the "neighbor explosion" problem of GNNs using quantized representations combined with a low-rank version of the graph convolution matrix. We show that such a compact low-rank version of the gigantic convolution matrix is sufficient both theoretically and experimentally. In company with VQ, we design a novel approximated message passing algorithm and a nontrivial back-propagation rule for our framework. Experiments on various types of GNN backbones demonstrate the scalability and competitive performance of our framework on large-graph node classification and link prediction benchmarks.

Sampling reduces this burden, but can be awkward for layers using distant or global information and does not accelerate inference. VQ-GNN addresses scaling through compact representations of global node information, targeting convolution-based graph neural networks.

Within each layer, vector quantization learns and updates a small collection of reference vectors representing global node embeddings. These quantized representations combine with a low-rank graph convolution matrix to avoid neighborhood explosion while effectively preserving the messages contributing to a minibatch. The framework includes an approximate message-passing algorithm and a specialized backpropagation rule for learning with this representation.

The authors provide theoretical and experimental support for the sufficiency of the compact low-rank convolution representation. Experiments across multiple graph-network backbones show scalability and competitive performance on large-graph node classification and link prediction. The findings support compressing the representation of message passing as a broadly applicable route to scaling convolution-based graph models.
summary.tldr: VQ-GNN scales convolution-based graph networks using quantized node representations and low-rank message passing.

title: VQ-GNN: A Universal Framework to Scale up Graph Neural Networks using Vector Quantization

abstract: Gradient inversion attack (or input recovery from gradient) is an emerging threat to the security and privacy preservation of Federated learning, whereby malicious eavesdroppers or participants in the protocol can recover (partially) the clients' private data. This paper evaluates existing attacks and defenses. We find that some attacks make strong assumptions about the setup. Relaxing such assumptions can substantially weaken these attacks. We then evaluate the benefits of three proposed defense mechanisms against gradient inversion attacks. We show the trade-offs of privacy leakage and data utility of these defense methods, and find that combining them in an appropriate manner makes the attack less effective, even under the original strong assumptions. We also estimate the computation cost of end-to-end recovery of a single image under each evaluated defense. Our findings suggest that the state-of-the-art attacks can currently be defended against with minor data utility loss, as summarized in a list of potential strategies.

paragraphs: Federated learning can expose information through shared gradients even when clients keep their original data private. Gradient inversion attacks attempt to reconstruct those inputs, at least partially, from gradient information. This paper evaluates existing attacks and defenses, focusing on how attack assumptions and protective measures affect the resulting privacy risk.

The authors find that some attacks rely on strong assumptions about the learning setup. Relaxing those assumptions can substantially reduce attack effectiveness. They also evaluate three proposed defenses and examine their tradeoffs between privacy leakage and data utility. Combining the defenses appropriately makes reconstruction less effective even when the attacks retain their original favorable assumptions.

The analysis additionally estimates the computational cost of recovering a single image from beginning to end under each evaluated defense. This adds a practical dimension to the comparison beyond whether reconstruction is possible. The findings suggest that the state-of-the-art attacks evaluated in the paper can be resisted with only minor utility loss. That conclusion concerns these assessed attacks and configurations, rather than establishing immunity to all possible gradient-based privacy attacks.
summary.tldr: Evaluated gradient inversion attacks weaken under relaxed assumptions and suitable defense combinations, suggesting protection with minor data-utility loss.

title: Evaluating Gradient Inversion Attacks and Defenses in Federated Learning

abstract: Advances in unsupervised learning of object-representations have culminated in the development of a broad range of methods for unsupervised object segmentation and interpretable object-centric scene generation. These methods, however, are limited to simulated and real-world datasets with limited visual complexity. Moreover, object representations are often inferred using RNNs which do not scale well to large images or iterative refinement which avoids imposing an unnatural ordering on objects in an image but requires the a priori initialisation of a fixed number of object representations. In contrast to established paradigms, this work proposes an embedding-based approach in which embeddings of pixels are clustered in a differentiable fashion using a stochastic stick-breaking process. Similar to iterative refinement, this clustering procedure also leads to randomly ordered object representations, but without the need of initialising a fixed number of clusters a priori. This is used to develop a new model, GENESIS-v2, which can infer a variable number of object representations without using RNNs or iterative refinement. We show that GENESIS-v2 performs strongly in comparison to recent baselines in terms of unsupervised image segmentation and object-centric scene generation on established synthetic datasets as well as more complex real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Learning object representations without supervision can support both image segmentation and scene generation organized around individual objects. Existing approaches face difficulties with visually complex images and with how they construct object representations. Recurrent models impose a sequence and scale poorly to large images, while iterative refinement requires initializing a fixed number of representations.

GENESIS-v2 instead learns pixel embeddings and groups them through differentiable clustering based on a stochastic stick-breaking process. This procedure produces randomly ordered object representations without initializing a fixed number of clusters in advance. The resulting model can infer a variable number of objects without recurrent networks or iterative refinement, directly addressing the representation choices highlighted by the authors.

The paper evaluates the model on established synthetic datasets and more complex real-world datasets. It reports strong performance relative to recent baselines for unsupervised segmentation and object-centric scene generation. These findings support embedding-based clustering as a practical route to flexible object representations, with evidence extending beyond the simpler visual settings that motivated the work.
summary.tldr: GENESIS-v2 uses differentiable pixel clustering to infer a variable number of unordered object representations without recurrent networks or iterative refinement.

title: GENESIS-V2: Inferring Unordered Object Representations without Iterative Refinement

abstract: We consider a line-search method for continuous optimization under a stochastic setting where the function values and gradients are available only through inexact probabilistic zeroth and first-order oracles. These oracles capture multiple standard settings including expected loss minimization and zeroth-order optimization. Moreover, our framework is very general and allows the function and gradient estimates to be biased. The proposed algorithm is simple to describe, easy to implement, and uses these oracles in a similar way as the standard deterministic line search uses exact function and gradient values. Under fairly general conditions on the oracles, we derive a high probability tail bound on the iteration complexity of the algorithm when applied to non-convex smooth functions. These results are stronger than those for other existing stochastic line search methods and apply in more general settings.

paragraphs: Line search adjusts optimization steps using information about the objective and its gradient. This paper considers the harder setting where those quantities are available only through probabilistic, inexact estimates. Its framework includes expected-loss minimization and zeroth-order optimization, and it permits biased estimates of both function values and gradients.

The proposed algorithm uses these information sources in a manner similar to deterministic line search with exact quantities. This preserves a simple algorithmic structure while accommodating uncertainty in the observations. Allowing bias broadens the covered settings beyond ones where each estimate must be correct on average.

Under fairly general conditions on the information sources, the authors derive a high-probability tail bound on iteration complexity for smooth nonconvex objectives. Such a bound controls the probability of requiring unusually many iterations, rather than describing only average behavior. The paper reports stronger results than existing stochastic line-search analyses and applicability to more general settings, with those guarantees remaining conditional on the required oracle properties.
summary.tldr: A stochastic line-search method receives high-probability iteration bounds even when function and gradient estimates can be biased.

title: High Probability Complexity Bounds for Line Search Based on Stochastic Oracles

abstract: We study the role of the representation of state-action value functions in regret minimization in finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with linear structure. We first derive a necessary condition on the representation, called universally spanning optimal features (UNISOFT), to achieve constant regret in any MDP with linear reward function. This result encompasses the well-known settings of low-rank MDPs and, more generally, zero inherent Bellman error (also known as the Bellman closure assumption). We then demonstrate that this condition is also sufficient for these classes of problems by deriving a constant regret bound for two optimistic algorithms (LSVI-UCB and ELEANOR). Finally, we propose an algorithm for representation selection and we prove that it achieves constant regret when one of the given representations, or a suitable combination of them, satisfies the UNISOFT condition.

paragraphs: In reinforcement learning, the representation of state-action values can affect how much performance an agent loses while learning. This paper studies finite-horizon Markov decision processes with linear structure and asks when regret can remain bounded by a constant, rather than continuing to increase as learning proceeds.

The authors derive a necessary representation condition called universally spanning optimal features, or UNISOFT, for constant regret in any MDP with a linear reward function. They then establish sufficiency for low-rank MDPs and the more general class with zero inherent Bellman error. For these classes, they prove constant-regret bounds for the optimistic algorithms LSVI-UCB and ELEANOR.

The paper also develops an algorithm that selects among supplied representations. It achieves constant regret when one representation, or a suitable combination of them, satisfies UNISOFT. The result links learning efficiency to a precise property of the available features. Its guarantee is conditional: representation selection delivers the stated bound when the candidate collection contains the required structure, either directly or through combination.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes representation conditions for constant regret in linear MDPs and proves a conditional guarantee for selecting suitable representations.

title: Reinforcement Learning in Linear MDPs: Constant Regret and Representation Selection

abstract: Automated machine learning (AutoML) can make data scientists more productive. But if machine learning is totally automated, that leaves no room for data scientists to apply their intuition. Hence, data scientists often prefer not total but gradual automation, where they control certain choices and AutoML explores the rest. Unfortunately, gradual AutoML is cumbersome with state-of-the-art tools, requiring large non-compositional code changes. More concise compositional code can be achieved with combinators, a powerful concept from functional programming. This paper introduces a small set of orthogonal combinators for composing machine-learning operators into pipelines. It describes a translation scheme from pipelines and associated hyperparameter schemas to search spaces for AutoML optimizers. On that foundation, this paper presents Lale, an open-source sklearn-compatible AutoML library, and evaluates it with a user study.

paragraphs: Automated machine learning can explore modeling choices, but practitioners often want to keep control over some decisions. This paper addresses gradual automation: a data scientist specifies selected parts of a workflow while an automated optimizer searches the remaining choices. Existing tools can make changes to that boundary cumbersome, requiring substantial rewrites.

The proposed solution uses a small set of combinators, reusable composition mechanisms drawn from functional programming, to assemble machine-learning operators into pipelines. The combinators are orthogonal, giving distinct building blocks for expressing workflows. A translation scheme then converts the pipelines and their hyperparameter schemas into search spaces that AutoML optimizers can explore.

The authors implement these ideas in Lale, an open-source library compatible with scikit-learn, and evaluate it through a user study. The contribution is a programming foundation for mixing human judgment with automated search. By connecting compositional pipeline descriptions to optimizer search spaces, the approach supports workflows in which the practitioner can adjust which decisions remain fixed and which are automated.
summary.tldr: Lale uses composable pipeline building blocks to let practitioners fix selected modeling decisions while AutoML searches the rest.

title: Pipeline Combinators for Gradual AutoML

abstract: Recent success in deep learning has partially been driven by training increasingly overparametrized networks on ever larger datasets. It is therefore natural to ask: how much of the data is superfluous, which examples are important for generalization, and how do we find them? In this work, we make the striking observation that, in standard vision datasets, simple scores averaged over several weight initializations can be used to identify important examples very early in training. We propose two such scores—the Gradient Normed (GraNd) and the Error L2-Norm (EL2N) scores—and demonstrate their efficacy on a range of architectures and datasets by pruning significant fractions of training data without sacrificing test accuracy. In fact, using EL2N scores calculated a few epochs into training, we can prune half of the CIFAR10 training set while slightly improving test accuracy. Furthermore, for a given dataset, EL2N scores from one architecture or hyperparameter configuration generalize to other configurations. Compared to recent work that prunes data by discarding examples that are rarely forgotten over the course of training, our scores use only local information early in training. We also use our scores to detect noisy examples and study training dynamics through the lens of important examples—we investigate how the data distribution shapes the loss surface and identify subspaces of the model’s data representation that are relatively stable over training.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether useful training examples can be identified before a neural network has completed training. On standard vision datasets, the authors find that simple scores computed early and averaged across several weight initializations can identify examples that matter for generalization. This makes data selection possible without observing the entire training trajectory.

The proposed scores are GraNd, based on gradient norms, and EL2N, based on the size of prediction errors. Across the evaluated architectures and datasets, these scores support removing substantial portions of training data without reducing test accuracy. For a given dataset, EL2N scores also transfer across architectures or hyperparameter configurations. The authors additionally use the scores to detect noisy examples and examine how data shapes training dynamics and learned representations. Together, the findings present early training behavior as a useful signal for both selecting data and studying its influence.
summary.tldr: Simple scores measured early in training identify useful examples and enable substantial data pruning without sacrificing test accuracy in the reported experiments.

title: Deep Learning on a Data Diet: Finding Important Examples Early in Training

abstract: Federated learning, which shares the weights of the neural network across clients, is gaining attention in the healthcare sector as it enables training on a large corpus of decentralized data while maintaining data privacy. For example, this enables neural network training for COVID-19 diagnosis on chest X-ray (CXR) images without collecting patient CXR data across multiple hospitals. Unfortunately, the exchange of the weights quickly consumes the network bandwidth if highly expressive network architecture is employed. So-called split learning partially solves this problem by dividing a neural network into a client and a server part, so that the client part of the network takes up less extensive computation resources and bandwidth. However, it is not clear how to find the optimal split without sacrificing the overall network performance. To amalgamate these methods and thereby maximize their distinct strengths, here we show that the Vision Transformer, a recently developed deep learning architecture with straightforward decomposable configuration, is ideally suitable for split learning without sacrificing performance. Even under the non-independent and identically distributed data distribution which emulates a real collaboration between hospitals using CXR datasets from multiple sources, the proposed framework was able to attain performance comparable to data-centralized training. In addition, the proposed framework along with heterogeneous multi-task clients also improves individual task performances including the diagnosis of COVID-19, eliminating the need for sharing large weights with innumerable parameters. Our results affirm the suitability of Transformer for collaborative learning in medical imaging and pave the way forward for future real-world implementations.

However, it is not clear how to find the optimal split without sacrificing the overall network performance. Even under the non-independent and identically distributed data distribution which emulates a real collaboration between hospitals using CXR datasets from multiple sources, the proposed framework was able to attain performance comparable to data-centralized training. In addition, the proposed framework along with heterogeneous multi-task clients also improves individual task performances including the diagnosis of COVID-19, eliminating the need for sharing large weights with innumerable parameters. Our results affirm the suitability of Transformer for collaborative learning in medical imaging and pave the way forward for future real-world implementations.

paragraphs: Collaborative medical-image training can use data held at different hospitals without gathering patient images in one place. Federated learning supports this arrangement by exchanging network weights, but large models can impose substantial communication costs. Split learning divides a model between clients and a server, creating a related challenge: choosing a division that preserves performance.

The paper combines these approaches using a Vision Transformer. Its readily decomposable architecture provides a basis for separating client and server computation while retaining model performance. The framework is evaluated using chest X-ray datasets from multiple sources, including uneven data distributions intended to resemble collaboration between hospitals.

In those experiments, the framework achieves performance comparable to centralized training. It also improves individual task performance, including COVID-19 diagnosis, when participating clients have different tasks, while avoiding the exchange of large parameter sets. The findings support the suitability of Transformers for this form of collaborative medical-image learning and provide evidence for the proposed architecture under heterogeneous data and task conditions.
summary.tldr: A federated split Vision Transformer supports collaborative chest X-ray learning with reduced weight-sharing demands and performance comparable to centralized training.

title: Federated Split Task-Agnostic Vision Transformer for COVID-19 CXR Diagnosis

abstract: Images, captured by a camera, play a critical role in training Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). Usually, we assume the images acquired by cameras are consistent with the ones perceived by human eyes. However, due to the different physical mechanisms between human-vision and computer-vision systems, the final perceived images could be very different in some cases, for example shooting on digital monitors. In this paper, we find a special phenomenon in digital image processing, the moiré effect, that could cause unnoticed security threats to DNNs. Based on it, we propose a Moiré Attack (MA) that generates the physical-world moiré pattern adding to the images by mimicking the shooting process of digital devices. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed digital Moiré Attack (MA) is a perfect camouflage for attackers to tamper with DNNs with a high success rate ($100.0\%$ for untargeted and $97.0\%$ for targeted attack with the noise budget $\epsilon=4$), high transferability rate across different models, and high robustness under various defenses. Furthermore, MA owns great stealthiness because the moiré effect is unavoidable due to the camera's inner physical structure, which therefore hardly attracts the awareness of humans. Our code is available at https://github.com/Dantong88/Moire_Attack.

paragraphs: An image photographed from a digital screen can differ from what a person perceives directly. This paper investigates the security implications of moiré patterns arising in that process. The authors argue that familiar capture artifacts can conceal changes that substantially affect a neural network's interpretation of an image.

Their Moiré Attack generates patterns by mimicking the process of photographing digital devices. This connects the attack's appearance to a physical image-formation phenomenon. Its proposed stealth comes from the possibility that people will interpret the resulting pattern as an ordinary camera artifact and consequently overlook its adversarial role.

In the reported digital experiments, the attack achieves 100.0% untargeted success and 97.0% targeted success with a noise budget of four. The authors also report strong transfer across models and robustness under various defenses. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of the evaluated digital attack and identify screen photography as a potential source of deceptive visual artifacts. The stated results do not make every occurrence of moiré evidence of an attack.
summary.tldr: A digital attack that mimics screen-photography moiré patterns achieves high reported success while resembling a familiar capture artifact.

title: Morié Attack (MA): A New Potential Risk of Screen Photos

abstract: Multi-hop reasoning (i.e., reasoning across two or more documents) is a key ingredient for NLP models that leverage large corpora to exhibit broad knowledge. To retrieve evidence passages, multi-hop models must contend with a fast-growing search space across the hops, represent complex queries that combine multiple information needs, and resolve ambiguity about the best order in which to hop between training passages. We tackle these problems via Baleen, a system that improves the accuracy of multi-hop retrieval while learning robustly from weak training signals in the many-hop setting. To tame the search space, we propose condensed retrieval, a pipeline that summarizes the retrieved passages after each hop into a single compact context. To model complex queries, we introduce a focused late interaction retriever that allows different parts of the same query representation to match disparate relevant passages. Lastly, to infer the hopping dependencies among unordered training passages, we devise latent hop ordering, a weak-supervision strategy in which the trained retriever itself selects the sequence of hops. We evaluate Baleen on retrieval for two-hop question answering and many-hop claim verification, establishing state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Answering a question or checking a claim can require combining evidence from several documents. Each retrieval step opens more possible paths, while the query may contain several distinct information needs. Training adds another difficulty: relevant passages may be known without specifying the order in which a system should retrieve them. Baleen addresses these problems together.

Its condensed retrieval pipeline summarizes passages after each step into one compact context, keeping the growing evidence collection manageable. A focused late interaction retriever lets different parts of a query match different relevant passages. This supports queries whose information needs cannot all be satisfied by the same piece of text.

For training, Baleen uses latent hop ordering: the retriever itself chooses a sequence through otherwise unordered evidence passages. This makes weak supervision useful even when reasoning requires many steps. Evaluations on retrieval for two-hop question answering and many-hop claim verification report state-of-the-art performance, supporting the combined use of compact context, flexible matching, and learned retrieval order.
summary.tldr: Baleen improves multi-hop evidence retrieval by condensing context, matching distinct query needs, and learning the order of retrieval steps.

title: Baleen: Robust Multi-Hop Reasoning at Scale via Condensed Retrieval

abstract: With the recent expanding attention of machine learning researchers and practitioners to fairness, there is a void of a common framework to analyze and compare the capabilities of proposed models in deep representation learning. In this paper, we evaluate different fairness methods trained with deep neural networks on a common synthetic dataset and a real-world dataset to obtain better insights on how these methods work. In particular, we train about 3000 different models in various setups, including imbalanced and correlated data configurations, to verify the limits of the current models and better understand in which setups they are subject to failure. Our results show that the bias of models increase as datasets become more imbalanced or datasets attributes become more correlated, the level of dominance of correlated sensitive dataset features impact bias, and the sensitive information remains in the latent representation even when bias-mitigation algorithms are applied. Overall, we present a dataset, propose various challenging evaluation setups, and rigorously evaluate recent promising bias-mitigation algorithms in a common framework and publicly release this benchmark, hoping the research community would take it as a common entry point for fair deep learning.

paragraphs: Methods for reducing bias in deep representation learning are difficult to compare when they are evaluated under different conditions. This paper creates a common benchmarking framework and tests fairness methods on both synthetic and real-world data. The aim is to understand how these approaches behave and identify settings in which they fail.

The authors train about 3,000 models across configurations that vary data imbalance and correlations between attributes. In their experiments, model bias increases as the data become more imbalanced or attributes become more correlated. They also find that the dominance of correlated sensitive features affects bias, showing that the structure of the data matters when interpreting mitigation results.

Another reported finding is that sensitive information remains in learned representations even after bias-mitigation algorithms are applied. This highlights a distinction between applying a mitigation method and removing sensitive information from the representation. The released dataset, challenging configurations, and common evaluation framework provide resources for examining these behaviors systematically across the evaluated methods.
summary.tldr: A shared benchmark finds that data imbalance and attribute correlations challenge bias mitigation, while sensitive information persists in learned representations.

title: Benchmarking Bias Mitigation Algorithms in Representation Learning through Fairness Metrics

abstract: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) promises a non-intrusive way to measure real-time brain activity and build responsive brain-computer interfaces. A primary barrier to realizing this technology's potential has been that observed fNIRS signals vary significantly across human users. Building models that generalize well to never-before-seen users has been difficult; a large amount of subject-specific data has been needed to train effective models. To help overcome this barrier, we introduce the largest open-access dataset of its kind, containing multivariate fNIRS recordings from 68 participants, each with labeled segments indicating four possible mental workload intensity levels. Labels were collected via a controlled setting in which subjects performed standard n-back tasks to induce desired working memory levels. We propose a benchmark analysis of this dataset with a standardized training and evaluation protocol, which allows future researchers to report comparable numbers and fairly assess generalization potential while avoiding any overlap or leakage between train and test data. Using this dataset and benchmark, we show how models trained using abundant fNIRS data from many other participants can effectively classify a new target subject's data, thus reducing calibration and setup time for new subjects. We further show how performance improves as the size of the available dataset grows, while also analyzing error rates across key subpopulations to audit equity concerns. We share our open-access Tufts fNIRS to Mental Workload (fNIRS2MW) dataset and open-source code as a step toward advancing brain computer interfaces.

These findings support collecting and sharing multi-participant data as a practical route toward interfaces that transfer more effectively to new users.
summary.tldr: The Tufts benchmark shows that shared fNIRS data from many participants can support mental-workload classification for new users with less calibration.

title: The Tufts fNIRS Mental Workload Dataset & Benchmark for Brain-Computer Interfaces that Generalize

abstract: Bayesian coresets approximate a posterior distribution by building a small weighted subset of the data points. Any inference procedure that is too computationally expensive to be run on the full posterior can instead be run inexpensively on the coreset, with results that approximate those on the full data. However, current approaches are limited by either a significant run-time or the need for the user to specify a low-cost approximation to the full posterior. We propose a Bayesian coreset construction algorithm that first selects a uniformly random subset of data, and then optimizes the weights using a novel quasi-Newton method. Our algorithm is a simple to implement, black-box method, that does not require the user to specify a low-cost posterior approximation. It is the first to come with a general high-probability bound on the KL divergence of the output coreset posterior. Experiments demonstrate that our method provides significant improvements in coreset quality against alternatives with comparable construction times, with far less storage cost and user input required.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference can become expensive when it must use an entire dataset. A coreset replaces that dataset with a small weighted selection of observations, producing an approximate posterior on which inference is cheaper. Existing construction methods can themselves be slow or require users to supply an inexpensive approximation to the full posterior.

This paper proposes a two-stage construction method. It first selects observations uniformly at random, then adjusts their weights using a new quasi-Newton optimization method. The resulting approach is described as simple to implement and usable as a black box, without requiring the user to design a separate low-cost posterior approximation.

The authors provide a general high-probability bound on the KL divergence of the resulting coreset posterior, giving a probabilistic characterization of approximation quality. Experiments show better coresets than alternatives with comparable construction times, alongside substantially lower storage requirements and less user input. The approach therefore addresses the cost of constructing the approximation as well as the cost of subsequently using it.
summary.tldr: Random subsampling followed by quasi-Newton weight optimization produces efficient Bayesian coresets with a high-probability approximation bound.

title: Fast Bayesian Coresets via Subsampling and Quasi-Newton Refinement

abstract: We introduce Meta-Album, an image classification meta-dataset designed to facilitate few-shot learning, transfer learning, meta-learning, among other tasks. It includes 40 open datasets, each having at least 20 classes with 40 examples per class, with verified licences. They stem from diverse domains, such as ecology (fauna and flora), manufacturing (textures, vehicles), human actions, and optical character recognition, featuring various image scales (microscopic, human scales, remote sensing). All datasets are preprocessed, annotated, and formatted uniformly, and come in 3 versions (Micro $\subset$ Mini $\subset$ Extended) to match users’ computational resources. We showcase the utility of the first 30 datasets on few-shot learning problems. The other 10 will be released shortly after. Meta-Album is already more diverse and larger (in number of datasets) than similar efforts, and we are committed to keep enlarging it via a series of competitions. As competitions terminate, their test data are released, thus creating a rolling benchmark, available through OpenML.org. Our website https://meta-album.github.io/ contains the source code of challenge winning methods, baseline methods, data loaders, and instructions for contributing either new datasets or algorithms to our expandable meta-dataset.

paragraphs: Meta-Album collects image-classification datasets to support research on learning from few examples, transferring knowledge, and learning across tasks. It contains 40 open datasets with verified licenses, each offering at least 20 classes and 40 examples per class. Its domains range from plants and animals to textures, vehicles, human actions, and character recognition.

The collection also spans different image scales, including microscopic imagery and remote sensing. All datasets are preprocessed, annotated, and placed in a common format. The paper demonstrates few-shot learning uses for the first 30 datasets and describes the remaining 10 as forthcoming. It also presents a plan to expand the collection through competitions whose test data become public afterward, creating a rolling benchmark through OpenML. Code, baseline methods, data loaders, and contribution instructions support reuse. The contribution is a diverse, standardized research resource with an explicit mechanism for continued expansion.
summary.tldr: Meta-Album standardizes diverse image datasets into scalable versions for few-shot learning, transfer learning, and an expanding benchmark.

title: Meta-Album: Multi-domain Meta-Dataset for Few-Shot Image Classification

abstract: In the last decade, recent successes in deep clustering majorly involved the mutual information (MI) as an unsupervised objective for training neural networks with increasing regularisations. While the quality of the regularisations have been largely discussed for improvements, little attention has been dedicated to the relevance of MI as a clustering objective. In this paper, we first highlight how the maximisation of MI does not lead to satisfying clusters. We identified the Kullback-Leibler divergence as the main reason of this behaviour. Hence, we generalise the mutual information by changing its core distance, introducing the generalised mutual information (GEMINI): a set of metrics for unsupervised neural network training. Unlike MI, some GEMINIs do not require regularisations when training. Some of these metrics are geometry-aware thanks to distances or kernels in the data space. Finally, we highlight that GEMINIs can automatically select a relevant number of clusters, a property that has been little studied in deep clustering context where the number of clusters is a priori unknown.

paragraphs: Mutual information is widely used to train deep clustering models, often with substantial regularization. This paper examines the objective itself and argues that maximizing it can produce unsatisfactory clusters, identifying its Kullback–Leibler-divergence structure as a source of the behavior.

The authors introduce generalized mutual information, or GEMINI, by replacing that core distance. The resulting family supplies unsupervised objectives, some of which incorporate data geometry through distances or kernels. Some variants do not require the regularizers used with ordinary mutual information.

The paper also highlights automatic selection of a relevant number of clusters, an important issue when the cluster count is unknown beforehand. The abstract gives no dataset results or universal cluster-recovery guarantee. Its contribution is a family of alternative objectives and an analysis of their properties, inviting evaluation of clustering quality through more than the choice of regularization alone.
summary.tldr: GEMINI replaces mutual information’s core divergence to build more flexible clustering objectives.

title: Generalised Mutual Information for Discriminative Clustering

abstract: Continuous hidden Markov models (HMMs) assume that observations are generated from a mixture of Gaussian densities, limiting their ability to model more complex distributions. In this work, we address this shortcoming and propose novel continuous HMM models, dubbed FlowHMMs, that enable learning general continuous observation densities without constraining them to follow a Gaussian distribution or their mixtures. To that end, we leverage deep flow-based architectures that model complex, non-Gaussian functions and propose two variants of training a FlowHMM model. The first one, based on gradient-based technique, can be applied directly to continuous multidimensional data, yet its application to larger data sequences remains computationally expensive. Therefore, we also present a second approach to training our FlowHMM that relies on the co-occurrence matrix of discretized observations and considers the joint distribution of pairs of co-observed values, hence rendering the training time independent of the training sequence length. As a result, we obtain a model that can be flexibly adapted to the characteristics and dimensionality of the data. We perform a variety of experiments in which we compare both training strategies with a baseline of Gaussian mixture models. We show, that in terms of quality of the recovered probability distribution, accuracy of prediction of hidden states, and likelihood of unseen data, our approach outperforms the standard Gaussian methods.

paragraphs: FlowHMM extends continuous hidden Markov modeling to observation distributions that need not follow Gaussian forms or Gaussian mixtures. The paper uses deep flow-based architectures to represent more complex densities while retaining hidden-state modeling. Its aim is to make the observation model adaptable to the shape and dimensionality of the data.

The authors propose two training strategies. One applies gradient-based learning directly to continuous multidimensional observations, but remains computationally expensive for longer sequences. The other works with a co-occurrence matrix built from discretized observations and models pairs of co-observed values. In that formulation, training time is independent of the training sequence length.

Experiments compare both strategies with Gaussian mixture baselines. The authors report improvements in recovering probability distributions, predicting hidden states, and assigning likelihood to unseen data. These findings support the value of more flexible observation densities across several evaluation criteria. The two training routes also address a practical choice between working directly with continuous sequences and learning from their discretized co-occurrence representation.
summary.tldr: FlowHMM uses flow-based observation densities and two training strategies to improve continuous hidden Markov modeling beyond Gaussian mixtures.

title: FlowHMM: Flow-based continuous hidden Markov models

abstract: Unlike matrix completion, tensor completion does not have an algorithm that is known to achieve the information-theoretic sample complexity rate. This paper develops a new algorithm for the special case of completion for nonnegative tensors. We prove that our algorithm converges in a linear (in numerical tolerance) number of oracle steps, while achieving the information-theoretic rate. Our approach is to define a new norm for nonnegative tensors using the gauge of a particular 0-1 polytope; integer linear programming can, in turn, be used to solve linear separation problems over this polytope. We combine this insight with a variant of the Frank-Wolfe algorithm to construct our numerical algorithm, and we demonstrate its effectiveness and scalability through computational experiments using a laptop on tensors with up to one-hundred million entries.

This paper develops a new algorithm for the special case of completion for nonnegative tensors. We prove that our algorithm converges in a linear (in numerical tolerance) number of oracle steps, while achieving the information-theoretic rate. Our approach is to define a new norm for nonnegative tensors using the gauge of a particular 0-1 polytope; integer linear programming can, in turn, be used to solve linear separation problems over this polytope. We combine this insight with a variant of the Frank-Wolfe algorithm to construct our numerical algorithm, and we demonstrate its effectiveness and scalability through computational experiments using a laptop on tensors with up to one-hundred million entries.

paragraphs: Tensor completion reconstructs missing entries in a multidimensional array from observed entries. The paper addresses the special case where entries are nonnegative. Its starting point is a gap with matrix completion: for general tensor completion, no algorithm is known to achieve the information-theoretic sample complexity rate.

The authors introduce a norm for nonnegative tensors using the gauge of a particular polytope defined by zero-one structure. Integer linear programming solves the associated linear separation problems. Combining that geometric construction with a variant of the Frank-Wolfe algorithm yields a numerical method that connects the statistical completion objective to discrete optimization.

The paper proves that the method achieves the information-theoretic rate and gives an oracle-step convergence guarantee described as linear in numerical tolerance. Computational experiments demonstrate effectiveness and scalability on tensors containing up to one hundred million entries using a laptop. The result joins a sample-efficiency guarantee with practical demonstrations, while the algorithm and theorem specifically target the nonnegative case.
summary.tldr: A nonnegative tensor-completion algorithm combines integer optimization with Frank-Wolfe updates and achieves the information-theoretic sample complexity rate.

title: Nonnegative Tensor Completion via Integer Optimization

abstract: Variational inequalities in general and saddle point problems in particular are increasingly relevant in machine learning applications, including adversarial learning, GANs, transport and robust optimization. With increasing data and problem sizes necessary to train high performing models across various applications, we need to rely on parallel and distributed computing. However, in distributed training, communication among the compute nodes is a key bottleneck during training, and this problem is exacerbated for high dimensional and over-parameterized models. Due to these considerations, it is important to equip existing methods with strategies that would allow to reduce the volume of transmitted information during training while obtaining a model of comparable quality. In this paper, we present the first theoretically grounded distributed methods for solving variational inequalities and saddle point problems using compressed communication: MASHA1 and MASHA2. Our theory and methods allow for the use of both unbiased (such as Rand$k$; MASHA1) and contractive (such as Top$k$; MASHA2) compressors. New algorithms support bidirectional compressions, and also can be modified for stochastic setting with batches and for federated learning with partial participation of clients. We empirically validated our conclusions using two experimental setups: a standard bilinear min-max problem, and large-scale distributed adversarial training of transformers.

paragraphs: Distributed learning spreads computation across machines, but exchanging updates can become a bottleneck, especially for large models. This paper addresses that communication cost for variational inequalities and saddle point problems. These formulations appear in adversarial learning, generative adversarial networks, transport, and robust optimization, where distributed methods need more than simply efficient local computation.

The authors introduce MASHA1 and MASHA2, described as the first theoretically grounded distributed methods for these problems using compressed communication. MASHA1 supports unbiased compressors, including Randk, while MASHA2 supports contractive compressors, including Topk. Supporting both classes provides alternative ways to reduce transmitted information within algorithms backed by theoretical guarantees.

Compression can operate in both communication directions. The methods can also be adapted to stochastic computation with batches and to federated learning where only some clients participate. Experiments examine a bilinear minimax problem and large-scale distributed adversarial training of transformers, empirically supporting the authors’ conclusions. The contribution is a framework for reducing communication in these optimization settings while retaining guarantees, rather than a compression technique tied to one model architecture.
summary.tldr: MASHA1 and MASHA2 provide theoretically grounded compressed communication for distributed variational inequalities and saddle point optimization.

title: Distributed Methods with Compressed Communication for Solving Variational Inequalities, with Theoretical Guarantees

abstract: Spiking neural networks have attracted increasing attention in recent years due to their potential of handling time-dependent data. Many algorithms and techniques have been developed; however, theoretical understandings of many aspects of spiking neural networks are far from clear. A recent work [Zhang and Zhou, 2021] disclosed that typical spiking neural networks could hardly work on spatio-temporal data due to their bifurcation dynamics and suggested that the self-connection structure has to be added. In this paper, we theoretically investigate the approximation ability and computational efficiency of spiking neural networks with self connections, and show that the self-connection structure enables spiking neural networks to approximate discrete dynamical systems using a polynomial number of parameters within polynomial time complexities. Our theoretical results may shed some insight for the future studies of spiking neural networks.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks are attractive for time-dependent data, but their theoretical capabilities remain incompletely understood. The paper builds on earlier work connecting difficulties on spatiotemporal data to bifurcation dynamics and suggesting the addition of self-connections. It investigates what networks with this structure can approximate and how much computation that approximation requires.

A self-connection lets a neuron connect back to itself, making it an explicit part of the network architecture considered in the analysis. The authors show that spiking networks with self-connections can approximate discrete dynamical systems. The result addresses both representational capacity and efficiency: the construction uses a polynomial number of parameters and has polynomial time complexity.

This provides a theoretical basis for studying self-connections as a useful architectural ingredient for temporal modeling. The significance lies in obtaining an approximation result together with resource bounds, rather than establishing representability alone. The authors present the findings as potential guidance for future spiking-network research, linking a proposed structural change to a provable capability for modeling evolving systems.
summary.tldr: Spiking networks with self-connections can approximate discrete dynamical systems with polynomial parameter counts and time complexity.

title: Theoretically Provable Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: There is mounting evidence of emergent phenomena in the capabilities of deep learning methods as we scale up datasets, model sizes, and training times. While there are some accounts of how these resources modulate statistical capacity, far less is known about their effect on the computational problem of model training. This work conducts such an exploration through the lens of learning a $k$-sparse parity of $n$ bits, a canonical discrete search problem which is statistically easy but computationally hard. Empirically, we find that a variety of neural networks successfully learn sparse parities, with discontinuous phase transitions in the training curves. On small instances, learning abruptly occurs at approximately $n^{O(k)}$ iterations; this nearly matches SQ lower bounds, despite the apparent lack of a sparse prior. Our theoretical analysis shows that these observations are not explained by a Langevin-like mechanism, whereby SGD "stumbles in the dark" until it finds the hidden set of features (a natural algorithm which also runs in $n^{O(k)}$ time). Instead, we show that SGD gradually amplifies the sparse solution via a Fourier gap in the population gradient, making continual progress that is invisible to loss and error metrics.

paragraphs: A model's training curve can appear stalled before performance suddenly improves. This paper investigates such behavior using sparse parity learning, where the answer depends on the parity of a hidden subset of input bits. The task is statistically easy but computationally hard, making it useful for separating the availability of information from the difficulty of finding a solution.

Empirically, several kinds of neural networks learn these parities with abrupt transitions in their training curves. On small instances, success occurs after roughly n^(O(k)) iterations for k relevant bits among n inputs. The authors report that this nearly matches statistical-query lower bounds, despite the networks' apparent lack of a prior favoring sparse solutions.

The findings show how an apparently sudden learning event can emerge from a sustained underlying optimization process.
summary.tldr: Sparse-parity experiments and theory reveal gradual SGD progress that can remain hidden until loss and error improve abruptly.

title: Hidden Progress in Deep Learning: SGD Learns Parities Near the Computational Limit

abstract: In this paper, we study the statistical limits in terms of Sobolev norms of gradient descent for solving inverse problem from randomly sampled noisy observations using a general class of objective functions. Our class of objective functions includes Sobolev training for kernel regression, Deep Ritz Methods (DRM), and Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINN) for solving elliptic partial differential equations (PDEs) as special cases. We consider a potentially infinite-dimensional parameterization of our model using a suitable Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space and a continuous parameterization of problem hardness through the definition of kernel integral operators. We prove that gradient descent over this objective function can also achieve statistical optimality and the optimal number of passes over the data increases with sample size. Based on our theory, we explain an implicit acceleration of using a Sobolev norm as the objective function for training, inferring that the optimal number of epochs of DRM becomes larger than the number of PINN when both the data size and the hardness of tasks increase, although both DRM and PINN can achieve statistical optimality.

paragraphs: This paper studies how accurately gradient descent can solve inverse problems from randomly sampled, noisy observations. It measures error using Sobolev norms and considers a broad family of training objectives. That family includes Sobolev training for kernel regression, Deep Ritz Methods, and physics-informed neural networks for elliptic partial differential equations.

The analysis uses a suitable reproducing kernel Hilbert space, allowing a potentially infinite-dimensional model. Kernel integral operators describe varying levels of problem difficulty. Within this framework, the authors prove that gradient descent can attain statistical optimality and that the optimal number of passes through the data increases with sample size.

The theory also explains an implicit acceleration associated with training using a Sobolev norm. As both dataset size and task difficulty increase, it implies that Deep Ritz Methods need more epochs at their optimal stopping point than physics-informed neural networks, although both can be statistically optimal. This distinguishes the accuracy attainable from the data from the training effort needed to reach it under the analyzed objectives.
summary.tldr: A unified analysis links statistically optimal gradient-descent solutions of elliptic inverse problems to objective-dependent training duration and Sobolev acceleration.

title: Sobolev Acceleration and Statistical Optimality for Learning Elliptic Equations via Gradient Descent

abstract: Motivated by the achievements in model-based methods and the advances in deep networks, we propose a novel enhanced latent space blind model based deep unfolding network, namely ScaoedNet, for complex real image denoising. It is derived by introducing latent space, noise information, and guidance constraint into the denoising cost function. A self-correction alternative optimization algorithm is proposed to split the novel cost function into three alternative subproblems, i.e., guidance representation (GR), degradation estimation (DE) and reconstruction (RE) subproblems. Finally, we implement the optimization process by a deep unfolding network consisting of GR, DE and RE networks. For higher performance of the DE network, a novel parameter-free noise feature adaptive enhancement (NFAE) layer is proposed. To synchronously and dynamically realize internal-external feature information mining in the RE network, a novel feature multi-modulation attention (FM2A) module is proposed. Our approach thereby leverages the advantages of deep learning, while also benefiting from the principled denoising provided by the classical model-based formulation. To the best of our knowledge, our enhanced latent space blind model, optimization scheme, NFAE and FM2A have not been reported in the previous literature. Experimental results show the promising performance of ScaoedNet on real image denoising. Code is available at https://github.com/chaoren88/ScaoedNet.

paragraphs: ScaoedNet addresses real image denoising by connecting a model-based optimization formulation with a learned neural network. The authors build a denoising cost function that includes a latent space, information about noise, and a guidance constraint. This gives the network’s design an explicit connection to the task of reconstructing a cleaner image.

A self-correction optimization algorithm alternates between three subproblems: guidance representation, degradation estimation, and reconstruction. The authors turn that optimization process into a deep unfolding network, with a corresponding network for each subproblem. The resulting architecture follows the structure of the proposed denoising procedure while using learned components to carry it out.

Two additional components support this design. A parameter-free noise feature enhancement layer improves degradation estimation, while a feature multi-modulation attention module supports dynamic use of internal and external feature information during reconstruction. Experiments show promising real-image denoising performance. The stated contribution is this combination of a principled objective, alternating optimization, and specialized neural components.
summary.tldr: ScaoedNet turns an alternating denoising optimization procedure into a neural network with specialized noise-estimation and reconstruction components.

title: Enhanced Latent Space Blind Model for Real Image Denoising via Alternative Optimization

abstract: In the theory of lossy compression, the rate-distortion (R-D) function $R(D)$ describes how much a data source can be compressed (in bit-rate) at any given level of fidelity (distortion). Obtaining $R(D)$ for a given data source establishes the fundamental performance limit for all compression algorithms. We propose a new method to estimate $R(D)$ from the perspective of optimal transport. Unlike the classic Blahut--Arimoto algorithm which fixes the support of the reproduction distribution in advance, our Wasserstein gradient descent algorithm learns the support of the optimal reproduction distribution by moving particles. We prove its local convergence and analyze the sample complexity of our R-D estimator based on a connection to entropic optimal transport. Experimentally, we obtain comparable or tighter bounds than state-of-the-art neural network methods on low-rate sources while requiring considerably less tuning and computation effort. We also highlight a connection to maximum-likelihood deconvolution and introduce a new class of sources that can be used as test cases with known solutions to the R-D problem.

paragraphs: Lossy compression trades a smaller representation against some distortion of the original data. The rate-distortion function describes the fundamental relationship between these quantities for a data source. Estimating it provides a reference for what compression algorithms could achieve, rather than measuring only the performance of one particular compressor.

This paper estimates that function using optimal transport and Wasserstein gradient descent. The classic Blahut–Arimoto approach fixes the possible values of the reproduction distribution in advance. The proposed method instead moves particles to learn where those values should lie. The authors prove local convergence and analyze sample complexity through a connection to entropic optimal transport.

On low-rate sources, the experiments produce bounds comparable to or tighter than those from state-of-the-art neural approaches, with substantially less tuning and computation. The convergence claim is local, while the empirical comparison concerns the tested low-rate setting. The paper additionally connects the estimator to maximum-likelihood deconvolution and introduces sources with known rate-distortion solutions, providing further test cases for evaluating estimators.
summary.tldr: Moving particles with Wasserstein gradient descent estimates compression limits while learning the reproduction distribution's support.

title: Estimating the Rate-Distortion Function by Wasserstein Gradient Descent

abstract: Electronic Health Records (EHRs), which contain patients' medical histories in various multi-modal formats, often overlook the potential for joint reasoning across imaging and table modalities underexplored in current EHR Question Answering (QA) systems. In this paper, we introduce EHRXQA, a novel multi-modal question answering dataset combining structured EHRs and chest X-ray images. To develop our dataset, we first construct two uni-modal resources: 1) The MIMIC- CXR-VQA dataset, our newly created medical visual question answering (VQA) benchmark, specifically designed to augment the imaging modality in EHR QA, and 2) EHRSQL (MIMIC-IV), a refashioned version of a previously established table-based EHR QA dataset. By integrating these two uni-modal resources, we successfully construct a multi-modal EHR QA dataset that necessitates both uni-modal and cross-modal reasoning. To address the unique challenges of multi-modal questions within EHRs, we propose a NeuralSQL-based strategy equipped with an external VQA API. This pioneering endeavor enhances engagement with multi-modal EHR sources and we believe that our dataset can catalyze advances in real-world medical scenarios such as clinical decision-making and research. EHRXQA is available at https://github.com/baeseongsu/ehrxqa.

EHRXQA is a dataset designed to study this joint reasoning problem. It combines structured electronic health records with chest X-ray images, supporting questions that require one modality or both.

The authors first construct two component resources. MIMIC-CXR-VQA is a new visual question-answering benchmark for chest X-rays. EHRSQL for MIMIC-IV adapts an existing dataset for questions over record tables. Integrating these resources creates a setting in which a system must connect visual evidence with information stored in structured records.

The paper also proposes a NeuralSQL-based strategy equipped with an external visual question-answering API to address multimodal questions. This supplies an approach for connecting table-oriented reasoning with image analysis. The dataset's main contribution is a concrete basis for developing and studying such systems. Benefits for clinical decision-making and medical research are presented as potential future applications of this research direction.
summary.tldr: EHRXQA combines health-record tables and chest X-rays to study questions requiring structured, visual, or joint reasoning.

title: EHRXQA: A Multi-Modal Question Answering Dataset for Electronic Health Records with Chest X-ray Images

abstract: Most advanced unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) methods rely on modeling feature representations of frozen encoder networks pre-trained on large-scale datasets, e.g. ImageNet. However, the features extracted from the encoders that are borrowed from natural image domains coincide little with the features required in the target UAD domain, such as industrial inspection and medical imaging. In this paper, we propose a novel epistemic UAD method, namely ReContrast, which optimizes the entire network to reduce biases towards the pre-trained image domain and orients the network in the target domain. We start with a feature reconstruction approach that detects anomalies from errors. Essentially, the elements of contrastive learning are elegantly embedded in feature reconstruction to prevent the network from training instability, pattern collapse, and identical shortcut, while simultaneously optimizing both the encoder and decoder on the target domain. To demonstrate our transfer ability on various image domains, we conduct extensive experiments across two popular industrial defect detection benchmarks and three medical image UAD tasks, which shows our superiority over current state-of-the-art methods.
