paragraphs: Many unsupervised anomaly detectors use features from a frozen encoder pretrained on natural images. Those features may fit industrial inspection or medical imaging poorly. ReContrast addresses this mismatch by adapting the whole network to the target domain, reducing its dependence on representations shaped by the original pretraining domain.

The method begins with feature reconstruction, where reconstruction errors provide evidence of anomalies. It incorporates elements of contrastive learning so that the encoder and decoder can be optimized together. These elements are designed to prevent unstable training, collapsed patterns, and an identical shortcut, problems that would undermine the usefulness of reconstruction errors.

The authors test ReContrast on two industrial defect-detection benchmarks and three medical-image anomaly-detection tasks, reporting improvements over current leading methods. The findings support joint adaptation of feature extraction and reconstruction across the examined domains. The key contribution is enabling that adaptation while preserving a useful anomaly signal, rather than treating the pretrained encoder's representation as fixed throughout target-domain learning.
summary.tldr: ReContrast combines contrastive learning with feature reconstruction to adapt entire anomaly-detection networks to industrial and medical image domains.

title: ReContrast: Domain-Specific Anomaly Detection via Contrastive Reconstruction

abstract: Spectral embedding is a powerful graph embedding technique that has received a lot of attention recently due to its effectiveness on Graph Transformers. However, from a theoretical perspective, the universal expressive power of spectral embedding comes at the price of losing two important invariance properties of graphs, sign and basis invariance, which also limits its effectiveness on graph data. To remedy this issue, many previous methods developed costly approaches to learn new invariants and suffer from high computation complexity. In this work, we explore a minimal approach that resolves the ambiguity issues by directly finding canonical directions for the eigenvectors, named Laplacian Canonization (LC). As a pure pre-processing method, LC is light-weighted and can be applied to any existing GNNs. We provide a thorough investigation, from theory to algorithm, on this approach, and discover an efficient algorithm named Maximal Axis Projection (MAP) that works for both sign and basis invariance and successfully canonizes more than 90\% of all eigenvectors. Experiments on real-world benchmark datasets like ZINC, MOLTOX21, and MOLPCBA show that MAP consistently outperforms existing methods while bringing minimal computation overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/PKU-ML/LaplacianCanonization.

paragraphs: Spectral graph embeddings use eigenvectors to represent graph structure, but those vectors can have ambiguous signs and bases. These ambiguities complicate how graph models use the representation. Previous approaches have learned new invariant representations, often adding considerable computational cost. This paper instead investigates resolving the ambiguity directly before the graph model receives its input.

Laplacian Canonization seeks canonical directions for the eigenvectors. It operates as lightweight preprocessing and can be applied to existing graph neural networks. The authors develop the approach theoretically and algorithmically, producing Maximal Axis Projection, or MAP, which handles both sign and basis invariance.

MAP successfully canonizes more than 90% of eigenvectors in the reported results. On real-world benchmarks including ZINC, MOLTOX21, and MOLPCBA, it consistently outperforms existing methods while adding little computation. The result supports preprocessing as an effective way to improve spectral representations. The reported canonization rate also preserves an important qualification: successful treatment of most eigenvectors is not a claim that every eigenvector ambiguity is always resolved.
summary.tldr: Laplacian Canonization resolves spectral eigenvector ambiguities through lightweight preprocessing, improving graph benchmarks with minimal overhead.

title: Laplacian Canonization: A Minimalist Approach to Sign and Basis Invariant Spectral Embedding

abstract: Decision trees have gained popularity as interpretable surrogate models for learning-based control policies. However, providing safety guarantees for systems controlled by decision trees is an open challenge. We show that the problem is undecidable even for systems with the simplest dynamics, and PSPACE-complete for finite-horizon properties. The latter can be verified for discrete-time systems via bounded model checking. However, for continuous-time systems, such an approach requires discretization, thereby weakening the guarantees for the original system. This paper presents the first algorithm to directly verify decision-tree controlled system in continuous time. The key aspect of our method is exploiting the decision-tree structure to propagate a set-based approximation through the decision nodes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by verifying safety of several decision trees distilled to imitate neural-network policies for nonlinear systems.

paragraphs: Decision trees can make learned control policies easier to interpret, but readable decisions do not by themselves establish system safety. This paper studies the difficulty of verifying systems controlled by such trees. It shows undecidability even with very simple dynamics and PSPACE-completeness for finite-horizon properties, establishing substantial computational obstacles to general verification.

For discrete-time systems, bounded model checking can address finite-horizon properties. Applying that route to continuous-time systems requires discretization, which weakens guarantees about the original system. The authors instead introduce an algorithm that works directly in continuous time. It exploits the tree’s decision structure to propagate a set-based approximation through the decision nodes.

Working with sets lets the verification procedure reason about collections of possible system states as the policy branches. The authors demonstrate the approach by verifying several decision-tree controllers distilled from neural-network policies for nonlinear systems. These demonstrations show that useful verification is possible despite the general hardness results. The central advance is exploiting the controller’s structure while avoiding the guarantee weakening associated with first discretizing continuous dynamics.
summary.tldr: A structure-aware algorithm verifies decision-tree controllers directly in continuous time by propagating sets through their decision nodes.

title: Safety Verification of Decision-Tree Policies in Continuous Time

abstract: The mean-field Langevin dynamics (MFLD) is a nonlinear generalization of the Langevin dynamics that incorporates a distribution-dependent drift, and it naturally arises from the optimization of two-layer neural networks via (noisy) gradient descent. Recent works have shown that MFLD globally minimizes an entropy-regularized convex functional in the space of measures. However, all prior analyses assumed the infinite-particle or continuous-time limit, and cannot handle stochastic gradient updates. We provide a general framework to prove a uniform-in-time propagation of chaos for MFLD that takes into account the errors due to finite-particle approximation, time-discretization, and stochastic gradient. To demonstrate the wide applicability of our framework, we establish quantitative convergence rate guarantees to the regularized global optimal solution for $(i)$ a wide range of learning problems such as mean-field neural network and MMD minimization, and $(ii)$ different gradient estimators including SGD and SVRG. Despite the generality of our results, we achieve an improved convergence rate in both the SGD and SVRG settings when specialized to the standard Langevin dynamics.

Recent works have shown that MFLD globally minimizes an entropy-regularized convex functional in the space of measures. However, all prior analyses assumed the infinite-particle or continuous-time limit, and cannot handle stochastic gradient updates. We provide a general framework to prove a uniform-in-time propagation of chaos for MFLD that takes into account the errors due to finite-particle approximation, time-discretization, and stochastic gradient. To demonstrate the wide applicability of our framework, we establish quantitative convergence rate guarantees to the regularized global optimal solution for $(i)$ a wide range of learning problems such as mean-field neural network and MMD minimization, and $(ii)$ different gradient estimators including SGD and SVRG. Despite the generality of our results, we achieve an improved convergence rate in both the SGD and SVRG settings when specialized to the standard Langevin dynamics.

paragraphs: Mean-field Langevin dynamics describes noisy optimization in which each particle's motion depends on the population's distribution. It arises naturally in the study of two-layer neural networks. Earlier results showed global minimization of an entropy-regularized convex objective over distributions, but relied on infinitely many particles or continuous time and did not accommodate stochastic gradient updates.

This paper develops an analysis that accounts jointly for three practical approximations: a finite particle population, discrete time steps, and stochastic gradients. Its uniform-in-time propagation-of-chaos result controls the relationship between the finite system and its mean-field description throughout time. This connects the idealized dynamics to algorithms that operate with finite resources.

The framework yields quantitative convergence guarantees to the regularized global optimum for learning problems including mean-field neural networks and maximum mean discrepancy minimization. It accommodates both ordinary stochastic gradients and the variance-reduced estimator SVRG. When specialized to standard Langevin dynamics, the analysis also improves convergence rates for both estimators. The guaranteed target is the regularized optimum, preserving the distinction between that objective and an unregularized learning problem.
summary.tldr: A unified convergence analysis brings mean-field Langevin guarantees closer to practical algorithms with finite particles, discrete updates, and stochastic gradients.

title: Convergence of mean-field Langevin dynamics: time-space discretization, stochastic gradient, and variance reduction

abstract: Existing analyses of neural network training often operate under the unrealistic assumption of an extremely small learning rate. This lies in stark contrast to practical wisdom and empirical studies, such as the work of J. Cohen et al. (ICLR 2021), which exhibit startling new phenomena (the "edge of stability"' or "unstable convergence") and potential benefits for generalization in the large learning rate regime. Despite a flurry of recent works on this topic, however, the latter effect is still poorly understood. In this paper, we take a step towards understanding genuinely non-convex training dynamics with large learning rates by performing a detailed analysis of gradient descent for simplified models of two-layer neural networks. For these models, we provably establish the edge of stability phenomenon and discover a sharp phase transition for the step size below which the neural network fails to learn ``threshold-like'' neurons (i.e., neurons with a non-zero first-layer bias). This elucidates one possible mechanism by which the edge of stability can in fact lead to better generalization, as threshold neurons are basic building blocks with useful inductive bias for many tasks.
originalAbstract: Existing analyses of neural network training often operate under the unrealistic assumption of an extremely small learning rate. This lies in stark contrast to practical wisdom and empirical studies, such as the work of J. Cohen et al. (ICLR 2021), which exhibit startling new phenomena (the "edge of stability"' or "unstable convergence") and potential benefits for generalization in the large learning rate regime. Despite a flurry of recent works on this topic, however, the latter effect is still poorly understood. In this paper, we take a step towards understanding genuinely non-convex training dynamics with large learning rates by performing a detailed analysis of gradient descent for simplified models of two-layer neural networks. For these models, we provably establish the edge of stability phenomenon and discover a sharp phase transition for the step size below which the neural network fails to learn ``threshold-like'' neurons (i.e., neurons with a non-zero first-layer bias). This elucidates one possible mechanism by which the edge of stability can in fact lead to better generalization, as threshold neurons are basic building blocks with useful inductive bias for many tasks.

paragraphs: Training theory often assumes learning rates are extremely small, even though larger rates produce distinctive behavior in practice. One such behavior is the edge of stability, also described as unstable convergence. This paper investigates that regime through a detailed analysis of gradient descent in simplified two-layer neural networks, aiming to explain a possible benefit of larger training steps.

For these models, the authors prove that edge-of-stability behavior occurs. They also identify a sharp transition in step size: below a threshold, the network fails to learn threshold-like neurons, defined here as neurons with nonzero first-layer bias. The finding links the optimization step size to the kind of features the network can learn.

Threshold neurons provide useful inductive biases for many tasks, so gaining access to them offers one possible explanation for improved generalization near the edge of stability. The conclusion is deliberately narrower than a universal claim about large learning rates. It establishes a mechanism within the analyzed models and shows how training dynamics can influence the building blocks available to the learned predictor.
summary.tldr: Analysis of simplified networks identifies a step-size transition that connects edge-of-stability training with learning threshold-like neurons.

title: Learning threshold neurons via edge of stability

abstract: Diffusion models have been successful on a range of conditional generation tasks including molecular design and text-to-image generation. However, these achievements have primarily depended on task-specific conditional training or error-prone heuristic approximations. Ideally, a conditional generation method should provide exact samples for a broad range of conditional distributions without requiring task-specific training. To this end, we introduce the Twisted Diffusion Sampler, or TDS. TDS is a sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithm that targets the conditional distributions of diffusion models through simulating a set of weighted particles. The main idea is to use twisting, an SMC technique that enjoys good computational efficiency, to incorporate heuristic approximations without compromising asymptotic exactness. We first find in simulation and in conditional image generation tasks that TDS provides a computational statistical trade-off, yielding more accurate approximations with many particles but with empirical improvements over heuristics with as few as two particles. We then turn to motif-scaffolding, a core task in protein design, using a TDS extension to Riemannian diffusion models; on benchmark tasks, TDS allows flexible conditioning criteria and often outperforms the state-of-the-art, conditionally trained model. Code can be found in https://github.com/blt2114/twisted_diffusion_sampler

paragraphs: Conditional generation asks a diffusion model to produce samples satisfying additional information or requirements. Existing approaches often need task-specific training or use heuristics that introduce approximation errors. The Twisted Diffusion Sampler, or TDS, targets conditional distributions through sequential Monte Carlo, maintaining a collection of weighted candidate samples called particles.

Its key ingredient is twisting, a technique that incorporates heuristic guidance while preserving asymptotic exactness. The distinction matters: heuristics can help guide computation without permanently defining the limiting distribution. Using more particles provides more accurate approximations, creating a trade-off between computational expense and statistical accuracy rather than guaranteeing exact finite-particle outputs.

In simulations and conditional image generation, TDS improves empirically on heuristic methods with as few as two particles. An extension to Riemannian diffusion models also addresses protein motif-scaffolding, where the method supports flexible conditioning criteria. On those benchmark tasks, it often outperforms a leading conditionally trained model. The results connect a principled sampling guarantee with practical gains across different forms of conditional generation.
summary.tldr: TDS uses weighted particles and heuristic guidance for diffusion conditioning while preserving asymptotic exactness.

title: Practical and Asymptotically Exact Conditional Sampling in Diffusion Models

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) has received considerable attention in recent years due to its attractive capability of learning policies from offline datasets without environmental interactions. Despite some success in the single-agent setting, offline multi-agent RL (MARL) remains to be a challenge. The large joint state-action space and the coupled multi-agent behaviors pose extra complexities for offline policy optimization. Most existing offline MARL studies simply apply offline data-related regularizations on individual agents, without fully considering the multi-agent system at the global level. In this work, we present OMIGA, a new offline multi-agent RL algorithm with implicit global-to-local value regularization. OMIGA provides a principled framework to convert global-level value regularization into equivalent implicit local value regularizations and simultaneously enables in-sample learning, thus elegantly bridging multi-agent value decomposition and policy learning with offline regularizations. Based on comprehensive experiments on the offline multi-agent MuJoCo and StarCraft II micro-management tasks, we show that OMIGA achieves superior performance over the state-of-the-art offline MARL methods in almost all tasks.

paragraphs: Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning must learn coordinated behavior from an existing dataset without further interaction with the environment. This is difficult because agents’ decisions are coupled and their joint state-action space is large. Applying data-related regularization separately to each agent can miss constraints that matter for the system as a whole.

OMIGA starts with value regularization at the global level and converts it into equivalent implicit regularizations for individual agents. This provides a principled connection between the team-level learning objective and local learning. The framework also enables in-sample learning, bringing together multi-agent value decomposition, policy learning, and the regularization needed when learning from fixed data.

The authors evaluate OMIGA on offline multi-agent MuJoCo and StarCraft II micromanagement tasks. It outperforms the state-of-the-art offline multi-agent methods in almost all evaluated tasks. These findings support organizing regularization globally while making it usable locally, so that individual policy updates reflect the coupled nature of the overall multi-agent problem.
summary.tldr: OMIGA converts global value regularization into equivalent local regularizations to improve learning from offline multi-agent datasets.

title: Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Implicit Global-to-Local Value Regularization

abstract: We study online adaptive policy selection in systems with time-varying costs and dynamics. We develop the Gradient-based Adaptive Policy Selection (GAPS) algorithm together with a general analytical framework for online policy selection via online optimization. Under our proposed notion of contractive policy classes, we show that GAPS approximates the behavior of an ideal online gradient descent algorithm on the policy parameters while requiring less information and computation. When convexity holds, our algorithm is the first to achieve optimal policy regret. When convexity does not hold, we provide the first local regret bound for online policy selection. Our numerical experiments show that GAPS can adapt to changing environments more quickly than existing benchmarks.

paragraphs: A policy operating in a changing system must adapt as both costs and dynamics evolve. This paper studies online policy selection in that setting, treating policy adjustment as an online optimization problem. It introduces Gradient-based Adaptive Policy Selection, or GAPS, alongside an analytical framework for understanding its behavior.

The key condition is a proposed notion of contractive policy classes. Under this condition, GAPS approximates an ideal online gradient descent procedure over policy parameters while using less information and computation. That connection provides a way to analyze practical adaptive updates through a better-understood optimization procedure.

The guarantees depend on the problem's structure. When convexity holds, the authors establish optimal policy regret and describe this as the first such result. Without convexity, they provide a local regret bound, which is a different and more local performance statement. Numerical experiments show faster adaptation than existing benchmarks. Together, the results connect a contraction-based theoretical framework with observed responsiveness to environmental change.
summary.tldr: GAPS adapts policies in changing systems, with contraction-based regret guarantees and empirical improvements in adaptation speed.

title: Online Adaptive Policy Selection in Time-Varying Systems: No-Regret via Contractive Perturbations

abstract: ``Effective robustness'' measures the extra out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness beyond what can be predicted from the in-distribution (ID) performance. Existing effective robustness evaluations typically use a single test set such as ImageNet to evaluate the ID accuracy. This becomes problematic when evaluating models trained on different data distributions, e.g., comparing models trained on ImageNet vs. zero-shot language-image pre-trained models trained on LAION. In this paper, we propose a new evaluation metric to evaluate and compare the effective robustness of models trained on different data. To do this, we control for the accuracy on multiple ID test sets that cover the training distributions for all the evaluated models. Our new evaluation metric provides a better estimate of effective robustness when there are models with different training data. It may also explain the surprising effective robustness gains of zero-shot CLIP-like models exhibited in prior works that used ImageNet as the only ID test set, while the gains diminish under our new evaluation. Additional artifacts including interactive visualizations are provided at https://shizhouxing.github.io/effective-robustness.

paragraphs: Effective robustness measures how much better a model handles shifted data than its in-distribution accuracy would predict. The comparison therefore depends on how in-distribution performance is measured. This paper argues that using one test set, such as ImageNet, becomes problematic when the models being compared were trained on substantially different data distributions.

The authors propose controlling for accuracy on multiple in-distribution test sets that collectively cover the evaluated models’ training distributions. This creates a broader reference for predicting out-of-distribution performance. The aim is to distinguish extra robustness from performance differences that become visible once the evaluation better represents each model’s training data.

Under this evaluation, the apparent effective-robustness advantages of zero-shot CLIP-like models diminish. The authors suggest that the revised reference may explain surprising gains reported when ImageNet was the only in-distribution test set. This is a qualified explanation about how robustness is measured: it shows that the estimated advantage depends on the comparison framework, rather than establishing that these models lack useful robustness.
summary.tldr: A robustness metric that accounts for multiple training distributions reduces the apparent extra robustness of zero-shot CLIP-like models.

title: Effective Robustness against Natural Distribution Shifts for Models with Different Training Data

abstract: In an era of widespread web scraping, unlearnable dataset methods have the potential to protect data privacy by preventing deep neural networks from generalizing. But in addition to a number of practical limitations that make their use unlikely, we make a number of findings that call into question their ability to safeguard data. First, it is widely believed that neural networks trained on unlearnable datasets only learn shortcuts, simpler rules that are not useful for generalization. In contrast, we find that networks actually can learn useful features that can be reweighed for high test performance, suggesting that image protection is not assured. Unlearnable datasets are also believed to induce learning shortcuts through linear separability of added perturbations. We provide a counterexample, demonstrating that linear separability of perturbations is not a necessary condition. To emphasize why linearly separable perturbations should not be relied upon, we propose an orthogonal projection attack which allows learning from unlearnable datasets published in ICML 2021 and ICLR 2023. Our proposed attack is significantly less complex than recently proposed techniques.

paragraphs: Unlearnable datasets add perturbations intended to stop neural networks from learning useful generalizable information. This paper questions the protection they provide by examining what trained networks actually retain. Contrary to the view that such networks learn only useless shortcuts, the authors find useful features that can be reweighted to obtain high test performance.

The paper also challenges an explanation of how these datasets work. Added perturbations are often believed to induce shortcuts because they are linearly separable. The authors provide a counterexample showing that linear separability is not necessary. This distinguishes a property that some perturbations possess from a condition that all successful unlearnability mechanisms must satisfy.

Finally, the authors introduce an orthogonal projection attack that enables learning from unlearnable datasets published in ICML 2021 and ICLR 2023. They report that the attack is substantially less complex than recently proposed alternatives. Together, the results show that suppressed initial generalization does not assure image protection: useful features can remain available, and the tested protective perturbations can be counteracted.
summary.tldr: Networks can retain useful features from unlearnable datasets, and a simple projection attack defeats protection in the tested datasets.

title: What Can We Learn from Unlearnable Datasets?

abstract: We present a novel language-driven ordering alignment method for ordinal classification. The labels in ordinal classification contain additional ordering relations, making them prone to overfitting when relying solely on training data. Recent developments in pre-trained vision-language models inspire us to leverage the rich ordinal priors in human language by converting the original task into a vision-language alignment task. Consequently, we propose L2RCLIP, which fully utilizes the language priors from two perspectives. First, we introduce a complementary prompt tuning technique called RankFormer, designed to enhance the ordering relation of original rank prompts. It employs token-level attention with residual-style prompt blending in the word embedding space. Second, to further incorporate language priors, we revisit the approximate bound optimization of vanilla cross-entropy loss and restructure it within the cross-modal embedding space. Consequently, we propose a cross-modal ordinal pairwise loss to refine the CLIP feature space, where texts and images maintain both semantic alignment and ordering alignment. Extensive experiments on three ordinal classification tasks, including facial age estimation, historical color image (HCI) classification, and aesthetic assessment demonstrate its promising performance.

paragraphs: Ordinal classification predicts categories that have an ordering, such as age levels or aesthetic ratings. Learning those relationships only from training examples can lead to overfitting. L2RCLIP uses ordering information already present in language by reframing ordinal classification as a vision-language alignment problem, drawing on a pretrained model's language priors.

The method has two complementary parts. RankFormer tunes rank prompts using token-level attention and residual-style blending in word-embedding space to strengthen their ordering relationships. A cross-modal ordinal pairwise loss then refines the shared image-text feature space. This loss comes from revisiting an approximate bound optimization of ordinary cross-entropy and restructuring it in the cross-modal embedding space.

Together, the components seek to preserve both semantic correspondence between images and text and the ordering among categories. Experiments cover facial age estimation, historical color image classification, and aesthetic assessment, with promising reported performance. The significance is that language supplies more than category names: its ordinal structure becomes part of both the prompt representation and the objective used to organize image and text features.
summary.tldr: L2RCLIP uses language-based ordering priors, tuned prompts, and a pairwise image-text loss to improve ordinal classification.

title: Learning-to-Rank Meets Language: Boosting Language-Driven Ordering Alignment for Ordinal Classification

abstract: Fr\'echet regression has emerged as a promising approach for regression analysis involving non-Euclidean response variables. However, its practical applicability has been hindered by its reliance on ideal scenarios with abundant and noiseless covariate data. In this paper, we present a novel estimation method that tackles these limitations by leveraging the low-rank structure inherent in the covariate matrix. Our proposed framework combines the concepts of global Fr\'echet regression and principal component regression, aiming to improve the efficiency and accuracy of the regression estimator. By incorporating the low-rank structure, our method enables more effective modeling and estimation, particularly in high-dimensional and errors-in-variables regression settings. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed estimator's large-sample properties, including a comprehensive rate analysis of bias, variance, and additional variations due to measurement errors. Furthermore, our numerical experiments provide empirical evidence that supports the theoretical findings, demonstrating the superior performance of our approach. Overall, this work introduces a promising framework for regression analysis of non-Euclidean variables, effectively addressing the challenges associated with limited and noisy covariate data, with potential applications in diverse fields.

paragraphs: Fréchet regression handles prediction problems whose response variables live in non-Euclidean spaces. The paper addresses a practical obstacle: methods relying on plentiful, error-free predictor measurements are harder to use when those measurements are limited or noisy. This becomes especially relevant when the predictor data have many dimensions.

The proposed estimator combines global Fréchet regression with principal component regression. It uses low-rank structure in the covariate matrix to improve estimation, representing the predictor information through a lower-dimensional structure. The availability of that structure is central to the approach. It provides a way to address measurement error while retaining a regression framework suited to non-Euclidean responses.

The authors analyze the estimator's large-sample behavior, separating rates for bias, variance, and extra variation caused by measurement errors. This distinguishes ordinary estimation uncertainty from the effect of noisy predictors. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and report superior performance for the proposed method. Together, the results support low-rank approximation as a useful strategy for the structured regression settings studied.
summary.tldr: Combining Fréchet regression with low-rank predictor approximation improves estimation with limited, noisy covariates, supported by theory and numerical experiments.

title: Errors-in-variables Fr\'echet Regression with Low-rank Covariate Approximation

abstract: Enzymes are important proteins that catalyze chemical reactions. In recent years, machine learning methods have emerged to predict enzyme function from sequence; however, there are no standardized benchmarks to evaluate these methods. We introduce CARE, a benchmark and dataset suite for the Classification And Retrieval of Enzymes (CARE). CARE centers on two tasks: (1) classification of a protein sequence by its enzyme commission (EC) number and (2) retrieval of an EC number given a chemical reaction. For each task, we design train-test splits to evaluate different kinds of out-of-distribution generalization that are relevant to real use cases. For the classification task, we provide baselines for state-of-the-art methods. Because the retrieval task has not been previously formalized, we propose a method called Contrastive Reaction-EnzymE Pretraining (CREEP) as one of the first baselines for this task and compare it to the recent method, CLIPZyme. CARE is available at https://github.com/jsunn-y/CARE/.

paragraphs: CARE provides a standardized way to evaluate machine learning methods for identifying enzyme functions. Enzymes are proteins that catalyze chemical reactions, and the benchmark connects their sequences and associated reactions to enzyme commission, or EC, numbers. Its motivation is that methods for predicting function from sequence need shared evaluation tasks and datasets.

The suite separates two questions. Classification asks which EC number belongs to a protein sequence. Retrieval asks which EC number corresponds to a chemical reaction. For both tasks, the authors design training and testing splits that examine different forms of generalization beyond the training distribution, chosen to reflect relevant practical uses.

CARE includes existing leading methods as classification baselines. For reaction-based retrieval, which the authors identify as a newly formalized task, they introduce Contrastive Reaction-EnzymE Pretraining, or CREEP, and compare it with CLIPZyme. The contribution is both a common testing framework and an initial basis for studying retrieval alongside sequence classification, without treating the two problems as interchangeable.
summary.tldr: CARE standardizes enzyme classification and reaction-based EC-number retrieval, with evaluation splits designed to test practical forms of generalization.

title: CARE: a Benchmark Suite for the Classification and Retrieval of Enzymes

abstract: Graph diffusion, which iteratively propagates real-valued substances among the graph, is used in numerous graph/network-involved applications. However, releasing diffusion vectors may reveal sensitive linking information in the data such as transaction information in financial network data. However, protecting the privacy of graph data is challenging due to its interconnected nature. This work proposes a novel graph diffusion framework with edge-level different privacy guarantees by using noisy diffusion iterates. The algorithm injects Laplace noise per diffusion iteration and adopts a degree-based thresholding function to mitigate the high sensitivity induced by low-degree nodes. Our privacy loss analysis is based on Privacy Amplification by Iteration (PABI), which to our best knowledge, is the first effort that analyzes PABI with Laplace noise and provides relevant applications. We also introduce a novel $\infty$-Wasserstein distance tracking method, which tightens the analysis of privacy leakage and makes PABI more applicable in practice. We evaluate this framework by applying it to Personalized Pagerank computation for ranking tasks. Experiments on real-world network data demonstrate the superiority of our method under stringent privacy conditions.

paragraphs: Graph diffusion repeatedly spreads numerical quantities through a network and produces vectors useful for applications such as ranking. Publishing those vectors can reveal sensitive connections, including financial transaction links. This paper develops a diffusion framework with edge-level differential privacy, targeting the information exposed about individual links in the graph.

The algorithm adds Laplace noise at every diffusion iteration. It also applies a thresholding function based on node degree to reduce the high sensitivity associated with nodes that have few connections. These two ingredients address both the release of information during repeated propagation and the disproportionate influence that some graph locations can have.

The privacy analysis uses Privacy Amplification by Iteration and introduces an infinity-Wasserstein distance tracking method to obtain tighter bounds on leakage. The authors identify their analysis of this amplification technique with Laplace noise as a first effort to their knowledge. Applied to Personalized PageRank ranking tasks, the framework outperforms the compared methods on real network data under stringent privacy requirements, supporting the practical value of its analysis and algorithm.
summary.tldr: Noisy diffusion steps and degree-based thresholding provide edge-level privacy while improving Personalized PageRank results under stringent privacy conditions.

title: Differentially Private Graph Diffusion with Applications in Personalized PageRanks

abstract: Diffusion models are powerful generative models, and this capability can also be applied to discrimination. The inner activations of a pre-trained diffusion model can serve as features for discriminative tasks, namely, diffusion feature. We discover that diffusion feature has been hindered by a hidden yet universal phenomenon that we call content shift. To be specific, there are content differences between features and the input image, such as the exact shape of a certain object. We locate the cause of content shift as one inherent characteristic of diffusion models, which suggests the broad existence of this phenomenon in diffusion feature. Further empirical study also indicates that its negative impact is not negligible even when content shift is not visually perceivable. Hence, we propose to suppress content shift to enhance the overall quality of diffusion features. Specifically, content shift is related to the information drift during the process of recovering an image from the noisy input, pointing out the possibility of turning off-the-shelf generation techniques into tools for content shift suppression. We further propose a practical guideline named GATE to efficiently evaluate the potential benefit of a technique and provide an implementation of our methodology. Despite the simplicity, the proposed approach has achieved superior results on various tasks and datasets, validating its potential as a generic booster for diffusion features. Our code is available at https://github.com/Darkbblue/diffusion-content-shift.

paragraphs: Pretrained diffusion models can supply internal features for discriminative tasks as well as generate images. This paper identifies a problem called content shift: the content represented by those features can differ from the input image, including differences in an object’s exact shape. The authors attribute the phenomenon to an inherent characteristic of diffusion models, suggesting it is broadly present.

Their empirical analysis finds that content shift can harm performance even when the discrepancy is not visually apparent. They connect it to information drift during recovery of an image from noisy input. That connection suggests using existing image-generation techniques to suppress the drift and improve the fidelity of features used for discrimination.

The authors introduce GATE, a practical guideline for efficiently assessing whether a generation technique is likely to help, and provide an implementation of the approach. They report superior results across multiple tasks and datasets despite the method’s simplicity. These results support content-shift suppression as a potentially general way to improve diffusion features, connecting the quality of image recovery to the usefulness of internal representations.
summary.tldr: Suppressing content drift with existing generation techniques improves diffusion-model features for discriminative tasks across the tested settings.

title: Suppress Content Shift: Better Diffusion Features via Off-the-Shelf Generation Techniques

abstract: The spiking camera is an emerging neuromorphic vision sensor that records high-speed motion scenes by asynchronously firing continuous binary spike streams. Prevailing image reconstruction methods, generating intermediate frames from these spike streams, often rely on complex step-by-step network architectures that overlook the intrinsic collaboration of spatio-temporal complementary information. In this paper, we propose an efficient spatio-temporal interactive reconstruction network to jointly perform inter-frame feature alignment and intra-frame feature filtering in a coarse-to-fine manner. Specifically, it starts by extracting hierarchical features from a concise hybrid spike representation, then refines the motion fields and target frames scale-by-scale, ultimately obtaining a full-resolution output. Meanwhile, we introduce a symmetric interactive attention block and a multi-motion field estimation block to further enhance the interaction capability of the overall network. Experiments on synthetic and real-captured data show that our approach exhibits excellent performance while maintaining low model complexity.

paragraphs: Spiking cameras record fast-moving scenes as asynchronous streams of binary spikes. Reconstructing conventional images from these streams requires combining information across both space and time. The paper argues that existing complex, sequential reconstruction networks do not fully exploit how these two sources of information can complement one another.

The proposed network jointly aligns features between frames and filters features within a frame. It begins with a compact hybrid representation of the spikes and extracts features at multiple scales. Motion fields and target images are then refined from coarse scales to finer ones until the network produces a full-resolution reconstruction. This design lets motion estimation and image reconstruction interact throughout refinement.

A symmetric interactive attention block and a multi-motion field estimation block further strengthen those interactions. Experiments on synthetic data and recordings from real cameras show strong reconstruction performance while maintaining low model complexity. The reported result supports coordinating spatial filtering and temporal alignment within one refinement process as an efficient way to reconstruct images from spike streams.
summary.tldr: A coarse-to-fine network jointly aligns temporal features and filters spatial features to reconstruct spiking-camera images with low model complexity.

title: Spatio-Temporal Interactive Learning for Efficient Image Reconstruction of Spiking Cameras

abstract: Generative models have shown great promise in generating 3D geometric systems, which is a fundamental problem in many natural science domains such as molecule and protein design. However, existing approaches only operate on static structures, neglecting the fact that physical systems are always dynamic in nature. In this work, we propose geometric trajectory diffusion models (GeoTDM), the first diffusion model for modeling the temporal distribution of 3D geometric trajectories. Modeling such distribution is challenging as it requires capturing both the complex spatial interactions with physical symmetries and temporal correspondence encapsulated in the dynamics. We theoretically justify that diffusion models with equivariant temporal kernels can lead to density with desired symmetry, and develop a novel transition kernel leveraging SE(3)-equivariant spatial convolution and temporal attention. Furthermore, to induce an expressive trajectory distribution for conditional generation, we introduce a generalized learnable geometric prior into the forward diffusion process to enhance temporal conditioning. We conduct extensive experiments on both unconditional and conditional generation in various scenarios, including physical simulation, molecular dynamics, and pedestrian motion. Empirical results on a wide suite of metrics demonstrate that GeoTDM can generate realistic geometric trajectories with significantly higher quality.

Such trajectories must capture both spatial interactions and correspondence across successive moments. The paper also emphasizes physical symmetries, so that the representation of a system’s motion respects the relevant geometric transformations.

The authors theoretically show that diffusion models using equivariant temporal kernels can produce densities with the desired symmetry. They build a transition kernel combining SE(3)-equivariant spatial convolution with temporal attention. These components address geometric relationships and temporal dependencies together. summary.tldr: GeoTDM combines symmetry-respecting spatial modeling and temporal attention to generate higher-quality three-dimensional trajectories in the evaluated settings.

title: Geometric Trajectory Diffusion Models

abstract: Few-shot 3D point cloud semantic segmentation aims to segment query point clouds with only a few annotated support point clouds. Existing prototype-based methods learn prototypes from the 3D support set to guide the segmentation of query point clouds. However, they encounter the challenge of low prototype quality due to constrained semantic information in the 3D support set and class information bias between support and query sets. To address these issues, in this paper, we propose a novel framework called Generated and Pseudo Content guided Prototype Refinement (GPCPR), which explicitly leverages LLM-generated content and reliable query context to enhance prototype quality. GPCPR achieves prototype refinement through two core components: LLM-driven Generated Content-guided Prototype Refinement (GCPR) and Pseudo Query Context-guided Prototype Refinement (PCPR). Specifically, GCPR integrates diverse and differentiated class descriptions generated by large language models to enrich prototypes with comprehensive semantic knowledge. PCPR further aggregates reliable class-specific pseudo-query context to mitigate class information bias and generate more suitable query-specific prototypes. Furthermore, we introduce a dual-distillation regularization term, enabling knowledge transfer between early-stage entities (prototypes or pseudo predictions) and their deeper counterparts to enhance refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our method, surpassing the state-of-the-art methods by up to 12.10% and 13.75% mIoU on S3DIS and ScanNet, respectively.

Prototype methods summarize each class from those examples and use the summaries to label a new cloud. Their effectiveness can suffer when the examples contain limited semantic information or represent classes differently from the query cloud.

GPCPR improves these summaries using two sources of additional information. One component incorporates varied class descriptions generated by a language model, enriching the prototypes’ semantic content. Another aggregates reliable class-specific context from pseudo predictions on the query, adapting prototypes to that particular cloud. A dual-distillation regularizer also transfers knowledge between earlier and deeper prototypes or pseudo predictions.

Experiments report gains over state-of-the-art methods of up to 12.10% mIoU on S3DIS and 13.75% on ScanNet. The results support combining descriptive class knowledge with evidence from the actual query. These sources address different weaknesses: generated descriptions broaden what a prototype expresses, while query context helps account for differences between the labeled examples and the cloud being segmented.
summary.tldr: GPCPR improves few-shot 3D segmentation by refining class prototypes with language-model descriptions and reliable context from the query cloud.

title: Generated and Pseudo Content guided Prototype Refinement for Few-shot Point Cloud Segmentation

abstract: We introduce OpenDebateEvidence, a comprehensive dataset for argument miningand summarization sourced from the American Competitive Debate community.This dataset includes over 3.5 million documents with rich metadata, making itone of the most extensive collections of debate evidence. OpenDebateEvidencecaptures the complexity of arguments in high school and college debates, pro-viding valuable resources for training and evaluation. Our extensive experimentsdemonstrate the efficacy of fine-tuning state-of-the-art large language models forargumentative abstractive summarization across various methods, models, anddatasets. By providing this comprehensive resource, we aim to advance com-putational argumentation and support practical applications for debaters, edu-cators, and researchers. OpenDebateEvidence is publicly available to supportfurther research and innovation in computational argumentation. Access it here:https://huggingface.co/datasets/Yusuf5/OpenCaselist.

paragraphs: Systems that analyze arguments need data reflecting how evidence is assembled and summarized in actual argumentative practice. OpenDebateEvidence provides a large collection drawn from the American competitive debate community. It contains more than 3.5 million documents with rich metadata and represents the complexity of arguments used in high school and college debates.

The dataset is intended for both argument mining and summarization, giving researchers material for training models and evaluating their behavior. Its debate setting supplies a shared application context for those tasks. The scale and accompanying metadata make it a substantial research resource for studying argumentative material across many documents within that setting.

The authors also conduct experiments on fine-tuning state-of-the-art language models for argumentative abstractive summarization, where models write summaries in newly generated language. Across methods, models, and datasets, they find that fine-tuning is effective. The paper therefore contributes both a publicly available evidence collection and experimental support for its associated modeling direction, with intended applications for debaters, educators, and researchers working on computational argumentation.
summary.tldr: OpenDebateEvidence provides over 3.5 million debate documents and supports research on argument mining and language-model summarization.

title: OpenDebateEvidence: A Massive-Scale Argument Mining and Summarization Dataset

abstract: Recently developed quasi-Bayesian (QB) methods \cite{fong2023martingale} proposed a stimulating change of paradigm in Bayesian computation by directly constructing the Bayesian predictive distribution through recursion, removing the need for expensive computations involved in sampling the Bayesian posterior distribution. This has proved to be data-efficient for univariate predictions, however, existing constructions for higher dimensional densities are only possible by relying on restrictive assumptions on the model's multivariate structure. Here, we propose a wholly different approach to extend Quasi-Bayesian prediction to high dimensions through the use of Sklar's theorem, by decomposing the predictive distribution into one-dimensional predictive marginals and a high-dimensional copula. We use the efficient recursive QB construction for the one-dimensional marginals and model the dependence using highly expressive vine copulas. Further, we tune hyperparameters using robust divergences (eg. energy score) and show that our proposed Quasi-Bayesian Vine (QB-Vine) is a fully non-parametric density estimator with \emph{an analytical form} and convergence rate independent of the dimension of the data in some situations. Our experiments illustrate that the QB-Vine is appropriate for high dimensional distributions ($\sim$64), needs very few samples to train ($\sim$200) and outperforms state-of-the-art methods with analytical forms for density estimation and supervised tasks by a considerable margin.

paragraphs: Quasi-Bayesian prediction constructs a predictive distribution recursively, avoiding costly posterior sampling. Existing approaches work well for one-dimensional prediction, but their extensions to higher dimensions require restrictive dependence assumptions. This paper introduces QB-Vine to separate the problem of modeling each variable from modeling relationships among variables.

Using Sklar's theorem, the method combines one-dimensional predictive marginals with a multivariate copula. Recursive quasi-Bayesian updates handle the marginals, while expressive vine copulas represent dependence. Hyperparameters are tuned with robust divergences such as the energy score. The resulting density estimator is fully nonparametric and has an analytical form.

The authors establish a dimension-independent convergence rate in some situations, rather than as a universal property. Experiments show applicability to distributions of around 64 dimensions with around 200 training samples. They also report substantial gains over state-of-the-art methods with analytical forms on density estimation and supervised tasks. The contribution is a flexible route to high-dimensional prediction that retains an explicitly available density.
summary.tldr: QB-Vine combines recursive one-dimensional predictions with vine copulas to obtain flexible high-dimensional densities in analytical form.

title: Quasi-Bayes meets Vines

abstract: Deep supervised models possess significant capability to assimilate extensive training data, thereby presenting an opportunity to enhance model performance through training on multiple datasets. However, conflicts arising from different label spaces among datasets may adversely affect model performance. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to automatically construct a unified label space across multiple datasets using graph neural networks. This enables semantic segmentation models to be trained simultaneously on multiple datasets, resulting in performance improvements. Unlike existing methods, our approach facilitates seamless training without the need for additional manual reannotation or taxonomy reconciliation. This significantly enhances the efficiency and effectiveness of multi-dataset segmentation model training. The results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms other multi-dataset training methods when trained on seven datasets simultaneously, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the WildDash 2 benchmark. Our code can be found in https://github.com/Mrhonor/AutoUniSeg.

paragraphs: Training a semantic segmentation model on multiple datasets offers access to more examples, but the datasets may use incompatible label systems. Since segmentation assigns categories to image regions, disagreements in those categories can interfere with learning. Simply pooling the available data therefore does not necessarily improve the resulting model.

The authors propose using graph neural networks to automatically construct a shared label space across datasets. This shared space lets a segmentation model learn from the datasets together without requiring people to reannotate their images or manually reconcile their category taxonomies. The method addresses the organization of supervision that makes joint training possible.

In experiments involving simultaneous training on seven datasets, the approach significantly outperforms other multi-dataset training methods. It also achieves state-of-the-art results on WildDash 2. These findings support automated label unification as a useful component of multi-dataset segmentation: the reported benefit combines improved prediction performance with reduced manual work in preparing otherwise incompatible datasets for joint use.
summary.tldr: Graph neural networks automatically unify dataset labels, enabling stronger joint semantic segmentation training without manual reannotation or taxonomy reconciliation.

title: Automated Label Unification for Multi-Dataset Semantic Segmentation with GNNs

abstract: This paper introduces an approach to endow generative diffusion processes the ability to satisfy and certify compliance with constraints and physical principles. The proposed method recast the traditional sampling process of generative diffusion models as a constrained optimization problem, steering the generated data distribution to remain within a specified region to ensure adherence to the given constraints.These capabilities are validated on applications featuring both convex and challenging, non-convex, constraints as well as ordinary differential equations, in domains spanning from synthesizing new materials with precise morphometric properties, generating physics-informed motion, optimizing paths in planning scenarios, and human motion synthesis.

paragraphs: This paper studies how diffusion models can generate outputs that satisfy specified constraints and physical principles. The goal includes certifying compliance, so a generated result can be assessed against the requirements imposed on it. This matters for tasks where the desired output must meet explicit mathematical or physical conditions.

The proposed approach reformulates diffusion sampling as a constrained optimization problem. It steers the generated distribution to stay within a specified admissible region. Constraints therefore become part of the generation procedure itself, giving the sampling process a direct way to account for properties that the output is required to possess.

The authors validate the approach on applications involving convex constraints, more challenging non-convex constraints, and ordinary differential equations. Their examples span materials with prescribed shape-related properties, motion informed by physical principles, path optimization, and human motion synthesis. These applications demonstrate the method across several kinds of requirements and output domains. The stated contribution is a framework connecting diffusion generation with explicit constraint satisfaction and certification.
summary.tldr: The paper reformulates diffusion sampling as constrained optimization to generate outputs that satisfy and certify specified requirements.

title: Constrained Synthesis with Projected Diffusion Models

abstract: Instruction tuning improves the reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs), with data quality and scalability being the crucial factors. Most instruction tuning data come from human crowd-sourcing or GPT-4 distillation. We propose a paradigm to efficiently harvest 10 million naturally existing instruction data from the pre-training web corpus to enhance LLM reasoning. Our approach involves (1) recalling relevant documents, (2) extracting instruction-response pairs, and (3) refining the extracted pairs using open-source LLMs. Fine-tuning base LLMs on this dataset, we build MAmmoTH2 models, which significantly boost performance on reasoning benchmarks. Notably, MAmmoTH2-7B’s (Mistral) performance increases from 11% to 36.7% on MATH and from 36% to 68.4% on GSM8K without training on any in-domain data. Further training MAmmoTH2 on public instruction tuning datasets yields MAmmoTH2-Plus, achieving state-of-the-art performance on several reasoning and chatbot benchmarks. Our work demonstrates how to harvest large-scale, high-quality instruction data without costly human annotation or GPT-4 distillation, providing a new paradigm for building better instruction tuning data.

The experiments demonstrate the value of extracting and refining web instructions at scale.
summary.tldr: MAmmoTH2 harvests 10 million web instruction examples and uses them to substantially improve language model reasoning.

title: MAmmoTH2: Scaling Instructions from the Web

abstract: We give the first polynomial-time, differentially node-private, and robust algorithm for estimating the edge density of Erdős-Rényi random graphs and their generalization, inhomogeneous random graphs. We further prove information-theoretical lower bounds, showing that the error rate of our algorithm is optimal up to logarithmic factors. Previous algorithms incur either exponential running time or suboptimal error rates.Two key ingredients of our algorithm are (1) a new sum-of-squares algorithm for robust edge density estimation, and (2) the reduction from privacy to robustness based on sum-of-squares exponential mechanisms due to Hopkins et al. (STOC 2023).

Previous algorithms incur either exponential running time or suboptimal error rates.Two key ingredients of our algorithm are (1) a new sum-of-squares algorithm for robust edge density estimation, and (2) the reduction from privacy to robustness based on sum-of-squares exponential mechanisms due to Hopkins et al. paragraphs: Estimating a graph's edge density means measuring how densely its nodes are connected. This paper addresses that task while combining differential node privacy, robustness, and efficient computation. Its setting covers Erdős–Rényi random graphs and the broader class of inhomogeneous random graphs.

The algorithm combines two ingredients. First, the authors develop a sum-of-squares algorithm for robust edge-density estimation. Second, they use an existing reduction that turns robustness into privacy through sum-of-squares exponential mechanisms. This connection allows a robust estimation method to form the basis of a private algorithm, bringing the two requirements into a common construction.

The resulting method runs in polynomial time, whereas previous algorithms required either exponential time or less favorable error rates. Information-theoretic lower bounds show that its error rate is optimal up to logarithmic factors. The significance is the simultaneous achievement of computational efficiency, node privacy, robustness, and near-optimal accuracy for the stated random-graph families. The lower bounds establish that the accuracy improvement approaches a fundamental statistical limit.
summary.tldr: A polynomial-time algorithm estimates random-graph edge density with node privacy, robustness, and error optimal up to logarithmic factors.

title: Private Edge Density Estimation for Random Graphs: Optimal, Efficient and Robust

abstract: In this paper, we formalize the active set ordering problem, which involves actively discovering a set of inputs based on their orderings determined by expensive evaluations of a blackbox function. We then propose the mean prediction (MP) algorithm and theoretically analyze it in terms of the regret of predicted pairwise orderings between inputs. Notably, as a special case of this framework, we can cast Bayesian optimization as an active set ordering problem by recognizing that maximizers can be identified solely by comparison rather than by precisely estimating the function evaluations. As a result, we are able to construct the popular Gaussian process upper confidence bound (GP-UCB) algorithm through the lens of ordering with several nuanced insights. We empirically validate the performance of our proposed solution using various synthetic functions and real-world datasets.

Notably, as a special case of this framework, we can cast Bayesian optimization as an active set ordering problem by recognizing that maximizers can be identified solely by comparison rather than by precisely estimating the function evaluations. paragraphs: An expensive black-box function may be useful mainly because it orders candidate inputs. This paper formalizes active set ordering, where the learner selects evaluations to discover those relationships rather than needing uniformly precise predictions of every function value.

The proposed mean-prediction algorithm is analyzed through regret on predicted pairwise orderings. Bayesian optimization appears as a special case because identifying a maximizer requires comparisons, even when exact objective values are not the ultimate goal.

The authors reconstruct the Gaussian-process upper-confidence-bound algorithm from this ordering perspective and draw additional insights from that interpretation. Experiments on synthetic functions and real-world datasets validate the proposed solution. The abstract does not give regret formulas or numerical gains. The contribution is both a general problem formulation and an algorithmic lens connecting ranking-oriented active evaluation with familiar Bayesian-optimization methods.
summary.tldr: Active set ordering studies which expensive evaluations are needed to infer useful rankings.

title: Active Set Ordering

abstract: Lately, there has been a surge in interest surrounding generative modeling of time series data. Most existing approaches are designed either to process short sequences or to handle long-range sequences. This dichotomy can be attributed to gradient issues with recurrent networks, computational costs associated with transformers, and limited expressiveness of state space models. Towards a unified generative model for varying-length time series, we propose in this work to transform sequences into images. By employing invertible transforms such as the delay embedding and the short-time Fourier transform, we unlock three main advantages: i) We can exploit advanced diffusion vision models; ii) We can remarkably process short- and long-range inputs within the same framework; and iii) We can harness recent and established tools proposed in the time series to image literature. We validate the effectiveness of our method through a comprehensive evaluation across multiple tasks, including unconditional generation, interpolation, and extrapolation. We show that our approach achieves consistently state-of-the-art results against strong baselines. In the unconditional generation tasks, we show remarkable mean improvements of $58.17$% over previous diffusion models in the short discriminative score and $132.61$% in the (ultra-)long classification scores. Code is at https://github.com/azencot-group/ImagenTime.

paragraphs: Generative time-series models often specialize in either short or long sequences. The paper links this split to difficulties such as recurrent-network gradients, transformer computation costs, and limited expressiveness in state space models. It proposes a common framework that first transforms a time series into an image-like representation, making image diffusion models available for sequence generation.

The method uses invertible transformations, including delay embedding and the short-time Fourier transform. Invertibility connects generated image representations back to time series. This design combines access to advanced visual diffusion models with established techniques for representing temporal data as images, while supporting both short and long inputs within the same framework.

These are improvements in the named evaluation scores, supporting the representation strategy across the tested sequence lengths and tasks.
summary.tldr: Invertible time-series-to-image transformations let one diffusion framework generate short and long sequences with strong reported results across several tasks.

title: Utilizing Image Transforms and Diffusion Models for Generative Modeling of Short and Long Time Series

abstract: Reward specification is one of the most tricky problems in Reinforcement Learning, which usually requires tedious hand engineering in practice. One promising approach to tackle this challenge is to adopt existing expert video demonstrations for policy learning. Some recent work investigates how to learn robot policies from only a single/few expert video demonstrations. For example, reward labeling via Optimal Transport (OT) has been shown to be an effective strategy to generate a proxy reward by measuring the alignment between the robot trajectory and the expert demonstrations. However, previous work mostly overlooks that the OT reward is invariant to temporal order information, which could bring extra noise to the reward signal. To address this issue, in this paper, we introduce the Temporal Optimal Transport (TemporalOT) reward to incorporate temporal order information for learning a more accurate OT-based proxy reward. Extensive experiments on the Meta-world benchmark tasks validate the efficacy of the proposed method. Our code is available at: https://github.com/fuyw/TemporalOT.

title: Robot Policy Learning with Temporal Optimal Transport Reward

abstract: Instruction following is crucial in contemporary LLM. However, when extended to multimodal setting, it often suffers from misalignment between specific textual instruction and targeted local region of an image. To achieve more accurate and nuanced multimodal instruction following, we introduce Instruction-guided Visual Masking (IVM), a new versatile visual grounding model that is compatible with diverse multimodal models, such as LMM and robot model. By constructing visual masks for instruction-irrelevant regions, IVM-enhanced multimodal models can effectively focus on task-relevant image regions to better align with complex instructions. Specifically, we design a visual masking data generation pipeline and create an IVM-Mix-1M dataset with 1 million image-instruction pairs. We further introduce a new learning technique, Discriminator Weighted Supervised Learning (DWSL) for preferential IVM training that prioritizes high-quality data samples. Experimental results on generic multimodal tasks such as VQA and embodied robotic control demonstrate the versatility of IVM, which as a plug-and-play tool, significantly boosts the performance of diverse multimodal models, yielding new state-of-the-art results across challenging multimodal benchmarks. Code, model and data are available at https://github.com/2toinf/IVM.

It provides a visual grounding component that can work with different multimodal systems, including robot models.

IVM constructs masks for image regions that are irrelevant to the instruction. This helps the receiving model focus on information needed for the task. To train the masking model, the authors develop a data-generation pipeline and create IVM-Mix-1M, containing one million image-instruction pairs. Their Discriminator Weighted Supervised Learning technique gives priority to higher-quality training examples.

Experiments cover visual question answering and embodied robotic control, demonstrating the method across different kinds of multimodal tasks. The authors report substantial improvements for diverse models and new leading results on challenging benchmarks. The contribution is a reusable masking tool whose instruction-dependent selection of visual information improves how existing models connect requests with relevant image content.
summary.tldr: IVM masks instruction-irrelevant image regions to improve visual question answering and robotic control across different multimodal models.

title: Instruction-Guided Visual Masking

abstract: Districting is a complex combinatorial problem that consists in partitioning a geographical area into small districts. In logistics, it is a major strategic decision determining operating costs for several years. Solving districting problems using traditional methods is intractable even for small geographical areas and existing heuristics often provide sub-optimal results. We present a structured learning approach to find high-quality solutions to real-world districting problems in a few minutes. It is based on integrating a combinatorial optimization layer, the capacitated minimum spanning tree problem, into a graph neural network architecture. To train this pipeline in a decision-aware fashion, we show how to construct target solutions embedded in a suitable space and learn from target solutions. Experiments show that our approach outperforms existing methods as it can significantly reduce costs on real-world cities.

DistrictNet aims to find high-quality solutions for real-world districting problems within a few minutes.

This brings a structured optimization problem directly into the learning architecture. To train the pipeline around the decisions it must ultimately make, the authors construct target solutions in a suitable representation and show how to learn from them.

Experiments on real-world cities report that DistrictNet outperforms existing methods and can significantly reduce costs. The result connects the learning procedure to the quality of the resulting geographic decisions, rather than evaluating a prediction in isolation. Its central contribution is the integration of learned representations, structured target solutions, and combinatorial optimization into a practical districting pipeline.
summary.tldr: DistrictNet combines a graph neural network with combinatorial optimization to produce lower-cost geographic districts in minutes.

title: DistrictNet: Decision-aware learning for geographical districting

abstract: Representing 3D scenes from multiview images remains a core challenge in computer vision and graphics, requiring both reliable rendering and reconstruction, which often conflicts due to the mismatched prioritization of image quality over precise underlying scene geometry. Although both neural implicit surfaces and explicit Gaussian primitives have advanced with neural rendering techniques, current methods impose strict constraints on density fields or primitive shapes, which enhances the affinity for geometric reconstruction at the sacrifice of rendering quality. To address this dilemma, we introduce GSDF, a dual-branch architecture combining 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and neural Signed Distance Fields (SDF). Our approach leverages mutual guidance and joint supervision during the training process to mutually enhance reconstruction and rendering. Specifically, our method guides the Gaussian primitives to locate near potential surfaces and accelerates the SDF convergence. This implicit mutual guidance ensures robustness and accuracy in both synthetic and real-world scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate that our method boosts the SDF optimization process to reconstruct more detailed geometry, while reducing floaters and blurry edge artifacts in rendering by aligning Gaussian primitives with the underlying geometry.

paragraphs: Building a 3D scene from multiple images requires both convincing rendered views and accurate geometry. These goals can conflict when a representation prioritizes image appearance over the underlying surface. The paper also describes how constraints intended to improve reconstruction can sacrifice rendering quality, motivating a method that improves the two together.

GSDF combines two branches: 3D Gaussian Splatting and a neural signed distance field. During training, the branches provide mutual guidance and share supervision. The method encourages Gaussian primitives to sit near potential surfaces while accelerating convergence of the signed distance field. This links the image-producing representation more closely to the geometry being reconstructed.

Experiments in synthetic and real-world scenarios show more detailed reconstructed geometry and improved rendering. In particular, aligning Gaussians with the underlying geometry reduces floating artifacts and blurry edges. The results support the paper's central strategy: use the complementary scene representations to improve one another during optimization, addressing reconstruction and rendering as connected parts of the same learning problem.
summary.tldr: GSDF jointly trains Gaussian splats and a signed distance field to improve reconstructed geometry and reduce rendering artifacts.

title: GSDF: 3DGS Meets SDF for Improved Neural Rendering and Reconstruction

abstract: Post-Translational Modifications (PTMs) are changes that occur in proteins after synthesis, influencing their structure, function, and cellular behavior. PTMs are essential in cell biology; they regulate protein function and stability, are involved in various cellular processes, and are linked to numerous diseases. A particularly interesting class of PTMs are chemical modifications such as phosphorylation introduced on amino acid side chains because they can drastically alter the physicochemical properties of the peptides once they are present. One or more PTMs can be attached to each amino acid of the peptide sequence. The most commonly applied technique to detect PTMs on proteins is bottom-up Mass Spectrometry-based proteomics (MS), where proteins are digested into peptides and subsequently analyzed using Tandem Mass Spectrometry (MS/MS). While an increasing number of machine learning models are published focusing on MS/MS-related property prediction of unmodified peptides, high-quality reference data for modified peptides is missing, impeding model development for this important class of peptides. To enable researchers to train machine learning models that can accurately predict the properties of modified peptides, we introduce four high-quality labeled datasets for applying machine and deep learning to tasks in MS-based proteomics. The four datasets comprise several subgroups of peptides with 1.2 million unique modified peptide sequences and 30 unique pairs of (amino-acid, PTM), covering both experimentally introduced and naturally occurring modifications on various amino acids. We evaluate the utility and importance of the dataset by providing benchmarking results on models trained with and without modifications and highlighting the impact of including modified sequences on downstream tasks. We demonstrate that predicting the properties of modified peptides is more challenging but has a broad impact since they are often the core of protein functionality and its regulation, and they have a potential role as biomarkers in clinical applications. Our datasets contribute to applied machine learning in proteomics by enabling the research community to experiment with methods to encode PTMs as model inputs and to benchmark against reference data for model comparison. With a proper data split for three common tasks in proteomics, we provide a robust way to evaluate model performance and assess generalization on unseen modified sequences.
