paragraphs: Regularized learning becomes harder to optimize when the penalty has a complex structure. This paper proposes a stochastic dual coordinate ascent method that uses the alternating direction method of multipliers, or ADMM, to handle such regularization. The intended scope includes a wide range of learning problems with structured penalties.

Ordinary ADMM is a batch method, while the proposed update needs only one or a few sample observations per iteration. This combines ADMM’s treatment of complex regularizers with stochastic updates that avoid requiring a full batch at every step. The method also naturally supports mini-batches, and the authors report that these can accelerate convergence.

Under assumptions described as mild, the paper proves exponential convergence. Numerical experiments also show efficient performance, providing empirical support alongside the theoretical rate. The convergence claim is conditional on those assumptions rather than a statement about every possible regularized objective. The main contribution is an optimization method that brings structured regularization and small-sample updates into the same algorithmic framework, with both convergence analysis and practical evaluation.
summary.tldr: An ADMM-based stochastic dual coordinate method handles complex regularization with small-sample updates and conditional exponential convergence.

title: Stochastic Dual Coordinate Ascent with Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers

abstract: We propose a unified framework for making a wide range of PCA-like algorithms – including the standard PCA, sparse PCA and non-negative sparse PCA, etc. – robust when facing a constant fraction of arbitrarily corrupted outliers. Our theoretic analysis establishes solid performance guarantees of the proposed framework: its estimation error is upper bounded by a term depending on the intrinsic parameters of the data model, the selected PCA-like algorithm and the fraction of outliers. Comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the outlier-robust PCA-like algorithms derived from our framework have outstanding performance.

paragraphs: Principal component methods seek structure in data, but corrupted observations can interfere with that estimation. This paper develops a common framework for making several related methods robust to outliers. Its scope includes ordinary PCA, sparse PCA, and non-negative sparse PCA, so the contribution extends across methods with different structural requirements.

The contamination setting permits a constant fraction of observations to be arbitrarily corrupted. This is a strong form of contamination: the corrupted observations need not follow a convenient noise pattern. The theoretical analysis bounds estimation error using properties of the underlying data model, the particular PCA-like method selected, and the fraction of outliers. Robustness therefore comes with a quantified dependence on both the problem and the contamination level.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets report strong performance for the algorithms produced by the framework. The main significance is the shared route to robustness: related PCA methods can be treated within one analysis, while their individual characteristics still enter the error guarantee.
summary.tldr: A unified framework makes several PCA variants robust to a constant fraction of arbitrarily corrupted observations, with estimation-error guarantees.

title: A Unified Framework for Outlier-Robust PCA-like Algorithms

abstract: Representational Similarity Learning (RSL) aims to discover features that are important in representing (human-judged) similarities among objects. RSL can be posed as a sparsity-regularized multi-task regression problem. Standard methods, like group lasso, may not select important features if they are strongly correlated with others. To address this shortcoming we present a new regularizer for multitask regression called Group Ordered Weighted \ell_1 (GrOWL). Another key contribution of our paper is a novel application to fMRI brain imaging. Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) is a tool for testing whether localized brain regions encode perceptual similarities. Using GrOWL, we propose a new approach called Network RSA that can discover arbitrarily structured brain networks (possibly widely distributed and non-local) that encode similarity information. We show, in theory and fMRI experiments, how GrOWL deals with strongly correlated covariates.

paragraphs: Representational Similarity Learning seeks features that explain human judgments about how similar objects are. It can be formulated as multitask regression with a sparsity penalty. A difficulty is that standard approaches such as group lasso may fail to select important features when those features are strongly correlated with others.

The authors introduce Group Ordered Weighted l1, or GrOWL, as a new regularizer for multitask regression that addresses this issue. They examine its handling of strongly correlated covariates through theory and fMRI experiments. The methodological goal is to improve feature discovery when useful information is shared among correlated predictors.

The paper also introduces Network RSA, an application of GrOWL to brain imaging. Conventional representational similarity analysis tests whether localized regions encode perceptual similarities. Network RSA can instead discover networks with arbitrary spatial structure, including widely distributed, non-local regions. This broadens the structures that can be considered when looking for similarity information in the brain and connects the regularization method to interpretable feature discovery in imaging data.
summary.tldr: GrOWL addresses correlated features in similarity learning and enables discovery of distributed brain networks encoding perceptual similarity.

title: Representational Similarity Learning with Application to Brain Networks

abstract: We examine the role of memorization in deep learning, drawing connections to capacity, generalization, and adversarial robustness. While deep networks are capable of memorizing noise data, our results suggest that they tend to prioritize learning simple patterns first. In our experiments, we expose qualitative differences in gradient-based optimization of deep neural networks (DNNs) on noise vs.~real data. We also demonstrate that for appropriately tuned explicit regularization (e.g.,~dropout) we can degrade DNN training performance on noise datasets without compromising generalization on real data. Our analysis suggests that the notions of effective capacity which are dataset independent are unlikely to explain the generalization performance of deep networks when trained with gradient based methods because training data itself plays an important role in determining the degree of memorization.

We also demonstrate that for appropriately tuned explicit regularization (e.g.,~dropout) we can degrade DNN training performance on noise datasets without compromising generalization on real data. Our analysis suggests that the notions of effective capacity which are dataset independent are unlikely to explain the generalization performance of deep networks when trained with gradient based methods because training data itself plays an important role in determining the degree of memorization.

paragraphs: A network's ability to memorize arbitrary data does not by itself explain what it learns during ordinary training. This paper investigates memorization alongside model capacity, generalization, and adversarial robustness. Its results suggest that deep networks tend to learn simple patterns before memorizing noise, making the course of training relevant to understanding their behavior.

The experiments identify qualitative differences between gradient-based training on real data and on noise. They also examine explicit regularization, including dropout. With appropriate tuning, regularization can make networks fit noise datasets less successfully without harming their ability to generalize on real data. The qualification about tuning matters: the finding concerns suitably chosen regularization.

Together, these observations suggest that memorization depends partly on the training data itself. The authors therefore question whether dataset-independent notions of effective capacity can explain generalization under gradient-based training. The contribution is evidence for an explanation that accounts for both what a network can represent and how learning unfolds on particular data.
summary.tldr: Experiments suggest that deep networks learn simple patterns first and that memorization depends on the data and training process.

title: A Closer Look at Memorization in Deep Networks

abstract: Persistence diagrams (PDs) play a key role in topological data analysis (TDA), in which they are routinely used to describe succinctly complex topological properties of complicated shapes. PDs enjoy strong stability properties and have proven their utility in various learning contexts. They do not, however, live in a space naturally endowed with a Hilbert structure and are usually compared with specific distances, such as the bottleneck distance. To incorporate PDs in a learning pipeline, several kernels have been proposed for PDs with a strong emphasis on the stability of the RKHS distance w.r.t. perturbations of the PDs. In this article, we use the Sliced Wasserstein approximation of the Wasserstein distance to define a new kernel for PDs, which is not only provably stable but also provably discriminative w.r.t. the Wasserstein distance $W^1_\infty$ between PDs. We also demonstrate its practicality, by developing an approximation technique to reduce kernel computation time, and show that our proposal compares favorably to existing kernels for PDs on several benchmarks.

paragraphs: Persistence diagrams summarize complex topological properties of shapes and are useful representations for learning. However, their natural comparisons do not directly provide the Hilbert-space structure used by many kernel methods. This paper develops a new kernel to make persistence diagrams easier to incorporate into a learning pipeline.

The construction uses the Sliced Wasserstein approximation to Wasserstein distance. The authors prove both stability and discriminative properties relative to the specified Wasserstein distance between diagrams. These properties address complementary needs: the comparison should tolerate small perturbations while retaining meaningful distinctions between diagrams.

The paper also develops an approximation technique that reduces kernel computation time. Benchmark experiments show favorable comparisons with existing persistence-diagram kernels. The contribution therefore combines mathematical properties of the representation with a way to make its computation more practical. Stability alone is not the entire goal; the stated discrimination guarantee also supports using the kernel to distinguish diagram structure, while the experiments assess its usefulness in learning settings.
summary.tldr: A Sliced Wasserstein kernel provides provably stable and discriminative persistence-diagram comparisons, with a faster approximation and favorable benchmark results.

title: Sliced Wasserstein Kernel for Persistence Diagrams

abstract: Although the convergence rates of existing variants of ADAGRAD have a better dependence on the number of iterations under the strong convexity condition, their iteration complexities have a explicitly linear dependence on the dimensionality of the problem. To alleviate this bad dependence, we propose a simple yet novel variant of ADAGRAD for stochastic (weakly) strongly convex optimization. Different from existing variants, the proposed variant (referred to as SADAGRAD) uses an adaptive restarting scheme in which (i) ADAGRAD serves as a sub-routine and is restarted periodically; (ii) the number of iterations for restarting ADAGRAD depends on the history of learning that incorporates knowledge of the geometry of the data. In addition to the adaptive proximal functions and adaptive number of iterations for restarting, we also develop a variant that is adaptive to the (implicit) strong convexity from the data, which together makes the proposed algorithm strongly adaptive. In terms of iteration complexity, in the worst case SADAGRAD has an O(1/\epsilon) for finding an \epsilon-optimal solution similar to other variants. However, it could enjoy faster convergence and much better dependence on the problem’s dimensionality when stochastic gradients are sparse. Extensive experiments on large-scale data sets demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed algorithms in comparison with several variants of ADAGRAD and stochastic gradient method.

paragraphs: Some ADAGRAD variants improve iteration dependence under strong convexity, yet their complexity still grows explicitly linearly with problem dimension. SADAGRAD addresses this issue for stochastic optimization under strong or weak strong convexity. Its central mechanism is an adaptive schedule for restarting ADAGRAD.

ADAGRAD serves as a subroutine that is periodically restarted. The restart timing depends on the learning history, incorporating information about the geometry of the data. Alongside adaptive proximal functions and adaptive restart lengths, the authors develop a version that adapts to strong convexity implicitly supplied by the data. Adaptation therefore operates at several levels of the optimization procedure.

In the worst case, SADAGRAD retains an O(1/epsilon) iteration complexity for finding an epsilon-optimal solution, comparable to other variants. When stochastic gradients are sparse, it could converge faster and have substantially better dependence on dimension. Large-scale experiments demonstrate efficiency against several ADAGRAD and stochastic gradient alternatives. The theoretical advantage is thus qualified by gradient structure, with empirical evidence supporting practical efficiency.
summary.tldr: SADAGRAD adaptively restarts ADAGRAD and can improve convergence and dimension dependence when stochastic gradients are sparse.

title: SADAGRAD: Strongly Adaptive Stochastic Gradient Methods

abstract: One of the biggest challenges in the research of generative adversarial networks (GANs) is assessing the quality of generated samples and detecting various levels of mode collapse. In this work, we construct a novel measure of performance of a GAN by comparing geometrical properties of the underlying data manifold and the generated one, which provides both qualitative and quantitative means for evaluation. Our algorithm can be applied to datasets of an arbitrary nature and is not limited to visual data. We test the obtained metric on various real-life models and datasets and demonstrate that our method provides new insights into properties of GANs.

Our algorithm can be applied to datasets of an arbitrary nature and is not limited to visual data. paragraphs: Evaluating a generative adversarial network involves assessing sample quality and whether the generator represents the variety present in the data. The latter concern includes mode collapse, where some forms of variation fail to appear in generated samples. This paper proposes an evaluation measure based on the geometry of real and generated data.

The method compares geometric properties of their underlying data manifolds, treating the structure of the two collections as evidence about the generator’s behavior. It provides both quantitative comparisons and qualitative ways to evaluate a model. This connects assessment of generated samples with how their collective structure relates to that of the source data.

The algorithm is designed for datasets of arbitrary nature, so its use is not restricted to images. The authors test it on several real-life models and datasets and report that it reveals new insights into GAN properties. Its stated contribution is an additional way to examine generative behavior, including the challenge of recognizing different levels of mode collapse.
summary.tldr: Geometry Score evaluates GANs by comparing the geometric structure of real and generated data, including data beyond images.

title: Geometry Score: A Method For Comparing Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: This paper studies semiparametric contextual bandits, a generalization of the linear stochastic bandit problem where the reward for a chosen action is modeled as a linear function of known action features confounded by a non-linear action-independent term. We design new algorithms that achieve $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{T})$ regret over $T$ rounds, when the linear function is $d$-dimensional, which matches the best known bounds for the simpler unconfounded case and improves on a recent result of Greenwald et al. (2017). Via an empirical evaluation, we show that our algorithms outperform prior approaches when there are non-linear confounding effects on the rewards. Technically, our algorithms use a new reward estimator inspired by doubly-robust approaches and our proofs require new concentration inequalities for self-normalized martingales.
originalAbstract: This paper studies semiparametric contextual bandits, a generalization of the linear stochastic bandit problem where the reward for a chosen action is modeled as a linear function of known action features confounded by a non-linear action-independent term. We design new algorithms that achieve $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{T})$ regret over $T$ rounds, when the linear function is $d$-dimensional, which matches the best known bounds for the simpler unconfounded case and improves on a recent result of Greenwald et al. (2017). Via an empirical evaluation, we show that our algorithms outperform prior approaches when there are non-linear confounding effects on the rewards. Technically, our algorithms use a new reward estimator inspired by doubly-robust approaches and our proofs require new concentration inequalities for self-normalized martingales.

paragraphs: A contextual bandit learns which action to choose from the rewards it observes. This paper considers rewards with two components: a linear function of known action features and an additional nonlinear term that does not depend on the action. The latter can complicate learning even though it is shared across actions.

The authors design algorithms with regret bounded by roughly d times the square root of T, up to logarithmic factors, for d-dimensional linear features over T rounds. Regret measures accumulated loss relative to better action choices. The bound matches the best known rate for the simpler setting without this confounding term and improves on the prior result identified in the abstract.

The algorithms use a new reward estimator inspired by doubly robust methods, supported by new concentration inequalities for self-normalized martingales. Empirical evaluations show better performance than prior approaches when rewards contain nonlinear confounding effects. Together, the theory and experiments show that the stated action-independent confounding structure can be handled without worsening the best known regret order.
summary.tldr: New contextual-bandit algorithms handle nonlinear action-independent confounding while matching the best known regret order for unconfounded linear bandits.

title: Semiparametric Contextual Bandits

abstract: We present a blended conditional gradient approach for minimizing a smooth convex function over a polytope P, combining the Frank{–}Wolfe algorithm (also called conditional gradient) with gradient-based steps, different from away steps and pairwise steps, but still achieving linear convergence for strongly convex functions, along with good practical performance. Our approach retains all favorable properties of conditional gradient algorithms, notably avoidance of projections onto P and maintenance of iterates as sparse convex combinations of a limited number of extreme points of P. The algorithm is lazy, making use of inexpensive inexact solutions of the linear programming subproblem that characterizes the conditional gradient approach. It decreases measures of optimality (primal and dual gaps) rapidly, both in the number of iterations and in wall-clock time, outperforming even the lazy conditional gradient algorithms of Braun et al. 2017. We also present a streamlined version of the algorithm that applies when P is the probability simplex.
originalAbstract: We present a blended conditional gradient approach for minimizing a smooth convex function over a polytope P, combining the Frank{–}Wolfe algorithm (also called conditional gradient) with gradient-based steps, different from away steps and pairwise steps, but still achieving linear convergence for strongly convex functions, along with good practical performance. Our approach retains all favorable properties of conditional gradient algorithms, notably avoidance of projections onto P and maintenance of iterates as sparse convex combinations of a limited number of extreme points of P. The algorithm is lazy, making use of inexpensive inexact solutions of the linear programming subproblem that characterizes the conditional gradient approach. It decreases measures of optimality (primal and dual gaps) rapidly, both in the number of iterations and in wall-clock time, outperforming even the lazy conditional gradient algorithms of Braun et al. 2017. We also present a streamlined version of the algorithm that applies when P is the probability simplex.

paragraphs: The paper addresses minimizing a smooth convex function over a polytope, a feasible region defined by flat boundaries. Its method blends Frank–Wolfe, also known as conditional gradient, with additional gradient-based steps. These added steps differ from away steps and pairwise steps, while the resulting algorithm retains linear convergence when the objective is strongly convex.

A practical attraction is that the algorithm avoids projecting points back onto the feasible region. It also represents each iterate as a sparse convex combination of a limited number of extreme points. Its lazy implementation uses inexpensive, inexact solutions to the linear programming subproblem that normally drives conditional gradient methods, reducing the need for costly exact work.

The authors report rapid reductions in both primal and dual gaps, which measure progress toward optimality, in iteration counts and elapsed time. Their comparisons outperform even the cited lazy conditional gradient methods. They also give a streamlined version for the probability simplex. The contribution combines these practical benefits with a convergence guarantee whose linear rate specifically requires strong convexity.
summary.tldr: Blending conditional gradients with gradient-based steps preserves sparse, projection-free optimization and achieves linear convergence for strongly convex objectives.

title: Blended Conditonal Gradients

abstract: We develop a framework of generalized multinomial models, which includes both the popular Plackett–Luce model and Bradley–Terry model as special cases. From a theoretical perspective, we prove that the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) under generalized multinomial models corresponds to the stationary distribution of an inhomogeneous Markov chain uniquely. Based on this property, we propose an iterative algorithm that is easy to implement and interpret, and is guaranteed to converge. Numerical experiments on synthetic data and real data demonstrate the advantages of our Markov chain based algorithm over existing ones. Our algorithm converges to the MLE with fewer iterations and at a faster convergence rate. The new algorithm is readily applicable to problems such as page ranking or sports ranking data.

paragraphs: This paper develops a common framework for generalized multinomial models used with ranking data. It includes the Plackett–Luce and Bradley–Terry models as special cases, bringing these established models into one treatment. The computational goal is to find the maximum likelihood estimate: the model parameters that best fit the observed data according to likelihood.

The key theoretical result connects that estimate uniquely to the stationary distribution of an inhomogeneous Markov chain. This converts the estimation problem into one with a useful Markov-chain interpretation. The authors use the connection to construct an iterative algorithm that they describe as straightforward to implement and interpret, with guaranteed convergence.

Experiments using synthetic and real data show advantages over existing algorithms: the proposed method reaches the maximum likelihood estimate in fewer iterations and at a faster convergence rate. The framework is readily applicable to page-ranking and sports-ranking problems. Its contribution combines a theoretical characterization of the estimator with a practical procedure for computing it more efficiently in the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: A Markov-chain characterization of ranking-model estimates yields a convergent iterative algorithm with faster convergence in reported experiments.

title: Fast Algorithm for Generalized Multinomial Models with Ranking Data

abstract: Machine-learned predictors, although achieving very good results for inputs resembling training data, cannot possibly provide perfect predictions in all situations. Still, decision-making systems that are based on such predictors need not only to benefit from good predictions but also to achieve a decent performance when the predictions are inadequate. In this paper, we propose a prediction setup for arbitrary metrical task systems (MTS) (e.g., caching, k-server and convex body chasing) and online matching on the line. We utilize results from the theory of online algorithms to show how to make the setup robust. Specifically for caching, we present an algorithm whose performance, as a function of the prediction error, is exponentially better than what is achievable for general MTS. Finally, we present an empirical evaluation of our methods on real world datasets, which suggests practicality.

paragraphs: Predictions can help systems make decisions before future requests are known, but their reliability can deteriorate on unfamiliar inputs. This paper studies online decision algorithms that can benefit from accurate advice while retaining reasonable performance when the advice is poor. Its setting includes problems governed by distances between possible system states.

The authors propose a prediction setup for arbitrary metrical task systems, covering examples such as caching, k-server, and convex body chasing. They also study online matching on a line. Results from online algorithm theory provide the basis for making the prediction setup robust, connecting learned advice with guarantees designed to handle unfavorable input sequences.

For caching specifically, the paper gives an algorithm whose dependence on prediction error is exponentially better than what can be achieved for general metrical task systems. This identifies a stronger opportunity within that particular problem. An evaluation using real-world datasets suggests the methods are practical, complementing the theoretical account of how performance responds to prediction quality.
summary.tldr: The paper develops robust prediction-assisted online algorithms, with especially strong prediction-error dependence for caching.

title: Online metric algorithms with untrusted predictions

abstract: The estimation of treatment effects is a pervasive problem in medicine. Existing methods for estimating treatment effects from longitudinal observational data assume that there are no hidden confounders, an assumption that is not testable in practice and, if it does not hold, leads to biased estimates. In this paper, we develop the Time Series Deconfounder, a method that leverages the assignment of multiple treatments over time to enable the estimation of treatment effects in the presence of multi-cause hidden confounders. The Time Series Deconfounder uses a novel recurrent neural network architecture with multitask output to build a factor model over time and infer latent variables that render the assigned treatments conditionally independent; then, it performs causal inference using these latent variables that act as substitutes for the multi-cause unobserved confounders. We provide a theoretical analysis for obtaining unbiased causal effects of time-varying exposures using the Time Series Deconfounder. Using both simulated and real data we show the effectiveness of our method in deconfounding the estimation of treatment responses over time.

paragraphs: Estimating treatment effects from longitudinal observations is difficult when unobserved factors influence both treatment assignment and outcomes. Existing methods commonly assume that such hidden confounders are absent. This paper develops the Time Series Deconfounder to address hidden confounders that affect multiple treatments, using patterns in treatment assignments over time.

The method builds a temporal factor model with a recurrent neural network and multitask outputs. It infers latent variables that make the assigned treatments conditionally independent. Those variables then enter causal inference as substitutes for the unobserved multi-cause confounders, connecting the treatment-assignment model to the estimation of treatment responses.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis for obtaining unbiased effects of time-varying exposures and demonstrate effectiveness on simulated and real data. The relevant scope is multi-cause hidden confounding, which supplies the shared assignment structure the method uses. The findings support recovering useful adjustment information from multiple treatment histories, with the theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations addressing how that information contributes to treatment-effect estimation over time.
summary.tldr: The Time Series Deconfounder infers latent adjustment variables from multiple treatment histories to address hidden multi-cause confounding.

title: Time Series Deconfounder: Estimating Treatment Effects over Time in the Presence of Hidden Confounders

abstract: As machine learning algorithms are increasingly deployed for high-impact automated decision making, ethical and increasingly also legal standards demand that they treat all individuals fairly, without discrimination based on their age, gender, race or other sensitive traits. In recent years much progress has been made on ensuring fairness and reducing bias in standard machine learning settings. Yet, for network embedding, with applications in vulnerable domains ranging from social network analysis to recommender systems, current options remain limited both in number and performance. We thus propose DeBayes: a conceptually elegant Bayesian method that is capable of learning debiased embeddings by using a biased prior. Our experiments show that these representations can then be used to perform link prediction that is significantly more fair in terms of popular metrics such as demographic parity and equalized opportunity.

paragraphs: Network embeddings represent entities in a network in a form that machine learning methods can use. Their applications include social network analysis and recommendation, where predictions can affect people. This paper addresses the limited options for reducing bias in these representations, particularly when sensitive traits such as age, gender, or race are relevant to concerns about discrimination.

The proposed method, DeBayes, takes a Bayesian approach to learning debiased embeddings. Its distinctive idea is to use a biased prior as part of that process. The prior therefore plays an explicit role in the debiasing method. The paper presents this as a way to obtain representations that can support fairer subsequent predictions about network connections.

Experiments evaluate the embeddings through link prediction and report significantly fairer results according to established measures, including demographic parity and equalized opportunity. Those findings concern the measured fairness of the resulting predictions. They support DeBayes as a useful approach to debiasing network representations, with the stated evidence centered on link prediction rather than every possible application of an embedding.
summary.tldr: DeBayes uses a biased Bayesian prior to learn network embeddings that yield fairer link predictions in the reported experiments.

title: DeBayes: a Bayesian Method for Debiasing Network Embeddings

abstract: Cross-domain alignment between two sets of entities (e.g., objects in an image, words in a sentence) is fundamental to both computer vision and natural language processing. Existing methods mainly focus on designing advanced attention mechanisms to simulate soft alignment, where no training signals are provided to explicitly encourage alignment. Plus, the learned attention matrices are often dense and difficult to interpret. We propose Graph Optimal Transport (GOT), a principled framework that builds upon recent advances in Optimal Transport (OT). In GOT, cross-domain alignment is formulated as a graph matching problem, by representing entities as a dynamically-constructed graph. Two types of OT distances are considered: (i) Wasserstein distance (WD) for node (entity) matching; and (ii) Gromov-Wasserstein distance (GWD) for edge (structure) matching. Both WD and GWD can be incorporated into existing neural network models, effectively acting as a drop-in regularizer. The inferred transport plan also yields sparse and self-normalized alignment, enhancing the interpretability of the learned model. Experiments show consistent outperformance of GOT over baselines across a wide range of tasks, including image-text retrieval, visual question answering, image captioning, machine translation, and text summarization.

paragraphs: Cross-domain alignment links entities from different kinds of data, such as image objects and sentence words. This paper argues that attention-based approaches often lack an explicit training signal for alignment and produce dense matrices that are difficult to interpret. Graph Optimal Transport supplies a direct alignment framework by treating the two entity sets as dynamically constructed graphs.

The method combines two kinds of matching. Wasserstein distance addresses correspondence between individual nodes, while Gromov-Wasserstein distance addresses correspondence between graph structures. These distances can be added to existing neural models as regularizers. The resulting transport plan supplies sparse, self-normalized alignments, making the inferred relationships easier to interpret than a dense set of attention weights.

The authors report consistent improvements over baselines in image-text retrieval, visual question answering, image captioning, machine translation, and text summarization. The common contribution across these applications is an explicit objective for aligning both entities and their relationships. This lets alignment influence training directly while also yielding a structured account of which elements are connected across domains.
summary.tldr: Graph Optimal Transport explicitly aligns entities and their relationships across domains, producing sparse alignments and improving several vision and language tasks.

title: Graph Optimal Transport for Cross-Domain Alignment

abstract: A fundamental challenge in contextual bandits is to develop flexible, general-purpose algorithms with computational requirements no worse than classical supervised learning tasks such as classification and regression. Algorithms based on regression have shown promising empirical success, but theoretical guarantees have remained elusive except in special cases. We provide the first universal and optimal reduction from contextual bandits to online regression. We show how to transform any oracle for online regression with a given value function class into an algorithm for contextual bandits with the induced policy class, with no overhead in runtime or memory requirements. We characterize the minimax rates for contextual bandits with general, potentially nonparametric function classes, and show that our algorithm is minimax optimal whenever the oracle obtains the optimal rate for regression. Compared to previous results, our algorithm requires no distributional assumptions beyond realizability, and works even when contexts are chosen adversarially.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits require a learner to choose actions using the information available in each context while learning from the rewards it observes. A central challenge is making this process as computationally manageable as supervised learning. Regression-based approaches had shown empirical promise, but broad theoretical guarantees were available only in special cases.

The paper provides a universal reduction that converts an online regression oracle into a contextual-bandit algorithm. Given a class of value functions for regression, the construction works with the policy class induced by those functions. The authors state that this conversion adds no runtime or memory overhead, connecting the practical computational demands of bandit learning directly to those of the regression oracle.

The authors also characterize minimax rates for general function classes, including potentially nonparametric ones. Their bandit algorithm achieves minimax optimality whenever its regression oracle achieves the optimal regression rate. The result requires realizability, but no further distributional assumptions, and allows adversarially selected contexts. Thus, the optimality guarantee is explicitly tied to both the modeling assumption and the quality of the regression oracle.
summary.tldr: An efficient reduction turns online regression into contextual-bandit learning, achieving minimax optimality when the regression oracle is optimal under realizability.

title: Beyond UCB: Optimal and Efficient Contextual Bandits with Regression Oracles

abstract: This paper is concerned with statistical estimation of two preferential attachment models: the Buckley-Osthus model and the block preferential attachment model. We prove that the maximum likelihood estimates for both models are consistent. We perform simulation studies to corroborate our theoretical findings. We also apply both models to study the evolution of a real-world network. A list of open problems are presented.
originalAbstract: This paper is concerned with statistical estimation of two preferential attachment models: the Buckley-Osthus model and the block preferential attachment model. We prove that the maximum likelihood estimates for both models are consistent. We perform simulation studies to corroborate our theoretical findings. We also apply both models to study the evolution of a real-world network. A list of open problems are presented.

paragraphs: This paper studies statistical estimation for two models of network growth: the Buckley-Osthus model and the block preferential attachment model. The focus is on learning model parameters from network observations. Estimation is the bridge between specifying a network model mathematically and using it to analyze an observed network.

The main theoretical result establishes consistency of maximum likelihood estimates for both models. Consistency means that, in the model's statistical setting, estimates approach the underlying parameters as the available information grows. It is an asymptotic reliability property, rather than a claim that estimates from every finite network are exact.

The authors conduct simulation studies that corroborate the theoretical findings and apply both models to the evolution of a real-world network. These components connect the estimation results to controlled experiments and an observed network history. The paper also presents open problems, placing its guarantees within an ongoing statistical investigation of these two preferential attachment models.
summary.tldr: The paper proves consistency of maximum likelihood estimation for two preferential attachment models and supports the results with simulations and a real-network application.

title: The Buckley-Osthus model and the block preferential attachment model: statistical analysis and application

abstract: We present three new algorithms for constructing differentially private synthetic data—a sanitized version of a sensitive dataset that approximately preserves the answers to a large collection of statistical queries. All three algorithms are \emph{oracle-efficient} in the sense that they are computationally efficient when given access to an optimization oracle. Such an oracle can be implemented using many existing (non-private) optimization tools such as sophisticated integer program solvers. While the accuracy of the synthetic data is contingent on the oracle’s optimization performance, the algorithms satisfy differential privacy even in the worst case. For all three algorithms, we provide theoretical guarantees for both accuracy and privacy. Through empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that our methods scale well with both the dimensionality of the data and the number of queries. Compared to the state-of-the-art method High-Dimensional Matrix Mechanism (McKenna et al. VLDB 2018), our algorithms provide better accuracy in the large workload and high privacy regime (corresponding to low privacy loss $\eps$).

paragraphs: Private synthetic data aims to replace a sensitive dataset with a sanitized version that approximately preserves answers to many statistical queries. This paper introduces three algorithms for that task. Each is computationally efficient when supplied with an optimization oracle, which can be implemented using existing non-private optimization tools such as integer programming solvers.

The paper separates the role of optimization quality from the privacy guarantee. How accurately the synthetic data preserves query answers depends on the oracle’s performance. Differential privacy, however, holds even in the worst case. The authors provide theoretical guarantees for accuracy and privacy for all three algorithms.

Empirical evaluations show good scaling as data dimensionality and the number of queries increase. In settings with large query workloads and strong privacy requirements, corresponding to small privacy-loss parameters, the methods outperform the High-Dimensional Matrix Mechanism in accuracy. The approach therefore offers a way to use powerful optimization software for private data release while retaining privacy protection independently of the optimizer’s success.
summary.tldr: Three private synthetic-data algorithms use optimization oracles to improve accuracy while guaranteeing privacy even when optimization performs poorly.

title: New Oracle-Efficient Algorithms for Private Synthetic Data Release

abstract: This paper builds on the connection between graph neural networks and traditional dynamical systems. We propose continuous graph neural networks (CGNN), which generalise existing graph neural networks with discrete dynamics in that they can be viewed as a specific discretisation scheme. The key idea is how to characterise the continuous dynamics of node representations, i.e. the derivatives of node representations, w.r.t. time.Inspired by existing diffusion-based methods on graphs (e.g. PageRank and epidemic models on social networks), we define the derivatives as a combination of the current node representations,the representations of neighbors, and the initial values of the nodes. We propose and analyse two possible dynamics on graphs{—}including each dimension of node representations (a.k.a. the feature channel) change independently or interact with each other{—}both with theoretical justification. The proposed continuous graph neural net-works are robust to over-smoothing and hence allow us to build deeper networks, which in turn are able to capture the long-range dependencies between nodes. Experimental results on the task of node classification demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach over competitive baselines.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks update node representations using information from the graph. This paper describes those updates through continuous dynamics, specifying how representations change with time. Existing networks with discrete updates can then be understood as particular discretizations of a broader continuous formulation.

Inspired by diffusion methods, the authors define each node's rate of change using its current representation, its neighbors' representations, and its initial values. They study two versions: one in which feature dimensions evolve independently and another in which those dimensions interact. Both versions receive theoretical analysis, making the choice of dynamics a central part of the architecture.

The proposed networks resist over-smoothing, the tendency for node representations to become too similar as information spreads. This allows deeper networks that can capture dependencies between more distant nodes. Node-classification experiments demonstrate effectiveness against competitive baselines. The contribution connects the design of graph updates to dynamical systems and uses that connection to address a concrete obstacle to learning from longer-range graph relationships.
summary.tldr: Continuous graph neural networks use theoretically analyzed dynamics to resist over-smoothing and capture longer-range node relationships.

title: Continuous Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Recent encoder-decoder approaches typically employ string decoders to convert images into serialized strings for image-to-markup. However, for tree-structured representational markup, string representations can hardly cope with the structural complexity. In this work, we first show via a set of toy problems that string decoders struggle to decode tree structures, especially as structural complexity increases, we then propose a tree-structured decoder that specifically aims at generating a tree-structured markup. Our decoders works sequentially, where at each step a child node and its parent node are simultaneously generated to form a sub-tree. This sub-tree is consequently used to construct the final tree structure in a recurrent manner. Key to the success of our tree decoder is twofold, (i) it strictly respects the parent-child relationship of trees, and (ii) it explicitly outputs trees as oppose to a linear string. Evaluated on both math formula recognition and chemical formula recognition, the proposed tree decoder is shown to greatly outperform strong string decoder baselines.

paragraphs: Converting an image into markup involves recovering both symbols and their organization. When the markup represents a tree, a decoder that produces a flat string must express that hierarchy indirectly. The paper first uses toy problems to show that string decoders struggle with tree structures, with difficulties becoming more pronounced as structural complexity increases.

The proposed decoder generates the tree explicitly. At each sequential step, it produces a child node together with its parent node, forming a small subtree. These subtrees are then incorporated recurrently into the developing output. This makes parent-child relationships part of the generation process itself, rather than information that must be recovered from a serialized sequence.

Evaluations on mathematical and chemical formula recognition show substantial improvements over strong string decoder baselines. The findings support matching the decoder’s output structure to the structure of the markup: explicitly maintaining tree relationships helps the model handle the organization that makes these recognition tasks difficult.
summary.tldr: An explicit tree decoder improves mathematical and chemical formula recognition by generating parent-child relationships directly.

title: A Tree-Structured Decoder for Image-to-Markup Generation

abstract: We examine the problem of causal response estimation for complex objects (e.g., text, images, genomics). In this setting, classical \emph{atomic} interventions are often not available (e.g., changes to characters, pixels, DNA base-pairs). Instead, we only have access to indirect or \emph{crude} interventions (e.g., enrolling in a writing program, modifying a scene, applying a gene therapy). In this work, we formalize this problem and provide an initial solution. Given a collection of candidate mediators, we propose (a) a two-step method for predicting the causal responses of crude interventions; and (b) a testing procedure to identify mediators of crude interventions. We demonstrate, on a range of simulated and real-world-inspired examples, that our approach allows us to efficiently estimate the effect of crude interventions with limited data from new treatment regimes.

paragraphs: For complex objects such as text, images, or genomes, available interventions may act indirectly. A writing program changes text through a broader process, just as a gene therapy can affect genetic material without providing isolated control over every component. This paper formalizes causal response estimation when these broader, crude interventions are the available actions.

Given a collection of candidate mediators, the authors propose a two-step method for predicting the causal responses to crude interventions. They also develop a testing procedure for identifying mediators of those interventions. These two components address related questions: what effect an intervention will have, and which candidate variables mediate its influence.

The approach is evaluated on simulated and real-world-inspired examples. Those demonstrations show efficient estimation of intervention effects using limited data from new treatment regimes. The contribution is presented as an initial solution to a practical causal problem: estimating the consequences of actions that operate on complex objects without assuming access to fine-grained interventions on their individual components.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes causal estimation for indirect interventions on complex objects and proposes methods to predict their effects and identify mediators.

title: Operationalizing Complex Causes: A Pragmatic View of Mediation

abstract: We consider the problem of training User Verification (UV) models in federated setup, where each user has access to the data of only one class and user embeddings cannot be shared with the server or other users. To address this problem, we propose Federated User Verification (FedUV), a framework in which users jointly learn a set of vectors and maximize the correlation of their instance embeddings with a secret linear combination of those vectors. We show that choosing the linear combinations from the codewords of an error-correcting code allows users to collaboratively train the model without revealing their embedding vectors. We present the experimental results for user verification with voice, face, and handwriting data and show that FedUV is on par with existing approaches, while not sharing the embeddings with other users or the server.

To address this problem, we propose Federated User Verification (FedUV), a framework in which users jointly learn a set of vectors and maximize the correlation of their instance embeddings with a secret linear combination of those vectors. We show that choosing the linear combinations from the codewords of an error-correcting code allows users to collaboratively train the model without revealing their embedding vectors. We present the experimental results for user verification with voice, face, and handwriting data and show that FedUV is on par with existing approaches, while not sharing the embeddings with other users or the server.

paragraphs: The paper addresses federated user verification under two explicit constraints: each user has examples from only one class, and user embeddings cannot be shared with either the server or other users. Embeddings are the model’s vector representations of examples. The challenge is to learn a verification model collaboratively while keeping those representations unshared.

Federated User Verification, or FedUV, has users jointly learn a collection of vectors. Each user trains their instance embeddings to correlate strongly with a secret linear combination of those shared vectors. The authors show that selecting these combinations from error-correcting codewords enables collaborative training without revealing the users’ embedding vectors.

Experiments evaluate verification using voice, face, and handwriting data. FedUV performs on par with existing approaches while maintaining the stated restriction on embedding sharing. The contribution is a way to organize the training objective around shared structure and private combinations, showing that competitive verification performance is possible in the evaluated setting despite each user’s restricted local data.
summary.tldr: FedUV uses secret combinations of jointly learned vectors to train competitive federated verification models without sharing user embeddings.

title: Federated Learning of User Verification Models Without Sharing Embeddings

abstract: Decentralization is a promising method of scaling up parallel machine learning systems. In this paper, we provide a tight lower bound on the iteration complexity for such methods in a stochastic non-convex setting. Our lower bound reveals a theoretical gap in known convergence rates of many existing decentralized training algorithms, such as D-PSGD. We prove by construction this lower bound is tight and achievable. Motivated by our insights, we further propose DeTAG, a practical gossip-style decentralized algorithm that achieves the lower bound with only a logarithm gap. Empirically, we compare DeTAG with other decentralized algorithms on image classification tasks, and we show DeTAG enjoys faster convergence compared to baselines, especially on unshuffled data and in sparse networks.

This paper studies the iteration complexity of decentralized methods in a stochastic, non-convex setting. It first establishes a lower bound that characterizes a fundamental requirement within that setting.

The bound reveals a gap in the known convergence rates of many existing algorithms, including D-PSGD. The authors then give a construction showing that the bound is achievable, establishing its tightness. This supplies a theoretical target against which decentralized training algorithms and their convergence guarantees can be assessed.

Guided by that analysis, the authors propose DeTAG, a practical gossip-style algorithm whose guarantee approaches the lower bound within a logarithmic gap. Image-classification experiments show faster convergence than the compared decentralized methods, especially with unshuffled data and sparse communication networks. The contribution combines an optimal-complexity characterization with a practical algorithm approaching it. The empirical results further indicate that the gains are particularly pronounced in the stated data and network conditions.
summary.tldr: A tight complexity bound motivates DeTAG, a decentralized training method that approaches the bound within a logarithmic gap.

title: Optimal Complexity in Decentralized Training

abstract: We propose to analyse the conditional distributional treatment effect (CoDiTE), which, in contrast to the more common conditional average treatment effect (CATE), is designed to encode a treatment’s distributional aspects beyond the mean. We first introduce a formal definition of the CoDiTE associated with a distance function between probability measures. Then we discuss the CoDiTE associated with the maximum mean discrepancy via kernel conditional mean embeddings, which, coupled with a hypothesis test, tells us whether there is any conditional distributional effect of the treatment. Finally, we investigate what kind of conditional distributional effect the treatment has, both in an exploratory manner via the conditional witness function, and in a quantitative manner via U-statistic regression, generalising the CATE to higher-order moments. Experiments on synthetic, semi-synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the merits of our approach.

paragraphs: A treatment’s average effect does not describe every way it can change outcomes. This paper studies conditional distributional treatment effects, which capture differences beyond the mean while accounting for conditioning information. Its starting point is a formal definition based on a distance between probability distributions, giving the broader question a mathematical target.

The authors then develop an instance based on maximum mean discrepancy, using kernel conditional mean embeddings to represent conditional distributions. Combined with a hypothesis test, this construction addresses whether there is evidence of a conditional distributional treatment effect. It separates detecting a difference from describing the particular form that difference takes.

To investigate that form, the paper offers two complementary tools. A conditional witness function supports exploratory analysis of distributional differences, while U-statistic regression quantifies effects involving higher-order moments, extending the familiar focus on conditional averages. Experiments with synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real datasets demonstrate the approach’s merits. Together, the components provide a framework for asking whether treatment changes an outcome distribution and then examining how it changes.
summary.tldr: The paper develops tools to detect and characterize conditional treatment effects beyond changes in average outcomes.

title: Conditional Distributional Treatment Effect with Kernel Conditional Mean Embeddings and U-Statistic Regression

abstract: We propose the k-Shortest-Path (k-SP) constraint: a novel constraint on the agent’s trajectory that improves the sample efficiency in sparse-reward MDPs. We show that any optimal policy necessarily satisfies the k-SP constraint. Notably, the k-SP constraint prevents the policy from exploring state-action pairs along the non-k-SP trajectories (e.g., going back and forth). However, in practice, excluding state-action pairs may hinder the convergence of RL algorithms. To overcome this, we propose a novel cost function that penalizes the policy violating SP constraint, instead of completely excluding it. Our numerical experiment in a tabular RL setting demonstrates that the SP-constraint can significantly reduce the trajectory space of policy. As a result, our constraint enables more sample efficient learning by suppressing redundant exploration and exploitation. Our experiments on MiniGrid, DeepMind Lab, Atari, and Fetch show that the proposed method significantly improves proximal policy optimization (PPO) and outperforms existing novelty-seeking exploration methods including count-based exploration even in continuous control tasks, indicating that it improves the sample efficiency by preventing the agent from taking redundant actions.

paragraphs: Sparse rewards leave reinforcement-learning agents with little guidance, making redundant actions especially costly. This paper proposes the k-Shortest-Path constraint on trajectories to suppress unnecessary behavior, such as repeatedly moving back and forth. The authors show that any optimal policy satisfies this constraint in the setting they study.

Applying the constraint as a strict exclusion rule would prevent exploration of state-action pairs on violating trajectories. However, that exclusion can interfere with the convergence of reinforcement-learning algorithms. The proposed practical approach instead introduces a cost that penalizes violations, allowing the constraint to guide learning without completely removing those possibilities.

A tabular experiment shows that the constraint can substantially reduce the trajectory space. Experiments on MiniGrid, DeepMind Lab, Atari, and Fetch report significant improvements to proximal policy optimization and better results than existing novelty-seeking methods, including count-based exploration. The findings extend to continuous control in the tested tasks. They support improving sample efficiency by reducing redundant exploration and exploitation, alongside the more familiar goal of seeking new experiences.
summary.tldr: Penalizing violations of a shortest-path constraint reduces redundant actions and improves sample efficiency in tested sparse-reward tasks.

title: Shortest-Path Constrained Reinforcement Learning for Sparse Reward Tasks

abstract: AlphaStar, the AI that reaches GrandMaster level in StarCraft II, is a remarkable milestone demonstrating what deep reinforcement learning can achieve in complex Real-Time Strategy (RTS) games. However, the complexities of the game, algorithms and systems, and especially the tremendous amount of computation needed are big obstacles for the community to conduct further research in this direction. We propose a deep reinforcement learning agent, StarCraft Commander (SCC). With order of magnitude less computation, it demonstrates top human performance defeating GrandMaster players in test matches and top professional players in a live event. Moreover, it shows strong robustness to various human strategies and discovers novel strategies unseen from human plays. In this paper, we’ll share the key insights and optimizations on efficient imitation learning and reinforcement learning for StarCraft II full game.

This paper introduces StarCraft Commander, or SCC, with efficiency as a central objective. It addresses the full game through improvements involving both imitation learning and reinforcement learning.

The authors report top-level human performance using an order of magnitude less computation than the demanding precedent motivating the work. SCC defeats GrandMaster players in test matches and top professional players at a live event. These results demonstrate strong play in the reported encounters while linking that performance to a substantially reduced computational requirement.

The agent also shows robustness against varied human strategies and discovers strategies not seen in human play. The paper presents key insights and optimizations behind its efficient training. Its contribution combines competitive gameplay with a reduction in the resources needed to obtain it, addressing one of the main obstacles that the authors identify for research on complex real-time strategy environments.
summary.tldr: SCC achieves top human-level StarCraft II performance with an order of magnitude less computation and efficient imitation and reinforcement learning.

title: SCC: an efficient deep reinforcement learning agent mastering the game of StarCraft II

abstract: In single-item auction design, it is well known due to Cremer and McLean that when bidders’ valuations are drawn from a correlated prior distribution, the auctioneer can extract full social surplus as revenue. However, in most real-world applications, the prior is usually unknown and can only be learned from historical data. In this work, we investigate the robustness of the optimal auction with correlated valuations via sample complexity analysis. We prove upper and lower bounds on the number of samples from the unknown prior required to learn a (1-epsilon)-approximately optimal auction. Our results reinforce the common belief that optimal correlated auctions are sensitive to the distribution parameters and hard to learn unless the prior distribution is well-behaved.

paragraphs: Auction design can exploit relationships between bidders’ valuations when their joint distribution is known. But practical auctioneers usually have historical observations instead of direct access to that distribution. This paper asks how much data is needed to learn a nearly optimal single-item auction when bidder valuations are correlated.

The authors analyze sample complexity: the number of observations from the unknown prior needed to achieve revenue within a factor of one minus epsilon of the optimum. They establish both upper and lower bounds. This examines the statistical demands of learning the auction, rather than treating the distribution of valuations as perfectly known from the outset.

The results reinforce the view that optimal auctions with correlated valuations can be sensitive to distribution parameters and difficult to learn unless the prior is well-behaved. The distinction matters because an auction’s theoretical revenue potential under a known prior does not by itself establish that historical data suffice to realize it. The paper makes that learning burden an explicit part of the analysis.
summary.tldr: Sample-complexity bounds show why nearly optimal auctions with correlated valuations can be difficult to learn from historical data.

title: Learning Optimal Auctions with Correlated Valuations from Samples

abstract: Model-agnostic meta learning (MAML) is currently one of the dominating approaches for few-shot meta-learning. Albeit its effectiveness, the optimization of MAML can be challenging due to the innate bilevel problem structure. Specifically, the loss landscape of MAML is much more complex with possibly more saddle points and local minimizers than its empirical risk minimization counterpart. To address this challenge, we leverage the recently invented sharpness-aware minimization and develop a sharpness-aware MAML approach that we term Sharp-MAML. We empirically demonstrate that Sharp-MAML and its computation-efficient variant can outperform the plain-vanilla MAML baseline (e.g., +3% accuracy on Mini-Imagenet). We complement the empirical study with the convergence rate analysis and the generalization bound of Sharp-MAML. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first empirical and theoretical study on sharpness-aware minimization in the context of bilevel learning.

paragraphs: Model-agnostic meta-learning, or MAML, trains models for adaptation from a small number of examples. Its optimization has two linked levels: learning within tasks and learning across tasks. This structure can produce a more complicated loss landscape than ordinary empirical risk minimization, potentially including more saddle points and local minima that make optimization challenging.

Sharp-MAML brings sharpness-aware minimization into this two-level setting. The approach makes the sharpness of the loss landscape part of the optimization strategy, addressing the difficulties associated with MAML’s structure. The paper also introduces a computation-efficient variant, so its investigation includes both the proposed method and a version designed to reduce computational demands.

Experiments show that Sharp-MAML and its efficient variant can outperform standard MAML, with a reported example of +3% accuracy on Mini-Imagenet. The authors complement these findings with a convergence-rate analysis and a generalization bound. Together, the contributions provide empirical and theoretical support for applying sharpness-aware optimization to bilevel learning, without implying that every task or training configuration receives the same improvement.
summary.tldr: Sharp-MAML applies sharpness-aware optimization to MAML, showing empirical gains alongside convergence and generalization analyses.

title: Sharp-MAML: Sharpness-Aware Model-Agnostic Meta Learning

abstract: When monitoring machine learning systems, two-sample tests of homogeneity form the foundation upon which existing approaches to drift detection build. They are used to test for evidence that the distribution underlying recent deployment data differs from that underlying the historical reference data. Often, however, various factors such as time-induced correlation mean that batches of recent deployment data are not expected to form an i.i.d. sample from the historical data distribution. Instead we may wish to test for differences in the distributions conditional on context that is permitted to change. To facilitate this we borrow machinery from the causal inference domain to develop a more general drift detection framework built upon a foundation of two-sample tests for conditional distributional treatment effects. We recommend a particular instantiation of the framework based on maximum conditional mean discrepancies. We then provide an empirical study demonstrating its effectiveness for various drift detection problems of practical interest, such as detecting drift in the distributions underlying subpopulations of data in a manner that is insensitive to their respective prevalences. The study additionally demonstrates applicability to ImageNet-scale vision problems.

paragraphs: Drift detectors typically compare recent deployment data with historical reference data to check whether their distributions differ. That comparison can be misleading when some changes are expected or permitted. For example, the proportions of different subpopulations may change even when the distribution within each subpopulation remains stable.

This paper reframes detection around distributions conditional on context. Instead of treating every difference between batches as relevant drift, it asks whether differences remain after accounting for context that may legitimately vary. The authors adapt tools from causal inference, using two-sample tests for conditional distributional treatment effects, and recommend an implementation based on maximum conditional mean discrepancies.

The empirical study demonstrates usefulness across several practical drift detection problems. In particular, the framework detects distribution changes within subpopulations while remaining insensitive to their relative prevalence. The authors also demonstrate applicability to ImageNet-scale vision tasks. These findings support monitoring that separates changes in the composition of incoming data from changes in the conditional distributions being monitored.
summary.tldr: Context-aware drift detection tests for distribution changes while accounting for contextual variation that is allowed to occur.

title: Context-Aware Drift Detection

abstract: Recent architectures for object detection adopt a Feature Pyramid Network as a backbone for deep feature extraction. Many works focus on the design of pyramid networks which produce richer feature representations. In this work, we opt to learn a dataset-specific architecture for Feature Pyramid Networks. With the proposed method, the network fuses features at multiple scales, it is efficient in terms of parameters and operations, and yields better results across a variety of tasks and datasets. Starting by a complex network, we adopt Variational Inference to prune redundant connections. Our model, integrated with standard detectors, outperforms the state-of-the-art feature fusion networks.

paragraphs: Feature Pyramid Networks combine features at multiple scales and are widely used in object-detection architectures. Much work focuses on manually designing richer pyramid structures. This paper instead learns a pyramid architecture specific to the dataset, making the arrangement of feature-fusion connections part of what the method learns.

The approach begins with a complex network and uses variational inference to prune redundant connections. The resulting network still fuses information across scales while improving efficiency in both parameter count and operations. Starting from a richer structure gives the method connections to select among as it learns which parts of the architecture to retain.

Integrated with standard detectors, the proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art feature-fusion networks in the reported evaluations. The authors also report improvements across a variety of tasks and datasets. These findings support learning the architecture of multiscale feature fusion through pruning, with efficiency and predictive performance evaluated together as outcomes of the same design process.
summary.tldr: Variational inference prunes a complex feature pyramid into a dataset-specific architecture that improves efficiency and reported detection performance.

title: Variational Feature Pyramid Networks

abstract: Group equivariance (e.g. SE(3) equivariance) is a critical physical symmetry in science, from classical and quantum physics to computational biology. It enables robust and accurate prediction under arbitrary reference transformations. In light of this, great efforts have been put on encoding this symmetry into deep neural networks, which has been shown to improve the generalization performance and data efficiency for downstream tasks. Constructing an equivariant neural network generally brings high computational costs to ensure expressiveness. Therefore, how to better trade-off the expressiveness and computational efficiency plays a core role in the design of the equivariant deep learning models. In this paper, we propose a framework to construct SE(3) equivariant graph neural networks that can approximate the geometric quantities efficiently. Inspired by differential geometry and physics, we introduce equivariant local complete frames to graph neural networks, such that tensor information at given orders can be projected onto the frames. The local frame is constructed to form an orthonormal basis that avoids direction degeneration and ensure completeness. Since the frames are built only by cross product operations, our method is computationally efficient. We evaluate our method on two tasks: Newton mechanics modeling and equilibrium molecule conformation generation. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves the best or competitive performance in two types of datasets.

paragraphs: Physical predictions should respond consistently when a scene is rotated or translated. SE(3) equivariance encodes that requirement in a model. Building expressive equivariant networks can be computationally expensive, so this paper studies how graph neural networks can represent geometric information efficiently while respecting these transformations.

The framework introduces complete local coordinate frames that themselves transform equivariantly. Each frame is an orthonormal basis, allowing tensor information of a given order to be projected onto it. The construction is designed to avoid losing directional information and to maintain completeness. Because the frames are built using cross-product operations, the authors present them as an efficient foundation for approximating geometric quantities.

The method is evaluated on modeling Newtonian mechanics and generating equilibrium molecular conformations. Across the two types of datasets, it achieves best or competitive performance. These results support local frames as a useful approach to balancing expressiveness and computation in geometric learning, with physical symmetry built directly into how the network represents information.
summary.tldr: Complete local coordinate frames provide an efficient way to build expressive graph networks that respect three-dimensional rotations and translations.

title: SE(3) Equivariant Graph Neural Networks with Complete Local Frames

abstract: Overparameterized neural networks enjoy great representation power on complex data, and more importantly yield sufficiently smooth output, which is crucial to their generalization and robustness. Most existing function approximation theories suggest that with sufficiently many parameters, neural networks can well approximate certain classes of functions in terms of the function value. The neural network themselves, however, can be highly nonsmooth. To bridge this gap, we take convolutional residual networks (ConvResNets) as an example, and prove that large ConvResNets can not only approximate a target function in terms of function value, but also exhibit sufficient first-order smoothness. Moreover, we extend our theory to approximating functions supported on a low-dimensional manifold. Our theory partially justifies the benefits of using deep and wide networks in practice. Numerical experiments on adversarial robust image classification are provided to support our theory.

paragraphs: Approximating a function accurately does not necessarily mean reproducing its smooth behavior. A neural network can give values close to the target while still changing sharply around those values. This paper studies that gap for convolutional residual networks, connecting their ability to represent functions with control over their first-order smoothness.

The authors prove that sufficiently large ConvResNets can approximate target function values while also meeting a first-order smoothness requirement. This strengthens the kind of approximation guarantee described in the abstract: the network's behavior between nearby inputs matters alongside the accuracy of its outputs. They also extend the analysis to functions supported on a low-dimensional manifold.

The results offer a partial theoretical explanation for the practical benefits of deep and wide networks. They concern what sufficiently large networks can represent, rather than establishing that every trained large network will be smooth or robust. Experiments involving adversarially robust image classification support the theory and connect its approximation perspective to a practical learning problem.
summary.tldr: Large convolutional residual networks can approximate function values while maintaining first-order smoothness, partially explaining benefits of overparameterization.

title: Benefits of Overparameterized Convolutional Residual Networks: Function Approximation under Smoothness Constraint

abstract: Incorporating symmetries can lead to highly data-efficient and generalizable models by defining equivalence classes of data samples related by transformations. However, characterizing how transformations act on input data is often difficult, limiting the applicability of equivariant models. We propose learning symmetric embedding networks (SENs) that encode an input space (e.g. images), where we do not know the effect of transformations (e.g. rotations), to a feature space that transforms in a known manner under these operations. This network can be trained end-to-end with an equivariant task network to learn an explicitly symmetric representation. We validate this approach in the context of equivariant transition models with 3 distinct forms of symmetry. Our experiments demonstrate that SENs facilitate the application of equivariant networks to data with complex symmetry representations. Moreover, doing so can yield improvements in accuracy and generalization relative to both fully-equivariant and non-equivariant baselines.
