paragraphs: Symmetry-aware models can share what they learn across examples related by transformations. Their use becomes difficult when the effect of a transformation on the input is hard to describe. For instance, a useful symmetry may exist even though its action on an image is not available in a convenient mathematical form.

The paper introduces symmetric embedding networks, or SENs, to bridge that gap. An SEN maps inputs into a feature space where transformations have a known action. It trains jointly with an equivariant task network, allowing the combined system to learn a representation with explicit symmetry while handling the more complicated input space.

The authors test this approach in transition models using three distinct forms of symmetry. Their experiments show that SENs make equivariant networks applicable to data with complex symmetry representations. They also find that the approach can improve accuracy and generalization relative to fully equivariant and non-equivariant alternatives. The contribution is a learned interface between difficult input transformations and structured models that can exploit symmetry.
summary.tldr: Symmetric embedding networks learn feature spaces with known transformation rules, enabling equivariant models to handle more complex inputs.

title: Learning Symmetric Embeddings for Equivariant World Models

abstract: We propose a method for training ordinary differential equations by using a control-theoretic Lyapunov condition for stability. Our approach, called LyaNet, is based on a novel Lyapunov loss formulation that encourages the inference dynamics to converge quickly to the correct prediction. Theoretically, we show that minimizing Lyapunov loss guarantees exponential convergence to the correct solution and enables a novel robustness guarantee. We also provide practical algorithms, including one that avoids the cost of backpropagating through a solver or using the adjoint method. Relative to standard Neural ODE training, we empirically find that LyaNet can offer improved prediction performance, faster convergence of inference dynamics, and improved adversarial robustness. Our code is available at https://github.com/ivandariojr/LyapunovLearning.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations make predictions through evolving dynamics. LyaNet trains those dynamics using a stability condition from control theory. Its Lyapunov loss encourages the inference trajectory to move quickly toward the correct prediction, making the behavior of the trajectory an explicit target of learning.

The authors prove that minimizing this loss guarantees exponential convergence to the correct solution and enables a robustness guarantee. Exponential convergence describes how quickly the dynamics approach the solution, so the theoretical result concerns the process of reaching a prediction as well as its destination. The paper also gives practical training algorithms, including one that avoids backpropagating through a differential-equation solver or using the adjoint method.

Compared with standard Neural ODE training, experiments find that LyaNet can improve predictive performance, accelerate convergence during inference, and increase adversarial robustness. These are reported empirical possibilities rather than universal improvements. The contribution connects a control-theoretic training objective, formal convergence behavior, and practical methods for learning the dynamics.
summary.tldr: LyaNet trains Neural ODEs with a Lyapunov loss that guarantees exponential convergence when minimized and can improve prediction, inference speed, and robustness.

title: LyaNet: A Lyapunov Framework for Training Neural ODEs

abstract: We study a nonparametric approach to Bayesian computation via feature means, where the expectation of prior features is updated to yield expected posterior features, based on regression from kernel or neural net features of the observations. All quantities involved in the Bayesian update are learned from observed data, making the method entirely model-free. The resulting algorithm is a novel instance of a kernel Bayes’ rule (KBR). Our approach is based on importance weighting, which results in superior numerical stability to the existing approach to KBR, which requires operator inversion. We show the convergence of the estimator using a novel consistency analysis on the importance weighting estimator in the infinity norm. We evaluate our KBR on challenging synthetic benchmarks, including a filtering problem with a state-space model involving high dimensional image observations. The proposed method yields uniformly better empirical performance than the existing KBR, and competitive performance with other competing methods. This paper represents that information through expected features: it updates prior feature averages into posterior feature averages. The method is a new form of kernel Bayes’ rule based on importance weighting. Across those experiments, the proposed method consistently outperforms the existing kernel Bayes’ rule and is competitive with other methods. The paper’s contribution combines a more stable way to perform feature-based Bayesian updates with a convergence result and empirical evidence on demanding observation spaces.
summary.tldr: Importance weighting yields a more numerically stable kernel Bayes’ rule, with estimator convergence and improved performance on the evaluated synthetic benchmarks.

title: Importance Weighted Kernel Bayes’ Rule

abstract: In this paper, we propose systematic and efficient gradient-based methods for both one-way and two-way partial AUC (pAUC) maximization that are applicable to deep learning. We propose new formulations of pAUC surrogate objectives by using the distributionally robust optimization (DRO) to define the loss for each individual positive data. We consider two formulations of DRO, one of which is based on conditional-value-at-risk (CVaR) that yields a non-smooth but exact estimator for pAUC, and another one is based on a KL divergence regularized DRO that yields an inexact but smooth (soft) estimator for pAUC. For both one-way and two-way pAUC maximization, we propose two algorithms and prove their convergence for optimizing their two formulations, respectively. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms for pAUC maximization for deep learning on various datasets.

paragraphs: The paper develops gradient-based methods for maximizing partial AUC in deep learning. It covers both one-way and two-way versions of the objective. Its central move is to formulate surrogate objectives through distributionally robust optimization, using that framework to define a loss for each individual positive example.

Two formulations offer different optimization properties. One uses conditional value at risk and yields an exact but non-smooth estimator of partial AUC. The other uses a KL-divergence-regularized robust objective and yields a smooth but inexact estimator. This makes the relationship between fidelity to the target quantity and smoothness of the optimization objective explicit.

The authors provide algorithms for the two formulations in both partial-AUC settings and establish convergence guarantees for optimizing them. These guarantees concern the proposed non-convex optimization procedures, without asserting that every run reaches a global optimum. Experiments on various datasets demonstrate the methods' effectiveness for deep learning, supporting the robust-optimization formulations as practical routes to partial-AUC maximization.
summary.tldr: Distributionally robust formulations enable gradient-based partial-AUC optimization with exact non-smooth or approximate smooth objectives and convergence guarantees.

title: When AUC meets DRO: Optimizing Partial AUC for Deep Learning with Non-Convex Convergence Guarantee

abstract: Finding the optimal pass sequence of compilation can lead to a significant reduction in program size. Prior works on compilation pass ordering have two major drawbacks. They either require an excessive budget (in terms of the number of compilation passes) at compile time or fail to generalize to unseen programs. In this work, instead of predicting passes sequentially, we directly learn a policy on the pass sequence space, which outperforms the default -Oz flag by an average of 4.5% over a large collection (4683) of unseen code repositories from diverse domains across 14 datasets. To achieve this, we first identify a small set (termed coreset) of pass sequences that generally optimize the size of most programs. Then, a policy is learned to pick the optimal sequences by predicting the normalized values of the pass sequences in the coreset. Our results demonstrate that existing human-designed compiler passes can be improved with a simple yet effective technique that leverages pass sequence space which contains dense rewards, while approaches operating on the individual pass space may suffer from issues of sparse reward, and do not generalize well to held-out programs from different domains. Website: https://rlcompopt.github.io.

paragraphs: The order of compiler optimization passes can substantially affect program size. Learning an effective ordering is difficult when methods require many passes during compilation or fail to transfer to unfamiliar programs. This paper approaches the problem by learning to choose whole pass sequences rather than predicting the next pass repeatedly.

The authors first identify a small collection of sequences, called a coreset, that generally reduce program size across many programs. A policy then predicts normalized values for the sequences in that collection and uses those predictions to select sequences. This organizes the decision around a compact set of complete alternatives.

Across 4,683 unseen code repositories from diverse domains and 14 datasets, the method improves on the default -Oz setting by an average of 4.5%. The authors connect its effectiveness to the denser rewards available in sequence space, while individual-pass approaches may face sparse rewards and poor cross-domain generalization. The results show that better selection and ordering can improve the use of existing human-designed compiler passes.
summary.tldr: Selecting among a small learned collection of compiler pass sequences improves program size over -Oz on diverse unseen repositories.

title: Learning Compiler Pass Orders using Coreset and Normalized Value Prediction

abstract: Bayesian inference offers principled tools to tackle many critical problems with modern neural networks such as poor calibration and generalization, and data inefficiency. However, scaling Bayesian inference to large architectures is challenging and requires restrictive approximations. Monte Carlo Dropout has been widely used as a relatively cheap way to approximate inference and estimate uncertainty with deep neural networks. Traditionally, the dropout mask is sampled independently from a fixed distribution. Recent research shows that the dropout mask can be seen as a latent variable, which can be inferred with variational inference. These methods face two important challenges: (a) the posterior distribution over masks can be highly multi-modal which can be difficult to approximate with standard variational inference and (b) it is not trivial to fully utilize sample-dependent information and correlation among dropout masks to improve posterior estimation. In this work, we propose GFlowOut to address these issues. GFlowOut leverages the recently proposed probabilistic framework of Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) to learn the posterior distribution over dropout masks. We empirically demonstrate that GFlowOut results in predictive distributions that generalize better to out-of-distribution data and provide uncertainty estimates which lead to better performance in downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo dropout provides a relatively inexpensive way to approximate Bayesian inference and estimate neural-network uncertainty. Traditional dropout draws masks independently from a fixed distribution. Treating masks as hidden variables to infer offers more flexibility, but learning their distribution introduces difficulties that simple variational approximations may struggle to handle.

The paper highlights two such difficulties. Many quite different masks can be plausible, giving the posterior distribution multiple modes. In addition, information specific to an input and correlations among masks are difficult to exploit fully. GFlowOut uses Generative Flow Networks to learn a posterior distribution over dropout masks and address these issues.

The reported experiments show predictive distributions that generalize better to data outside the training distribution. They also show that the resulting uncertainty estimates improve performance on downstream tasks. These are empirical findings about prediction and uncertainty quality, supporting learned mask distributions as a useful alternative to drawing every mask from the same fixed rule.
summary.tldr: GFlowOut learns dropout-mask distributions with Generative Flow Networks, improving reported out-of-distribution prediction and uncertainty-based downstream performance.

title: GFlowOut: Dropout with Generative Flow Networks

abstract: Deep graph clustering, which aims to group the nodes of a graph into disjoint clusters with deep neural networks, has achieved promising progress in recent years. However, the existing methods fail to scale to the large graph with million nodes. To solve this problem, a scalable deep graph clustering method (Dink-Net) is proposed with the idea of dilation and shrink. Firstly, by discriminating nodes, whether being corrupted by augmentations, representations are learned in a self-supervised manner. Meanwhile, the cluster centers are initialized as learnable neural parameters. Subsequently, the clustering distribution is optimized by minimizing the proposed cluster dilation loss and cluster shrink loss in an adversarial manner. By these settings, we unify the two-step clustering, i.e., representation learning and clustering optimization, into an end-to-end framework, guiding the network to learn clustering-friendly features. Besides, Dink-Net scales well to large graphs since the designed loss functions adopt the mini-batch data to optimize the clustering distribution even without performance drops. Both experimental results and theoretical analyses demonstrate the superiority of our method. Compared to the runner-up, Dink-Net achieves $9.62%$ NMI improvement on the ogbn-papers100M dataset with 111 million nodes and 1.6 billion edges. The source code is released: https://github.com/yueliu1999/Dink-Net. Besides, a collection (papers, codes, and datasets) of deep graph clustering is shared on GitHub https://github.com/yueliu1999/Awesome-Deep-Graph-Clustering.

paragraphs: Deep graph clustering groups graph nodes into separate clusters using learned representations. Scaling this process is difficult when graphs contain millions of nodes. Dink-Net addresses the problem by joining representation learning and cluster optimization in one end-to-end framework, so the features being learned are directly shaped by the clustering task.

The method first learns representations through a self-supervised task that distinguishes nodes corrupted by augmentations. Cluster centers are represented as learnable neural parameters. Two objectives, called cluster dilation and cluster shrink losses, then optimize the clustering distribution in an adversarial manner. Their design allows optimization using mini-batches rather than requiring the entire graph at once.

The paper reports that this mini-batch approach scales without performance degradation in its evaluations, supported by experiments and theoretical analysis. On ogbn-papers100M, containing 111 million nodes and 1.6 billion edges, Dink-Net achieves a reported 9.62% NMI improvement over the runner-up. The result connects the method’s scalability goal to clustering quality on a particularly large graph.
summary.tldr: Dink-Net combines representation learning and mini-batch cluster optimization to perform neural clustering on graphs with more than a hundred million nodes.

title: Dink-Net: Neural Clustering on Large Graphs

abstract: Dynamical systems with complex behaviours, e.g. immune system cells interacting with a pathogen, are commonly modelled by splitting the behaviour in different regimes, or modes , each with simpler dynamics, and then learn the switching behaviour from one mode to another. To achieve this, Switching Dynamical Systems (SDS) are a powerful tool that automatically discovers these modes and mode-switching behaviour from time series data. While effective, these methods focus on independent objects , where the modes of one object are independent of the modes of the other objects. In this paper, we focus on the more general interacting object setting for switching dynamical systems, where the per-object dynamics also depend on an unknown and dynamically changing subset of other objects and their modes. To this end, we propose a novel graph-based approach for switching dynamical systems, GRAph Switching dynamical Systems (GRASS), in which we use a dynamic graph to characterize interactions between objects and learn both intra-object and inter-object mode-switching behaviour. For benchmarking, we create two new datasets, a synthesized ODE-driven particles dataset and a real-world Salsa-couple dancing dataset. Experiments show that GRASS can consistently outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods. We will release code and data after acceptance.

paragraphs: Switching dynamical systems describe complicated behavior through simpler modes and transitions between those modes. Existing approaches can discover these patterns from time series, but commonly treat objects as independent: one object’s mode does not depend on the modes of others. That leaves out interactions that can shape how a system changes over time.

GRASS extends this setting to interacting objects whose dynamics depend on an unknown, changing subset of other objects and their modes. It uses a dynamic graph to represent those relationships. The model learns both switching within individual objects and switching behavior involving interactions between objects, making the changing relationships part of the modeling problem.

For evaluation, the authors introduce a synthetic particle dataset driven by ordinary differential equations and a real-world dataset of salsa couples dancing. Experiments report consistent improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods. The contribution is a way to learn changing behavioral modes together with changing interactions, rather than modeling each object’s transitions independently.
summary.tldr: GRASS uses a dynamic graph to learn behavioral modes and mode changes in systems of interacting objects.

title: Graph Switching Dynamical Systems

abstract: The entropic fictitious play (EFP) is a recently proposed algorithm that minimizes the sum of a convex functional and entropy in the space of measures — such an objective naturally arises in the optimization of a two-layer neural network in the mean-field regime. In this work, we provide a concise primal-dual analysis of EFP in the setting where the learning problem exhibits a finite-sum structure. We establish quantitative global convergence guarantees for both the continuous-time and discrete-time dynamics based on properties of a proximal Gibbs measure introduced in Nitanda et al. (2022). Furthermore, our primal-dual framework entails a memory-efficient particle-based implementation of the EFP update, and also suggests a connection to gradient boosting methods. We illustrate the efficiency of our novel implementation in experiments including neural network optimization and image synthesis.

paragraphs: Entropic fictitious play optimizes an objective defined over probability measures, combining a convex functional with an entropy term. Such objectives arise when studying two-layer neural networks in the mean-field regime. This paper examines the algorithm when the learning objective has a finite-sum structure, connecting its theoretical behavior to a more practical implementation.

The authors develop a primal-dual analysis using properties of a proximal Gibbs measure. They establish quantitative global convergence guarantees for both continuous-time dynamics and discrete updates. Covering both formulations connects an idealized evolution of the algorithm with the step-by-step process used in computation, within the finite-sum setting they analyze.

The same framework yields a memory-efficient implementation that represents the measure using particles. It also suggests a relationship with gradient boosting, connecting this optimization approach to another family of learning methods. Experiments involving neural-network optimization and image synthesis illustrate the implementation's efficiency. The contribution combines convergence analysis and an implementation strategy, showing how the mathematical formulation can inform the resources needed to run the algorithm.
summary.tldr: A primal-dual analysis gives entropic fictitious play global convergence guarantees and a memory-efficient particle implementation for finite-sum problems.

title: Primal and Dual Analysis of Entropic Fictitious Play for Finite-sum Problems

abstract: In this paper, we aim to optimize a contrastive loss with individualized temperatures in a principled manner. The common practice of using a global temperature parameter $\tau$ ignores the fact that “not all semantics are created equal", meaning that different anchor data may have different numbers of samples with similar semantics, especially when data exhibits long-tails. First, we propose a new robust contrastive loss inspired by distributionally robust optimization (DRO), providing us an intuition about the effect of $\tau$ and a mechanism for automatic temperature individualization. Then, we propose an efficient stochastic algorithm for optimizing the robust contrastive loss with a provable convergence guarantee without using large mini-batch sizes. Theoretical and experimental results show that our algorithm automatically learns a suitable $\tau$ for each sample. Specifically, samples with frequent semantics use large temperatures to keep local semantic structures, while samples with rare semantics use small temperatures to induce more separable features. Our method not only outperforms prior strong baselines (e.g., SimCLR, CLIP) on unimodal and bimodal tasks with larger improvements on imbalanced data but also is less sensitive to hyper-parameters. To our best knowledge, this is the first methodical approach to optimizing a contrastive loss with individualized temperatures. Our proposed algorithms are implemented in the LibAUC library at https://libauc.org.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning commonly uses one temperature parameter to control its loss across all training examples. This paper argues that a shared setting overlooks differences in how often similar meanings occur in the data. Those differences are particularly relevant for long-tailed datasets, where some semantic groups are common and others have relatively few examples.

The authors introduce a robust contrastive loss inspired by distributionally robust optimization. It supplies a mechanism for learning an individual temperature for each sample. They also develop an efficient stochastic optimization algorithm with a convergence guarantee that does not require large mini-batches. Theoretical and experimental results show the algorithm learning temperatures suited to different semantic frequencies.

Frequent semantics receive higher temperatures that preserve local semantic structure, while rare semantics receive lower temperatures that encourage more separable features. Experiments on unimodal and bimodal tasks outperform strong baselines including SimCLR and CLIP, with larger gains on imbalanced data and reduced hyperparameter sensitivity. The findings support adapting the contrastive objective to differences between examples.
summary.tldr: Automatically learning a temperature for each example improves contrastive learning, with especially strong gains on imbalanced data.

title: Not All Semantics are Created Equal: Contrastive Self-supervised Learning with Automatic Temperature Individualization

abstract: As previous representations for reinforcement learning cannot effectively incorporate a human-intuitive understanding of the 3D environment, they usually suffer from sub-optimal performances. In this paper, we present Semantic-aware Neural Radiance Fields for Reinforcement Learning (SNeRL), which jointly optimizes semantic-aware neural radiance fields (NeRF) with a convolutional encoder to learn 3D-aware neural implicit representation from multi-view images. We introduce 3D semantic and distilled feature fields in parallel to the RGB radiance fields in NeRF to learn semantic and object-centric representation for reinforcement learning. SNeRL outperforms not only previous pixel-based representations but also recent 3D-aware representations both in model-free and model-based reinforcement learning.

We introduce 3D semantic and distilled feature fields in parallel to the RGB radiance fields in NeRF to learn semantic and object-centric representation for reinforcement learning. SNeRL outperforms not only previous pixel-based representations but also recent 3D-aware representations both in model-free and model-based reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: An agent learning from images needs a useful representation of its environment. This paper focuses on representations that combine three-dimensional information with semantic and object-centered information. SNeRL learns such a representation from multiple views, aiming to address the weak incorporation of intuitive 3D understanding in previous reinforcement-learning representations.

The method jointly trains a convolutional encoder and semantic-aware neural radiance fields. Alongside the RGB radiance fields, it introduces fields for 3D semantics and distilled features. These parallel components allow the learned implicit representation to include semantic and object-related information together with the visual information represented by the radiance fields.

The reported comparisons show that SNeRL outperforms both earlier pixel-based representations and more recent 3D-aware representations in model-free and model-based reinforcement learning. Those results support enriching a 3D representation with semantic content for the evaluated learning settings. The key contribution is the joint representation-learning design, which brings multiple views, radiance information, semantic fields, and a convolutional encoder into one training approach.
summary.tldr: SNeRL combines semantic neural radiance fields and an image encoder to improve representations for model-free and model-based reinforcement learning.

title: SNeRL: Semantic-aware Neural Radiance Fields for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Typical machine learning applications always assume the data follows independent and identically distributed (IID) assumptions. In contrast, this assumption is frequently violated in real-world circumstances, leading to the Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization problem and a major drop in model robustness. To mitigate this issue, the invariant learning technique is leveraged to distinguish between spurious features and invariant features among all input features and to train the model purely on the basis of the invariant features. Numerous invariant learning strategies imply that the training data should contain domain information. Such information includes the environment index or auxiliary information acquired from prior knowledge. However, acquiring these information is typically impossible in practice. In this study, we present TIVA for environment-independent invariance learning, which requires no environment-specific information in training data. We discover and prove that, given certain mild data conditions, it is possible to train an environment partitioning policy based on attributes that are independent of the targets and then conduct invariant risk minimization. We examine our method in comparison to other baseline methods, which demonstrate superior performance and excellent robustness under OOD, using multiple benchmarks.

paragraphs: Models can lose robustness when deployment data differ from their training data. Invariant learning addresses this by trying to distinguish reliable features from spurious ones and learning from the reliable features. Many methods require environment labels or prior information about domains, which the authors identify as difficult to obtain in practice.

TIVA removes the requirement for environment-specific information in the training data. It learns a policy for partitioning environments using attributes independent of the targets, then performs invariant risk minimization. The authors prove that this strategy is possible under certain mild data conditions. The independence requirement and data conditions are part of the stated theoretical result.

Experiments on multiple benchmarks show better performance than the compared baselines and strong robustness under distribution shift. The contribution is therefore both methodological and conditional: it supplies a way to learn the partitions needed for invariant learning, along with a proof under stated conditions and empirical support for the resulting approach.
summary.tldr: TIVA learns environment partitions without supplied domain information and supports invariant learning under stated data conditions.

title: Provably Invariant Learning without Domain Information

abstract: Attribution methods shed light on the explainability of data-driven approaches such as deep learning models by uncovering the most influential features in a to-be-explained decision. While determining feature attributions via gradients delivers promising results, the internal access required for acquiring gradients can be impractical under safety concerns, thus limiting the applicability of gradient-based approaches. In response to such limited flexibility, this paper presents GEEX (gradient-estimation-based explanation), a method that produces gradient-like explanations through only query-level access. The proposed approach holds a set of fundamental properties for attribution methods, which are mathematically rigorously proved, ensuring the quality of its explanations. In addition to the theoretical analysis, with a focus on image data, the experimental results empirically demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over state-of-the-art black-box methods and its competitive performance compared to methods with full access.

paragraphs: Feature attribution methods aim to identify which parts of an input most influence a model's decision. Gradients can provide useful attribution signals, but computing them requires access to model internals. That access may be unavailable, including for safety-related reasons. GEEX is designed for the more restricted setting where an explainer can only submit queries and observe model outputs.

The method estimates gradients to produce gradient-like explanations through this query interface. This makes the access requirement central to the contribution: the explainer seeks information similar to that used by gradient-based methods without directly reading the model's internal derivatives. The authors also rigorously prove a set of fundamental attribution properties for the approach.

Experiments focus on image data and compare GEEX with both black-box methods and methods that have full model access. The paper reports superior results against state-of-the-art black-box alternatives and competitive performance against full-access methods. Together, the formal properties and image experiments support the usefulness of gradient estimation for explanations, without establishing universal equivalence to every white-box method.
summary.tldr: GEEX produces gradient-like feature explanations using only model queries, with proven attribution properties and competitive image results.

title: On Gradient-like Explanation under a Black-box Setting: When Black-box Explanations Become as Good as White-box

abstract: In this paper, we introduce MAAD, a novel, sample-efficient on-policy algorithm for Imitation Learning from Observations. MAAD utilizes a surrogate reward signal, which can be derived from various sources such as adversarial games, trajectory matching objectives, or optimal transport criteria. To compensate for the non-availability of expert actions, we rely on an inverse dynamics model that infers plausible actions distribution given the expert’s state-state transitions; we regularize the imitator’s policy by aligning it to the inferred action distribution. MAAD leads to significantly improved sample efficiency and stability. We demonstrate its effectiveness in a number of MuJoCo environments, both int the OpenAI Gym and the DeepMind Control Suite. We show that it requires considerable fewer interactions to achieve expert performance, outperforming current state-of-the-art on-policy methods. Remarkably, MAAD often stands out as the sole method capable of attaining expert performance levels, underscoring its simplicity and efficacy.

paragraphs: Imitation learning from observations must learn from expert behavior without seeing which actions the expert took. MAAD addresses this missing information using an inverse dynamics model. Given two successive expert states, this model infers a distribution over plausible actions that could explain the transition, providing an approximate action signal.

The learner is trained with a surrogate reward, which can come from adversarial games, trajectory matching, or optimal transport criteria. MAAD adds a regularizer that aligns the learner's policy with the inferred action distribution. The inferred distribution therefore complements the reward rather than serving as the only source of learning guidance.

The paper evaluates this on-policy algorithm in MuJoCo environments from OpenAI Gym and the DeepMind Control Suite. It reports greater stability and substantially improved sample efficiency relative to current state-of-the-art on-policy methods, requiring fewer environment interactions to reach expert performance. In many of the reported comparisons, MAAD alone reaches that level. The findings support using plausible action distributions to make observation-only imitation more effective in the tested environments.
summary.tldr: MAAD improves observation-only imitation by aligning the learner's policy with action distributions inferred from expert state transitions.

title: Mimicking Better by Matching the Approximate Action Distribution

abstract: Recent works have studied the design of algorithms for selecting representative sortition panels. However, the most central question remains unaddressed: Do these panels reflect the entire population’s opinion? We present a positive answer by adopting the concept of metric distortion from computational social choice, which aims to quantify how much a panel’s decision aligns with the ideal decision of the population when preferences and agents lie on a metric space. We show that uniform selection needs only logarithmically many agents in terms of the number of alternatives to achieve almost optimal distortion. We also show that Fair Greedy Capture, a selection algorithm introduced recently by Ebadian and Micha (2024), matches uniform selection’s guarantees of almost optimal distortion and also achieves constant ex-post distortion, ensuring a “best of both worlds” performance.

paragraphs: Selecting a representative panel raises a question beyond who gets a seat: how well will its decisions reflect the population’s preferences? This paper examines sortition panels using metric distortion, a concept from computational social choice. The analysis places agents and preferences in a metric space and measures how closely a panel’s decision approaches the population’s ideal decision.

The first result concerns uniform selection. The authors show that a panel containing only logarithmically many agents in the number of alternatives can achieve almost optimal distortion. This is a statement about decision quality within the metric model. It provides a positive answer to whether relatively small panels can make decisions that align well with the larger population.

The paper also analyzes Fair Greedy Capture, an existing selection algorithm. It matches uniform selection’s almost optimal distortion guarantees and additionally achieves constant ex-post distortion, a guarantee concerning the resulting panel. The combination matters because the algorithm supplies both kinds of protection rather than requiring a choice between them.
summary.tldr: Under a metric preference model, small randomly selected panels can achieve almost optimal decision distortion.

title: Can a Few Decide for Many? The Metric Distortion of Sortition

abstract: The Shapley value (SV) is a prevalent approach of allocating credit to machine learning (ML) entities to understand black box ML models. Enriching such interpretations with higher-order interactions is inevitable for complex systems, where the Shapley Interaction Index (SII) is a direct axiomatic extension of the SV. While it is well-known that the SV yields an optimal approximation of any game via a weighted least square (WLS) objective, an extension of this result to SII has been a long-standing open problem, which even led to the proposal of an alternative index. In this work, we characterize higher-order SII as a solution to a WLS problem, which constructs an optimal approximation via SII and k-Shapley values (k-SII). We prove this representation for the SV and pairwise SII and give empirically validated conjectures for higher orders. As a result, we propose KernelSHAP-IQ, a direct extension of KernelSHAP for SII, and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance for feature interactions.

paragraphs: Shapley values explain a model by allocating credit among its inputs or other contributing entities. Complex behavior also involves interactions: the contribution of several inputs together may not be captured by separate credits. The Shapley Interaction Index extends the Shapley-value framework to describe these joint effects.

For ordinary Shapley values, a known weighted least-squares formulation finds an optimal approximation to the underlying game. Extending that connection to Shapley interactions has been an open problem. This paper develops a weighted least-squares characterization that constructs approximations through the interaction index and k-Shapley values, providing an optimization route to richer explanations.

The strength of the mathematical evidence differs by interaction order. The authors prove the representation for ordinary Shapley values and pairwise interactions; for higher orders, they offer conjectures supported by empirical validation. The resulting KernelSHAP-IQ algorithm directly extends KernelSHAP to interaction estimation and demonstrates state-of-the-art feature-interaction performance. Its practical results accompany, but do not turn the higher-order conjectures into proofs.
summary.tldr: KernelSHAP-IQ estimates Shapley interactions through weighted least squares, with proofs for pairwise interactions and empirical support for higher-order conjectures.

title: KernelSHAP-IQ: Weighted Least Square Optimization for Shapley Interactions

abstract: We consider a cooperative learning scenario where a collection of networked agents with individually owned classifiers dynamically update their predictions, for the same classification task, through communication or observations of each other’s predictions. Clearly if highly influential vertices use erroneous classifiers, there will be a negative effect on the accuracy of all the agents in the network. We ask the following question: how can we optimally fix the prediction of a few classifiers so as maximize the overall accuracy in the entire network. To this end we consider an aggregate and an egalitarian objective function. We show a polynomial time algorithm for optimizing the aggregate objective function, and show that optimizing the egalitarian objective function is NP-hard. Furthermore, we develop approximation algorithms for the egalitarian improvement. The performance of all of our algorithms are guaranteed by mathematical analysis and backed by experiments on synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: In the setting studied here, networked agents each own a classifier for the same task and revise their predictions using what other agents communicate or predict. Errors can therefore spread through social influence. A highly influential agent with an inaccurate classifier may reduce accuracy across the network, making the placement of a limited number of corrections important.

The paper asks which classifiers should have their predictions fixed to obtain the greatest network-wide benefit. It considers two objectives: an aggregate objective concerned with overall accuracy and an egalitarian objective concerned with how improvements are distributed. Distinguishing them makes explicit that maximizing total benefit and pursuing a more egalitarian outcome are separate optimization goals.

The authors give a polynomial-time algorithm for the aggregate objective and prove that optimizing the egalitarian objective is NP-hard. They also develop approximation algorithms for egalitarian improvement. Mathematical analyses provide performance guarantees, while experiments on synthetic and real data support the algorithms. The results show how the chosen social objective changes the computational difficulty of targeted corrections.
summary.tldr: The paper develops algorithms for improving networked classifiers and shows that aggregate and egalitarian objectives have different computational difficulty.

title: Optimally Improving Cooperative Learning in a Social Setting

abstract: We propose a new procedure named PASOA, for Bayesian experimental design, that performs sequential design optimization by simultaneously providing accurate estimates of successive posterior distributions for parameter inference. The sequential design process is carried out via a contrastive estimation principle, using stochastic optimization and Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) samplers to maximise the Expected Information Gain (EIG). As larger information gains are obtained for larger distances between successive posterior distributions, this EIG objective may worsen classical SMC performance. To handle this issue, tempering is proposed to have both a large information gain and an accurate SMC sampling, that we show is crucial for performance. This novel combination of stochastic optimization and tempered SMC allows to jointly handle design optimization and parameter inference. We provide a proof that the obtained optimal design estimators benefit from some consistency property. Numerical experiments confirm the potential of the approach, which outperforms other recent existing procedures.

paragraphs: Bayesian experimental design chooses experiments to improve knowledge of unknown parameters. PASOA tackles two linked tasks: selecting the next design and accurately updating the posterior distribution after each step. It combines a contrastive estimation principle, stochastic optimization, and sequential Monte Carlo sampling to maximize expected information gain.

The difficulty is that informative experiments can move successive posterior distributions far apart. That movement can undermine ordinary sequential Monte Carlo, even though obtaining information is the design objective. PASOA uses tempering to handle the transition between distributions, aiming to preserve sampling accuracy while still selecting experiments with large information gains. The authors show that this component is crucial to performance.

The resulting procedure treats design optimization and parameter inference jointly, rather than assuming the posterior estimates will remain accurate automatically. The paper proves a consistency property for its optimal-design estimators. Numerical experiments demonstrate the approach's potential and report better performance than other recent procedures, supporting the combination of tempered sampling with stochastic design optimization.
summary.tldr: PASOA combines stochastic design optimization with tempered particle sampling to seek informative experiments while maintaining accurate posterior estimates.

title: PASOA- PArticle baSed Bayesian Optimal Adaptive design

abstract: Scene graph generation (SGG) is an important task in image understanding because it represents the relationships between objects in an image as a graph structure, making it possible to understand the semantic relationships between objects intuitively. Previous SGG studies used a message-passing neural networks (MPNN) to update features, which can effectively reflect information about surrounding objects. However, these studies have failed to reflect the co-occurrence of objects during SGG generation. In addition, they only addressed the long-tail problem of the training dataset from the perspectives of sampling and learning methods. To address these two problems, we propose CooK, which reflects the Co-occurrence Knowledge between objects, and the learnable term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-$l$-IDF) to solve the long-tail problem. We applied the proposed model to the SGG benchmark dataset, and the results showed a performance improvement of up to 3.8% compared with existing state-of-the-art models in SGGen subtask. The proposed method exhibits generalization ability from the results obtained, showing uniform performance improvement for all MPNN models.

paragraphs: Scene graph generation represents objects in an image and the relationships between them as a graph. Message-passing neural networks update object features using surrounding objects, but the paper identifies two gaps: insufficient use of object co-occurrence and an imbalanced training distribution with many rare cases.

The proposed strategy addresses these issues with two components. CooK incorporates knowledge about which objects occur together. A learnable term frequency–inverse document frequency mechanism, called TF-l-IDF, targets the long-tail distribution. This adds a frequency-based mechanism to approaches that previously addressed imbalance through sampling and learning methods.

On the scene graph generation benchmark, the authors report improvements of up to 3.8% over existing state-of-the-art models for the SGGen subtask. They also observe consistent improvements across the message-passing models evaluated, supporting the strategy’s applicability across those architectures. The findings suggest that explicitly representing co-occurrence and accounting for uneven frequencies can complement the neighborhood information already exchanged by message-passing networks.
summary.tldr: Object co-occurrence knowledge and learnable frequency weighting improve scene graph generation across the evaluated message-passing models.

title: Scene Graph Generation Strategy with Co-occurrence Knowledge and Learnable Term Frequency

abstract: One of the central problems of statistical learning theory is quantifying the generalization ability of learning algorithms within a probabilistic framework. Algorithmic stability is a powerful tool for deriving generalization bounds, however, it typically builds on a critical assumption that losses are bounded. In this paper, we relax this condition to unbounded loss functions with subweibull diameter. This gives new generalization bounds for algorithmic stability and also includes existing results of subgaussian and subexponential diameters as specific cases. Furthermore, we provide a refined stability analysis by developing generalization bounds which can be $\sqrt{n}$-times faster than the previous results, where $n$ is the sample size. Our main technical contribution is general concentration inequalities for subweibull random variables, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Generalization theory asks how reliably a learning algorithm’s performance on observed data carries over to new data. Algorithmic stability provides one way to study this question, but its usual analysis assumes that losses have a fixed upper bound. This paper extends that analysis to a broader setting in which losses can be unbounded.

The replacement condition is that the losses have a subweibull diameter, a probabilistic restriction governing their variability. Unbounded losses therefore remain subject to a specified tail condition. The resulting framework includes previously studied subgaussian and subexponential diameter conditions as special cases, bringing several forms of stability analysis into a common treatment.

The authors also refine the stability argument to obtain generalization bounds that can improve on earlier results by a factor of the square root of the sample size. This is a possible improvement under their analysis, rather than a universal rate for every learning problem. Their main technical contribution is a collection of concentration inequalities for subweibull random variables, which may also be useful beyond stability-based generalization.
summary.tldr: New stability bounds accommodate unbounded losses under subweibull conditions and can improve previous bounds by a square-root-of-sample-size factor.

title: Algorithmic Stability Unleashed: Generalization Bounds with Unbounded Losses

abstract: Various robust estimation methods or algorithms have been proposed to hedge against Byzantine failures in distributed learning. However, there is a lack of systematic approaches to provide theoretical guarantees of significance in detecting those Byzantine machines. In this paper, we develop a general detection procedure, ByMI, via error rate control to address this issue, which is applicable to many robust learning problems. The key idea is to apply the sample-splitting strategy on each worker machine to construct a score statistic integrated with a general robust estimation and then to utilize the symmetry property of those scores to derive a data-driven threshold. The proposed method is dimension insensitive and p-value free with the help of the symmetry property and can achieve false discovery rate control under mild conditions. Numerical experiments on both synthetic and real data validate the theoretical results and demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method on Byzantine machine identification.

In this paper, we develop a general detection procedure, ByMI, via error rate control to address this issue, which is applicable to many robust learning problems. The key idea is to apply the sample-splitting strategy on each worker machine to construct a score statistic integrated with a general robust estimation and then to utilize the symmetry property of those scores to derive a data-driven threshold. paragraphs: Distributed learning must sometimes operate despite worker machines that produce unreliable or adversarial outputs, known as Byzantine failures. Robust estimation methods aim to withstand these failures, but identifying which machines are responsible is a separate statistical problem. This paper develops ByMI to attach error-rate guarantees to that identification process.

ByMI splits the samples on each worker and uses the resulting pieces to construct a score statistic together with a general robust estimator. It then exploits symmetry in the scores to choose a detection threshold from the data. This symmetry-based construction avoids p-values, and the procedure is described as insensitive to dimension.

Under mild conditions, ByMI controls the false discovery rate: the expected proportion of incorrectly identified machines among those flagged. That guarantee does not require every individual identification to be correct. Experiments using synthetic and real data support the theoretical results and demonstrate effective identification. The procedure is designed to apply across many robust learning problems.
summary.tldr: ByMI identifies Byzantine workers using symmetry-based scores while controlling false discoveries under mild conditions.

title: ByMI: Byzantine Machine Identification with False Discovery Rate Control

abstract: We consider solving large scale nonconvex optimisation problems with nonnegativity constraints. Such problems arise frequently in machine learning, such as nonnegative least-squares, nonnegative matrix factorisation, as well as problems with sparsity-inducing regularisation. In such settings, first-order methods, despite their simplicity, can be prohibitively slow on ill-conditioned problems or become trapped near saddle regions, while most second-order alternatives involve non-trivially challenging subproblems. The two-metric projection framework, initially proposed by Bertsekas (1982), alleviates these issues and achieves the best of both worlds by combining projected gradient steps at the boundary of the feasible region with Newton steps in the interior in such a way that feasibility can be maintained by simple projection onto the nonnegative orthant. We develop extensions of the two-metric projection framework, which by inexactly solving the subproblems as well as employing non-positive curvature directions, are suitable for large scale and nonconvex settings. We obtain state-of-the-art convergence rates for various classes of non-convex problems and demonstrate competitive practical performance on a variety of problems.

paragraphs: The paper studies large nonconvex optimization problems whose variables must remain nonnegative. These include nonnegative least squares, matrix factorization, and some problems involving sparsity-inducing regularization. Simple gradient methods can progress slowly on ill-conditioned problems or linger near saddle regions, while methods using curvature often require difficult internal optimization steps.

The starting point is a two-metric projection framework. Near the boundary of the feasible region, it uses projected gradient steps; in the interior, it uses Newton steps. This division allows the method to use curvature information while preserving nonnegativity through a simple projection. The authors extend the framework by solving its subproblems approximately and incorporating directions of non-positive curvature.

These changes make the framework suitable for large-scale, nonconvex settings, where exact subproblem solutions can be demanding and saddle behavior matters. The authors establish state-of-the-art convergence rates for several classes of nonconvex problems and report competitive practical results across a variety of problems. The theoretical claims concern those problem classes, while the experiments demonstrate how the methods perform in practice.
summary.tldr: The paper extends projected Newton methods with approximate subproblem solutions and non-positive curvature directions for large nonconvex problems with nonnegative variables.

title: Inexact Newton-type Methods for Optimisation with Nonnegativity Constraints

abstract: This paper addresses the scarcity of large-scale datasets for accurate object-in-hand pose estimation, which is crucial for robotic in-hand manipulation within the "Perception-Planning-Control" paradigm. Specifically, we introduce VinT-6D, the first extensive multi-modal dataset integrating vision, touch, and proprioception, to enhance robotic manipulation. VinT-6D comprises 2 million VinT-Sim and 0.1 million VinT-Real entries, collected via simulations in Mujoco and Blender and a custom-designed real-world platform. This dataset is tailored for robotic hands, offering models with whole-hand tactile perception and high-quality, well-aligned data. To the best of our knowledge, the VinT-Real is the largest considering the collection difficulties in the real-world environment so it can bridge the gap of simulation to real compared to the previous works. Built upon VinT-6D, we present a benchmark method that shows significant improvements in performance by fusing multi-modal information. The project is available at https://VinT-6D.github.io/.

paragraphs: A robot manipulating an object within its hand needs to estimate the object's pose. This paper addresses the shortage of large datasets for that problem by introducing VinT-6D, which combines vision, touch, and proprioception. Together, these modalities provide visual information, contact information, and information about the robot's own configuration for learning object-in-hand perception.

The dataset contains two million simulated entries and 100,000 real entries. Simulation data come from Mujoco and Blender, while a custom platform collects the real-world component. The resource is tailored to robotic hands, includes whole-hand tactile perception, and emphasizes high-quality alignment between modalities. The authors describe the real component as the largest of its kind to their knowledge.

A benchmark method built on VinT-6D shows significant performance improvements from combining modalities. This supports the usefulness of integrating the available sensory information for pose estimation. The real-data component is also intended to help bridge simulation and real-world use. The main contribution is therefore both a substantial multimodal resource and evidence that its combined sensing channels improve the evaluated method.
summary.tldr: VinT-6D supplies aligned visual, tactile, and proprioceptive data for object-in-hand pose estimation, with a benchmark showing gains from combining modalities.

title: VinT-6D: A Large-Scale Object-in-hand Dataset from Vision, Touch and Proprioception

abstract: Selective classification enables models to make predictions only when they are sufficiently confident, aiming to enhance safety and reliability, which is important in high-stakes scenarios. Previous methods mainly use deep neural networks and focus on modifying the architecture of classification layers to enable the model to estimate the confidence of its prediction. This work provides a generalization bound for selective classification, disclosing that optimizing feature layers helps improve the performance of selective classification. Inspired by this theory, we propose to explicitly improve the selective classification model at the feature level for the first time, leading to a novel Confidence-aware Contrastive Learning method for Selective Classification, CCL-SC, which similarizes the features of homogeneous instances and differentiates the features of heterogeneous instances, with the strength controlled by the model’s confidence. The experimental results on typical datasets, i.e., CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CelebA, and ImageNet, show that CCL-SC achieves significantly lower selective risk than state-of-the-art methods, across almost all coverage degrees. Moreover, it can be combined with existing methods to bring further improvement.

paragraphs: Selective classification allows a model to decline predictions when its confidence is insufficient. Its goal is to improve reliability among the predictions it does make. While earlier approaches mainly modify the final classification layers to estimate confidence, this paper investigates how the learned feature representation can improve the decision to predict or abstain.

A generalization bound motivates optimizing the feature layers. The proposed method, Confidence-aware Contrastive Learning for Selective Classification, brings features of homogeneous instances closer together and pushes heterogeneous instances apart. The model’s confidence controls the strength of these adjustments. Confidence therefore influences how the representation is learned, rather than serving only as a threshold applied after classification.

On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CelebA, and ImageNet, the method achieves lower selective risk than state-of-the-art alternatives across almost all tested coverage levels. Coverage describes how often the model chooses to predict, so the result concerns reliability across different amounts of abstention. The method can also be combined with existing approaches to improve performance further.
summary.tldr: Confidence-aware feature learning improves the accuracy of predictions retained by selective classifiers across almost all tested coverage levels.

title: Confidence-aware Contrastive Learning for Selective Classification

abstract: Diffusion models exhibit powerful generative capabilities enabling noise mapping to data via reverse stochastic differential equations. However, in image restoration, the focus is on the mapping relationship from low-quality to high-quality images. Regarding this issue, we introduce the Generalized Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Bridge (GOUB) model. By leveraging the natural mean-reverting property of the generalized OU process and further eliminating the variance of its steady-state distribution through the Doob’s h–transform, we achieve diffusion mappings from point to point enabling the recovery of high-quality images from low-quality ones. Moreover, we unravel the fundamental mathematical essence shared by various bridge models, all of which are special instances of GOUB and empirically demonstrate the optimality of our proposed models. Additionally, we present the corresponding Mean-ODE model adept at capturing both pixel-level details and structural perceptions. Experimental outcomes showcase the state-of-the-art performance achieved by both models across diverse tasks, including inpainting, deraining, and super-resolution. Code is available at https://github.com/Hammour-steak/GOUB.

title: Image Restoration Through Generalized Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Bridge

abstract: Link prediction—a task of distinguishing actual hidden edges from random unconnected node pairs—is one of the quintessential tasks in graph machine learning. Despite being widely accepted as a universal benchmark and a downstream task for representation learning, the link prediction benchmark’s validity has rarely been questioned. Here, we show that the common edge sampling procedure in the link prediction task has an implicit bias toward high-degree nodes. This produces a highly skewed evaluation that favors methods overly dependent on node degree. In fact a “null” link prediction method based solely on node degree can yield nearly optimal performance in this setting. We propose a degree-corrected link prediction benchmark that offers a more reasonable assessment and better aligns with the performance on the recommendation task. Finally, we demonstrate that the degree-corrected benchmark can more effectively train graph machine-learning models by reducing overfitting to node degrees and facilitating the learning of relevant structures in graphs.

paragraphs: Link prediction evaluates whether a model can distinguish hidden graph edges from node pairs that are not connected. This paper questions a common way of constructing that evaluation. The authors show that the usual edge-sampling procedure implicitly favors high-degree nodes, meaning nodes with many connections receive a systematically different role in the benchmark.

That bias can reward methods that rely heavily on degree instead of learning richer graph structure. In the studied setting, a null method using node degree alone can achieve nearly optimal performance. The result matters because a strong benchmark score may partly reflect the sampling procedure rather than the structural understanding the benchmark is intended to measure.

The authors propose a degree-corrected benchmark that gives a more reasonable assessment and better matches performance on recommendation tasks. They also demonstrate benefits when using the corrected setup to train graph models. Reducing the incentive to overfit node degrees helps the models learn relevant graph structures, so the correction affects both evaluation quality and what training encourages.
summary.tldr: Common link-prediction sampling can reward degree-based shortcuts, while a degree-corrected benchmark improves assessment and encourages learning relevant graph structure.

title: Implicit degree bias in the link prediction task

abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular technique for interpreting language model activations, and there is extensive recent work on improving SAE effectiveness. However, most prior work evaluates progress using unsupervised proxy metrics with unclear practical relevance. We introduce SAEBench, a comprehensive evaluation suite that measures SAE performance across eight diverse metrics, spanning interpretability, feature disentanglement and practical applications like unlearning. To enable systematic comparison, we open-source a suite of over 200 SAEs across seven recently proposed SAE architectures and training algorithms. Our evaluation reveals that gains on proxy metrics do not reliably translate to better practical performance. For instance, while Matryoshka SAEs slightly underperform on existing proxy metrics, they substantially outperform other architectures on feature disentanglement metrics; moreover, this advantage grows with SAE scale. By providing a standardized framework for measuring progress in SAE development, SAEBench enables researchers to study scaling trends and make nuanced comparisons between different SAE architectures and training methodologies. Our interactive interface enables researchers to flexibly visualize relationships between metrics across hundreds of open-source SAEs at www.neuronpedia.org/sae-bench

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders are used to interpret language-model activations, but their progress is often measured with indirect, unsupervised metrics. This paper introduces SAEBench to examine whether improvements on those proxies correspond to better interpretability and practical usefulness. Its eight metrics cover interpretation, separation of features, and applications such as unlearning.

The authors release more than 200 sparse autoencoders spanning seven architectures and training algorithms, enabling systematic comparisons. Their evaluation finds that better proxy scores do not reliably imply better practical performance. For example, Matryoshka autoencoders score slightly worse on existing proxies but substantially better on feature disentanglement, with that advantage increasing as the autoencoders scale.

The benchmark makes these differences visible within a standardized evaluation framework. An interactive interface also supports exploring relationships among metrics across the released models. The contribution is a richer basis for judging architectural and training changes: a method’s strengths can vary by the property being measured, and scaling trends may look different when evaluation moves beyond the usual proxy objectives.
summary.tldr: SAEBench evaluates sparse autoencoders across eight metrics and shows that proxy improvements do not reliably predict practical gains.

title: SAEBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Sparse Autoencoders in Language Model Interpretability

abstract: Macro placement is a vital step in digital circuit design that defines the physical location of large collections of components, known as macros, on a 2D chip. Because key performance metrics of the chip are determined by the placement, optimizing it is crucial. Existing learning-based methods typically fall short because of their reliance on reinforcement learning (RL), which is slow and struggles to generalize, requiring online training on each new circuit. Instead, we train a diffusion model capable of placing new circuits zero-shot, using guided sampling in lieu of RL to optimize placement quality. To enable such models to train at scale, we designed a capable yet efficient architecture for the denoising model, and propose a novel algorithm to generate large synthetic datasets for pre-training. To allow zero-shot transfer to real circuits, we empirically study the design decisions of our dataset generation algorithm, and identify several key factors enabling generalization. When trained on our synthetic data, our models generate high-quality placements on unseen, realistic circuits, achieving competitive performance on placement benchmarks compared to state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Macro placement determines where large groups of components sit on a chip, making it an important influence on chip performance. Existing learning-based approaches often use reinforcement learning and require online training for each new circuit. This paper investigates a diffusion model that can produce placements for previously unseen circuits without that circuit-specific training.

The model uses guided sampling to improve placement quality during generation. To make training at scale feasible, the authors design an efficient denoising architecture and an algorithm for producing large synthetic training datasets. Synthetic data generation is a central part of the method because the learned placement behavior must transfer to realistic circuits.

The authors empirically examine dataset-generation choices and identify factors that enable this transfer. Models trained on their synthetic data produce high-quality placements on unseen realistic circuits and achieve competitive results against state-of-the-art placement methods. The contribution connects scalable synthetic training with zero-shot placement, showing that the evaluated circuits can be handled by a pretrained generator while sampling guidance directs the quality of its outputs.
summary.tldr: A diffusion model trained on synthetic circuits generates competitive macro placements for unseen realistic circuits without circuit-specific training.

title: Chip Placement with Diffusion Models

abstract: As Large Language Model (LLM) context windows expand, the necessity of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for integrating external knowledge is debated. Existing RAG vs. long-context (LC) LLM comparisons are often inconclusive due to benchmark limitations. We introduce LaRA, a novel benchmark with 2326 test cases across four QA tasks and three long context types, for rigorous evaluation. Our analysis of eleven LLMs reveals the optimal choice between RAG and LC depends on a complex interplay of model capabilities, context length, task type, and retrieval characteristics, offering actionable guidelines for practitioners. Our code and dataset is provided at:https://github.com/Alibaba-NLP/LaRA

paragraphs: As language models accept longer inputs, practitioners face a choice about how to supply external information: retrieve selected material or use a long-context model. Existing comparisons have left this choice unsettled, in part because their benchmarks provide limited evidence. LaRA introduces a benchmark designed to examine the decision across a broader set of conditions.

The benchmark contains 2,326 test cases spanning four question-answering tasks and three types of long context. The authors analyze eleven language models using this evaluation. This structure allows the comparison to consider differences among models, tasks, and context settings instead of treating retrieval and long-context processing as two options with a single fixed ranking.

The main finding is that the better choice depends jointly on model capabilities, context length, task type, and retrieval characteristics. The study offers practical guidelines based on those interactions. Its significance is the conditional nature of the result: larger context windows alone do not settle which approach is preferable, and the choice needs to reflect the particular information-processing task.
summary.tldr: LaRA finds that choosing between retrieval and long-context processing depends on the model, task, context length, and retrieval characteristics.

title: LaRA: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Long-Context LLMs – No Silver Bullet for LC or RAG Routing

abstract: Self-attention performs well in long context but has quadratic complexity. Existing RNN layers have linear complexity, but their performance in long context is limited by the expressive power of their hidden states. We present a practical framework for instantiating sequence modeling layers with linear complexity and expressive hidden states. The key idea is to make the hidden state a machine learning model itself, and the update rule a step of self-supervised learning. Since the hidden state is updated by training even on test sequences, our layers are called Test-Time Training (TTT) layers. We consider two instantiations: TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP, whose hidden state is a linear model and a two-layer MLP respectively. We evaluate our instantiations at the scale of 125M to 1.3B parameters, comparing with a strong Transformer and Mamba, a modern RNN. Similar to Transformer, TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP can keep reducing perplexity by conditioning on more tokens, while Mamba cannot after 16k context. TTT-MLP still faces challenges in memory I/O, but shows larger potential in long context, pointing to a promising direction for future research.

paragraphs: Self-attention handles long contexts effectively but has quadratic complexity, while recurrent layers offer linear complexity with less expressive hidden states. This paper proposes making the hidden state itself a machine learning model. Updating that state becomes a self-supervised learning step, allowing the sequence layer to adapt its internal model as it reads.

These Test-Time Training layers continue updating on test sequences, which gives the approach its name. The authors study TTT-Linear, whose state is a linear model, and TTT-MLP, whose state is a two-layer neural network. Both instantiate a framework intended to combine linear sequence-processing complexity with a richer form of recurrent memory.

Evaluations from 125 million to 1.3 billion parameters compare the layers with a strong Transformer and Mamba. Both TTT variants continue reducing perplexity with additional context, similarly to the Transformer, whereas Mamba stops benefiting beyond 16,000 tokens in these evaluations. TTT-MLP shows greater long-context potential but still encounters memory input/output challenges, distinguishing its modeling promise from its implementation efficiency.
summary.tldr: Test-Time Training layers use a learnable model as recurrent memory, enabling continued benefits from longer context with linear complexity.

title: Learning to (Learn at Test Time): RNNs with Expressive Hidden States

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) methods via joint embedding architectures have proven remarkably effective at capturing semantically rich representations with strong clustering properties, magically in the absence of label supervision. Despite this, few of them have explored leveraging these untapped properties to improve themselves. In this paper, we provide an evidence through various metrics that the encoder’s output encoding exhibits superior and more stable clustering properties compared to other components. Building on this insight, we propose a novel positive-feedback SSL method, termed Representation Self-Assignment (ReSA), which leverages the model’s clustering properties to promote learning in a self-guided manner. Extensive experiments on standard SSL benchmarks reveal that models pretrained with ReSA outperform other state-of-the-art SSL methods by a significant margin. Finally, we analyze how ReSA facilitates better clustering properties, demonstrating that it effectively enhances clustering performance at both fine-grained and coarse-grained levels, shaping representations that are inherently more structured and semantically meaningful.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning can produce representations that group semantically related examples despite receiving no class labels. This paper investigates how those clustering properties differ across components of joint embedding architectures. Using several metrics, the authors find that the encoder’s output has stronger and more stable clustering properties than the other components they examine.

They use that observation to develop Representation Self-Assignment, or ReSA. The method turns the model’s existing tendency to form clusters into guidance for further learning. Its positive-feedback design aims to strengthen useful representational structure through the structure already emerging in the model, making clustering an active learning resource rather than only a property measured after training.

On standard self-supervised-learning benchmarks, models pretrained with ReSA outperform other state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin. Further analysis reports improved clustering at both fine and coarse levels, meaning the benefits extend across different levels of grouping. Together, the findings connect where useful structure appears inside the architecture with a method for improving that structure during training.
summary.tldr: ReSA uses the encoder’s strong clustering structure to guide self-supervised learning, improving benchmark performance and clustering at multiple levels.

title: Clustering Properties of Self-Supervised Learning

abstract: Recent multi-modal audio-language models (ALMs) excel at text-audio retrieval but struggle with frame-wise audio understanding. Prior works use temporal-aware labels or unsupervised training to improve frame-wise capabilities, but they still lack fine-grained labeling capability to pinpoint when an event occurs. While traditional sound event detection models can precisely localize events, they are limited to pre-defined categories, making them ineffective for real-world scenarios with out-of-distribution events. In this work, we introduce FLAM, an open-vocabulary contrastive audio-language model capable of localizing specific sound events. FLAM employs a memory-efficient and calibrated frame-wise objective with logit adjustment to address spurious correlations, such as event dependencies and label imbalances during training. To enable frame-wise supervision, we leverage a large-scale dataset with diverse audio events, LLM-generated captions and simulation. Experimental results and case studies demonstrate that FLAM significantly improves the open-vocabulary localization capability while maintaining strong performance in global retrieval and downstream tasks.
