paragraphs: Finding an audio recording that matches a description is different from identifying exactly when the described sound occurs. Existing audio-language models are strong at retrieval but weaker at this fine-grained timing task. Traditional sound event detectors can locate events precisely, but their predefined categories restrict which sounds they can recognize.

FLAM combines audio-language matching with frame-wise sound localization in an open vocabulary setting. Its training objective operates at the frame level and is designed to be memory-efficient and calibrated. Logit adjustment addresses misleading training correlations, including events that tend to occur together and imbalances among labels. For frame-wise supervision, the work uses diverse audio events, language-model-generated captions, and simulation.

Experiments and case studies show significant improvements in open-vocabulary localization while maintaining strong global retrieval and downstream performance. This means the timing improvements do not come with a reported collapse in whole-recording understanding. The paper’s contribution is to train the model for both what a sound means and where it appears in time, beyond a fixed event-category list.
summary.tldr: FLAM improves open-vocabulary sound localization through calibrated frame-wise audio-language training while retaining strong retrieval performance.

title: FLAM: Frame-Wise Language-Audio Modeling

abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have significantly enhanced the ability of LLM-based systems to perform complex tasks through natural language processing and tool interaction. However, optimizing these LLM-based systems for specific tasks remains challenging, often requiring manual interventions like prompt engineering and hyperparameter tuning. Existing automatic optimization methods, such as textual feedback-based techniques (e.g., TextGrad), tend to focus on immediate feedback, analogous to using immediate derivatives in traditional numerical gradient descent. However, relying solely on such feedback can be limited when the adjustments made in response to this feedback are either too small or fluctuate irregularly, potentially slowing down or even stalling the optimization process. In this paper, we introduce $\textbf{REVOLVE}$, an optimization method that tracks how $\textbf{R}$esponses $\textbf{EVOLVE}$ across iterations in LLM systems. By focusing on the evolution of responses over time, REVOLVE enables more stable and effective optimization by making thoughtful, progressive adjustments at each step. Experiments across three tasks demonstrate the adaptability and efficiency of our proposal. Beyond its practical contributions, REVOLVE highlights a promising direction, where the rich knowledge from established optimization principles can be leveraged to enhance LLM systems, which paves the way for further advancements in this hybrid domain. Code is available at: https://llm-revolve.netlify.app.

paragraphs: Adapting a language-model system to a task often involves manual prompt changes and other tuning. Automatic methods can use textual feedback to guide those changes, but immediate feedback alone may produce adjustments that are too small or fluctuate irregularly. Such behavior can slow optimization or cause it to stall.

REVOLVE tracks how the system’s responses change across successive iterations. That response history guides progressive adjustments, extending the information available beyond the latest feedback. The paper connects this idea to established optimization principles: the course of previous changes can help inform the next update. The method is intended to make textual optimization more stable and effective.

Experiments across three tasks demonstrate REVOLVE’s adaptability and efficiency. The findings support response evolution as useful information for optimizing the evaluated language-model systems. The broader contribution is a way to connect textual feedback with a view of the optimization process over time, reducing reliance on isolated reactions to each iteration’s feedback.
summary.tldr: REVOLVE tracks changes in responses across iterations to guide more stable and effective optimization of language-model systems.

title: Revolve: Optimizing AI Systems by Tracking Response Evolution in Textual Optimization

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) using world models has found significant recent successes. However, when a sudden change to world mechanics or properties occurs then agent performance and reliability can dramatically decline. We refer to the sudden change in visual properties or state transitions as novelties. Implementing novelty detection within generated world model frameworks is a crucial task for protecting the agent when deployed. In this paper, we propose straightforward bounding approaches to incorporate novelty detection into world model RL agents by utilizing the misalignment of the world model’s hallucinated states and the true observed states as a novelty score. We provide effective approaches to detecting novelties in a distribution of transitions learned by an agent in a world model. Finally, we show the advantage of our work in a novel environment compared to traditional machine learning novelty detection methods as well as currently accepted RL-focused novelty detection algorithms.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents that use world models can perform poorly when the environment changes suddenly. The changes considered here include altered visual properties and altered rules for how states evolve. A model learned under earlier conditions may no longer describe the environment accurately, creating a need to detect novelty during deployment.

The paper uses disagreement between the world model's imagined states and the states actually observed by the agent as a novelty score. In this context, hallucinated states are the model's generated predictions. The proposed bounding approaches turn their misalignment with observations into a way to detect changes relative to the transition distribution the agent has learned.

The authors report effective novelty detection and an advantage in a novel environment over both traditional machine-learning detection methods and established reinforcement-learning approaches. The key idea is to draw detection evidence from predictions the world model already supplies. This connects novelty detection directly to whether the agent's learned account of the environment continues to match its experience.
summary.tldr: The method detects environmental novelty by measuring disagreement between a reinforcement-learning world model's predictions and observed states.

title: Novelty Detection in Reinforcement Learning with World Models

abstract: The peer review process in major artificial intelligence (AI) conferences faces unprecedented challenges with the surge of paper submissions (exceeding 10,000 submissions per venue), accompanied by growing concerns over review quality and reviewer responsibility. This position paper argues for **the need to transform the traditional one-way review system into a bi-directional feedback loop where authors evaluate review quality and reviewers earn formal accreditation, creating an accountability framework that promotes a sustainable, high-quality peer review system.** The current review system can be viewed as an interaction between three parties: the authors, reviewers, and system (i.e., conference), where we posit that all three parties share responsibility for the current problems. However, issues with authors can only be addressed through policy enforcement and detection tools, and ethical concerns can only be corrected through self-reflection. As such, this paper focuses on reforming reviewer accountability with systematic rewards through two key mechanisms: (1) a two-stage bi-directional review system that allows authors to evaluate reviews while minimizing retaliatory behavior, (2) a systematic reviewer reward system that incentivizes quality reviewing. We ask for the community's strong interest in these problems and the reforms that are needed to enhance the peer review process.

paragraphs: This position paper addresses pressure on AI conference peer review as submission volumes grow and concerns about review quality increase. The authors view the process as an interaction among authors, reviewers, and conferences, with responsibility shared across all three. Their proposed reform concentrates on making reviewers more accountable while recognizing and rewarding high-quality reviewing.

The first mechanism is a two-stage process in which authors can evaluate the reviews they receive. The intention is to create feedback in both directions while minimizing retaliation. The second mechanism is a systematic reward structure, including formal accreditation, that gives reviewers a reason to invest in useful, responsible assessments of submitted work.

These mechanisms connect information about review quality with incentives for improving it. The authors situate this focus alongside their view that author misconduct requires enforcement and detection, while ethical concerns also require self-reflection. The paper calls for community engagement with the reforms as a route toward sustainable peer review; it presents the design and its rationale rather than reporting a demonstrated conference-wide improvement.
summary.tldr: The authors propose author feedback on reviews and formal reviewer rewards to strengthen accountability in AI conference peer review.

title: Position: The AI Conference Peer Review Crisis Demands Author Feedback and Reviewer Rewards

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), with their event-driven and biologically inspired mechanisms, are well-suited for energy-efficient neuromorphic hardware. Neural coding, which is critical to SNNs, determines how information is represented via spikes. While Time-to-First-Spike (TTFS) coding uses a single spike per neuron to offer extreme sparsity and energy efficiency, it often suffers from unstable training and low accuracy due to its sparse firing. To address these challenges, we propose a training framework that incorporates parameter initialization, training normalization, a temporal output decoder, and a re-evaluation of the pooling layer. The proposed parameter initialization and training normalization mitigate signal diminishing and gradient vanishing, which helps stabilize training. Our output decoder aggregates temporal spikes to encourage earlier firing, thereby reducing latency. The re-evaluation of the pooling layer demonstrates that max-pooling violates single-spike constraints, which should be avoided, whereas average-pooling preserves them. Experiments show that our framework stabilizes and accelerates training, reduces latency, and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy for step-by-step TTFS SNNs on MNIST ($99.48%$), Fashion-MNIST ($92.90%$), CIFAR10 ($90.56%$), CIFAR100 ($70.27%$) and DVS Gesture ($95.83%$).

abstract: Operator splitting algorithms are a cornerstone of modern first-order optimization, decomposing complex problems into simpler subproblems solved via proximal operators. However, most functions lack closed-form proximal operators, which has long restricted these methods to a narrow set of problems. Hamilton-Jacobi-based proximal operator (HJ-Prox) is a recent derivative-free Monte Carlo technique based on Hamilton-Jacobi PDE theory, that approximates proximal operators numerically. In this work, we introduce a unified framework for operator splitting via HJ-Prox, which allows for deployment of operator splitting even when functions are not proximable. We prove that replacing exact proximal steps with HJ-Prox in algorithms such as proximal point, proximal gradient descent, Douglas–Rachford splitting, Davis–Yin splitting, and primal–dual hybrid gradient preserves convergence guarantees under mild assumptions. Numerical experiments demonstrate HJ-Prox is competitive and effective on a wide variety of statistical learning tasks.

This paper studies how numerical approximations can fill that gap while retaining convergence guarantees for the surrounding optimization algorithm.

The approximation is HJ-Prox, a derivative-free Monte Carlo method derived from Hamilton–Jacobi partial differential equation theory. The authors place it inside a unified operator-splitting framework. This permits approximate proximal steps for functions that are not directly proximable, extending the range of problems to which these methods can be applied.

Under assumptions described as mild, the paper proves convergence is preserved for several algorithms, including proximal point, proximal gradient descent, Douglas–Rachford, Davis–Yin, and primal–dual hybrid gradient. Numerical experiments report competitive and effective performance across statistical learning tasks. The central result is that using sampled numerical proximal approximations can be theoretically justified across multiple splitting schemes, provided the relevant assumptions hold.
summary.tldr: A unified framework uses HJ-Prox numerical approximations to extend operator splitting while preserving convergence under stated assumptions.

title: Operator Splitting with Hamilton-Jacobi-based Proximals

abstract: Modeling decision-making outside of controlled environments requires accounting for asynchronous, exogenous signals, such as notifications or algorithmic feeds, that dynamically alter user response times. Standard Drift-Diffusion Models (DDM) become analytically intractable when drift rates vary continuously with time. In this paper, we derive a closed-form analytical approximation for the first-passage time distribution of a single-boundary DDM with time-dependent drift, valid in the high-threshold regime. The main result allows us to analytically study the optimal timing of external signals to maximize the probability of a user response within our approximation framework. To evaluate our response time model, we conduct an extensive empirical comparison with state-of-the-art methods for user watch-time prediction and evaluation in simulated environments.

paragraphs: User decisions outside controlled experiments can be influenced by notifications, feeds, and other signals arriving at different times. A drift-diffusion model describes a decision process that progresses toward a response threshold, but these external influences make its drift vary over time. The resulting response-time distribution is difficult to handle analytically using standard formulations.

The paper derives a closed-form approximation for the first-passage time distribution: the distribution of times at which the process first reaches its response boundary. Its result applies to a single-boundary model with time-dependent drift in the high-threshold regime. These conditions matter because the analytical expression is an approximation for that setting, rather than an unrestricted solution for all drift-diffusion models.

The expression lets the authors analytically examine when an external signal should arrive to maximize response probability within their approximation framework. They also evaluate the response-time model through comparisons with state-of-the-art user watch-time prediction methods and simulated environments. The abstract describes this evaluation but does not state a comparative outcome; the explicit contribution is a tractable way to connect changing external signals with response timing.
summary.tldr: A high-threshold approximation makes time-dependent drift-diffusion response models analytically usable for studying the timing of external signals.

title: Approximating Drift-Diffusion Models for User Decisions under Nudging and External Information

abstract: Deep neural networks frequently exhibit overconfidence, undermining reliability in safety-critical applications. Existing adaptive methods rely on indirectly learned proxies of sample difficulty. We establish the logit margin as a direct and principled hardness indicator. We prove that margin constrains the feasible temperature range for a target confidence. Empirically, margin strongly correlates with decision boundary proximity and reveals systematic calibration patterns across difficulty levels. We further identify a fundamental flaw in NLL-based optimization: minimizing NLL can paradoxically worsen calibration. To address this, we introduce Charbonnier-SoftECE, a smooth objective that provably upper-bounds the smooth calibration error (smCE). Building on these insights, we propose SMART (Sample Margin-Aware Recalibration of Temperature), a lightweight method that learns a sample-wise margin-to-temperature mapping guided by our calibration-centric objective. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art calibration across CNNs and ViTs on standard, long-tailed, and distribution-shifted benchmarks, with minimal inference-time overhead. Code is available at: https://github.com/Misakaaaaaz/ICML2026-SMART.

paragraphs: A classifier's confidence can be poorly matched to how often it is correct. SMART addresses this calibration problem by making temperature adjustment depend on each sample's logit margin. The paper establishes margin as a direct indicator of sample difficulty and proves that it constrains which temperatures can produce a target confidence.

Empirically, margin correlates strongly with proximity to the decision boundary and reveals systematic calibration differences across difficulty levels. The authors also show that optimizing negative log-likelihood can worsen calibration. They introduce Charbonnier-SoftECE, a smooth objective with a proven upper bound on smooth calibration error, to focus optimization more directly on the desired confidence behavior.

SMART learns a lightweight mapping from sample margin to temperature using that objective. Experiments report state-of-the-art calibration across convolutional networks and vision transformers on standard, long-tailed, and distribution-shifted benchmarks, with minimal inference overhead. The findings connect a theoretically motivated difficulty signal with an objective aligned to calibration, rather than assuming that better likelihood automatically produces better-calibrated confidence.
summary.tldr: SMART calibrates predictions with sample-specific temperatures learned from logit margins and an objective that directly targets calibration error.

title: Sample Margin-Aware Recalibration of Temperature Scaling

abstract: Large language models allocate uniform computation across all tokens, ignoring that some sequences are trivially predictable while others require deep reasoning. We introduce ConceptMoE, which dynamically merges semantically similar tokens into concepts through learnable chunking at target compression ratio $R$. The MoE architecture enables controlled evaluation: reallocating saved computation to match baseline FLOPs and parameters isolates genuine architectural benefits. ConceptMoE consistently outperforms standard MoE, achieving +0.9 points on language pretraining, +2.3 on long context, and +0.6 on multimodal tasks. Continual training conversion with layer looping gains +5.5 points. Beyond performance, at $R=2$, ConceptMoE reduces attention computation by $R^2\times$ and KV cache by $R\times$, delivering prefill speedups up to 175% and decoding speedups up to 117%. The minimal architectural changes enable straightforward integration, demonstrating that adaptive concept-level processing fundamentally improves LLM effectiveness and efficiency.

The method learns to group semantically similar tokens into larger units called concepts, with a target compression ratio controlling how much the sequence is shortened.

The authors use a mixture-of-experts architecture to examine whether this change helps independently of model size or total computation. They redistribute the computation saved by compression so that comparisons match baseline FLOPs and parameter counts. This makes the evaluation informative about the architecture itself, rather than simply about spending more resources.

summary.tldr: ConceptMoE learns to compress tokens into concepts, improving reported task performance while reducing attention and cache costs.

title: ConceptMoE: Adaptive Token-to-Concept Compression for Implicit Compute Allocation

abstract: Compositional data analysis has gained increased attention due to the widespread occurrence of simplex-valued data, including microbiome data and financial portfolios. Existing compositional two-sample tests often require $\log$-transformations and only detect mean differences, motivating the need for a more general framework without relying on $\log$-based methods. There is a close connection between compositional data and directional statistics, and we construct a unified non-parametric two-sample test framework. Our work is based on a studentized energy statistic constructed from spherical harmonics theory over a fixed dimensional underlying space, incorporating U-statistics theory and recent developments of studentization for both compositional and directional data. We establish asymptotic normality for our spherical harmonics based test statistics, thus avoiding the need for permutation tests or bootstrap procedures. Our proposed framework sheds new light on the connections between Non-Euclidean data analysis and classical asymptotic high-dimensional data techniques.

paragraphs: Comparing two groups becomes more complicated when observations are compositions or directions. Compositions represent parts of a whole, as in microbiome proportions or portfolio allocations. Their geometry differs from that of unrestricted numerical vectors. The paper seeks a common testing framework for compositional and directional data without depending on logarithmic transformations or restricting attention to mean differences.

The proposed test combines an energy statistic with spherical harmonics, mathematical functions suited to spherical geometry. It then studentizes the statistic, scaling it to account for variability. The construction draws on U-statistics theory and recent studentization methods, working in an underlying space whose dimension is fixed.

The authors establish that their test statistics approach a normal distribution asymptotically. This supplies a route to statistical calibration without permutation tests or bootstrap procedures. The result matters because it links geometry-aware comparisons to familiar asymptotic inference. Its stated justification is an asymptotic one, within the fixed-dimensional framework, and the broader contribution is a unified approach to two kinds of non-Euclidean observations.
summary.tldr: A geometry-aware two-sample test unifies compositional and directional data analysis and uses asymptotic normality to avoid resampling-based calibration.

title: A Studentized Spherical Harmonics–Based Nonparametric Two-Sample Test for Compositional and Directional Data

abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has shifted time series analysis from narrow analytics to general-purpose reasoning. Yet, existing benchmarks cover only a small set of health time series modalities and tasks, failing to reflect the diverse domains and extensive temporal dependencies inherent in real-world physiological modeling. To bridge these gaps, we introduce HEARTS (Health Reasoning over Time Series), a unified benchmark for evaluating hierarchical reasoning capabilities of LLMs over general health time series. HEARTS integrates 16 real-world datasets across 12 health domains and 20 signal modalities, and defines a comprehensive taxonomy of 110 tasks grouped into four core capabilities: Perception, Inference, Generation, and Deduction. Evaluating 14 state-of-the-art LLMs on more than 20K test samples reveals intriguing findings. First, LLMs substantially underperform specialized models, and their performance is only weakly related to general reasoning scores. Moreover, LLMs often rely on simple heuristics and struggle with multi-step temporal reasoning. Finally, performance declines with increasing temporal complexity, with similar failure modes within model families, indicating that scaling alone is insufficient. By making these gaps measurable, HEARTS provides a standardized testbed and living benchmark for developing next-generation LLM agents capable of reasoning over diverse health signals.

summary.tldr: HEARTS benchmarks diverse health time-series reasoning and finds major gaps between general-purpose language models and specialized models.

title: HEARTS: Benchmarking LLM Reasoning on Health Time Series

abstract: Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) is a fundamental NP-hard problem that has garnered significant attention from both academia and industry. The Branch-and-Bound (B&B) algorithm is the dominant approach for solving MILPs, where branching decisions play a critical role and have recently been enhanced by neural methods. However, these methods still struggle with semantic variation across depths, the scarcity of upstream nodes, and the costly collection of strong branching samples. To address these issues, we propose SC-MILP, a Dynamic Stratified Contrastive Training Framework for MILP Branching. Our method groups B&B nodes based on their feature distributions and learns depth-aware, fine-grained node representations through dynamic stratified contrastive training. To address data scarcity and imbalance at upstream nodes, we introduce an upstream-augmented MILP derivation procedure that generates both theoretically equivalent and perturbed instances. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world MILP benchmarks, including large-scale instances, show that SC-MILP significantly improves branching accuracy, reduces solving time, with particularly strong gains at upstream nodes.

paragraphs: Mixed integer linear programs are commonly solved with branch-and-bound, where branching choices strongly affect the search. Neural branching methods must interpret nodes at different depths, even though node meaning and feature distributions vary across the tree. Training also faces a shortage of upstream nodes and expensive strong-branching examples.

SC-MILP addresses these difficulties through dynamic grouping and targeted data augmentation. It groups nodes according to their feature distributions, then uses stratified contrastive training to learn detailed representations sensitive to search depth. This makes the representation-learning process account for variation among nodes rather than treating all training examples as interchangeable.

An upstream augmentation procedure generates both theoretically equivalent and perturbed MILP instances to address the scarcity and imbalance of early-tree training data. Experiments cover synthetic and real-world benchmarks, including large problems, and report better branching accuracy and shorter solving times. Gains are particularly strong at upstream nodes. The results connect improved training coverage and depth-sensitive representations with more effective branching decisions during optimization.
summary.tldr: SC-MILP improves learned branching through depth-sensitive contrastive training and augmentation aimed at scarce upstream search nodes.

title: Dynamic Stratified Contrastive Learning with Upstream Augmentation for MILP Branching

abstract: We study online change point detection for multivariate inhomogeneous Poisson point process time series. This setting arises commonly in applications such as earthquake seismology, climate monitoring, and epidemic surveillance, yet remains underexplored in the machine learning and statistics literature. We propose a method that uses low-rank matrices to represent the multivariate Poisson intensity functions, resulting in an adaptive nonparametric detection procedure. Our algorithm is single-pass and requires only constant computational cost per new observation, independent of the elapsed length of the time series. We provide theoretical guarantees to control the overall false alarm probability and characterize the detection delay under temporal dependence. We also develop a new Matrix Bernstein inequality for temporally dependent Poisson point process time series, which may be of independent interest. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our method is both statistically robust and computationally efficient.

Such a setting appears in areas including earthquake monitoring, climate observation, and epidemic surveillance. The task is to recognize a change promptly while controlling how often the system raises a false alarm.

The computational cost of each new observation remains constant with respect to elapsed series length, so processing a later observation does not become more expensive simply because the monitoring history has grown.

They also derive a Matrix Bernstein inequality for temporally dependent Poisson event series as part of the theoretical contribution. Numerical experiments demonstrate statistical robustness and computational efficiency. Together, the results address both reliable change detection and the practical need to keep ongoing monitoring computationally manageable.
summary.tldr: The paper develops an online detector for changing multivariate event rates with false-alarm guarantees and constant processing cost per observation.

title: Online Change Point Detection for Multivariate Inhomogeneous Poisson Processes Time Series

abstract: Video Diffusion Models (VDMs) is constrained by immense computational costs. While offline calibration-based acceleration suffers from calibration data dependency, prohibitive calibration duration, and susceptibility to distribution shifts, offline calibration-free methods eliminate these hurdles. However, since they rely on instantaneous zero-order approximations where the mapping between input and output differences varies in real-time, they are susceptible to observational noise and ignore the intrinsic momentum within the diffusion trajectory. In this paper, we propose NaviCache, a plug-and-play test-time self-calibration method re-conceptualizing feature evolution as an Inertial Navigation System (INS) problem. NaviCache bridges the fundamental domain gap and the non-stationary nature of diffusion by modeling the relative coupling between input and output variations. We introduce a dual-state estimation architecture that adaptively tracks the feature change ratio and its latent drift, initialized via a specialized Initial Alignment phase. By integrating a time-dependent noise schedule with an uncertainty-aware Measurement Update mechanism, NaviCache provides a theoretically grounded mechanism for error-bounded block skipping. Extensive experiments on the HunyuanVideo, Wan, and Open-Sora series demonstrate that NaviCache exhibits more accurate error judgment for block skipping and achieves outstanding comprehensive performance.

paragraphs: NaviCache accelerates video diffusion by improving decisions about when computational blocks can be skipped. Offline calibration can be costly and sensitive to distribution changes. Existing approaches that avoid offline calibration instead rely on immediate approximations, which the paper argues are vulnerable to noise and fail to capture momentum in evolving diffusion features.

A dedicated initial alignment phase establishes these estimates. Subsequent updates combine a time-dependent noise schedule with uncertainty-aware measurements, allowing the estimates to adapt as the diffusion process changes.

This tracking mechanism provides a theoretically grounded approach to block skipping with bounded error. summary.tldr: NaviCache tracks feature-change dynamics and uncertainty during video generation to make more accurate, error-bounded block-skipping decisions.

title: NaviCache: Test-Time Self-Calibration Caching for Video Generation

abstract: A wide range of optimization problems can often be written in terms of generalized convex functions (GCFs). When this structure is present, it can convert certain nested bilevel objectives into single-level problems amenable to standard first-order optimization methods. We provide a new differentiable layer with a convex parameter space and show (Theorems 5.1 and 5.2) that it and its gradient are universal approximators for GCFs and their gradients. We demonstrate how this parameterization can be leveraged in practice by (i) learning optimal transport maps with general cost functions and (ii) learning optimal auctions of multiple goods. In both these cases, we show how our layer can be used to convert the existing bilevel or min-max formulations into single-level problems that can be solved efficiently with first-order methods.

The representation therefore addresses both the functions being learned and the gradients needed to optimize with them.

The paper demonstrates the layer in learning optimal transport maps with general cost functions and in learning optimal auctions for multiple goods. In both applications, it converts existing bilevel or min-max formulations into single-level problems that can be solved efficiently with first-order methods. The simplification relies on the relevant generalized convex structure being present; the contribution provides a representation that makes this structure usable in the demonstrated optimization tasks.
summary.tldr: A differentiable layer universally approximates generalized convex functions and gradients, enabling single-level formulations for demonstrated transport and auction problems.

title: Universal Representation of Generalized Convex Functions and their Gradients

abstract: Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning (URL) aims to pre-train scalable, skill-conditioned policies without extrinsic rewards, serving as a foundation for downstream control tasks. Despite recent progress, we argue that current off-policy URL methods are limited by two critical, overlooked bottlenecks: (1) non-stationarity skill semantic and (2) brittle generalization. To address these challenges, we propose GenDa (Generalizable Data-efficient Agent), a unified framework for robust unsupervised reinforcement learning. First, we introduce a skill relabeling mechanism to mitigate non-stationarity and significantly improve sample efficiency for pretraining. Second, we propose a Complementary Information Bottleneck(CIB), encouraging the learned skill policy to focus on ego-centric features and become robust to distribution shifts for downstream tasks. Through various experiments, we demonstrate that GenDa significantly enhances the scalability of URL with superior generality and sample efficiency. Our source codes are available in the supplementary materials.

paragraphs: Unsupervised reinforcement learning pretrains policies to perform different skills without task-provided rewards, creating a starting point for later control tasks. This paper identifies two obstacles in existing off-policy approaches: the meaning of a skill changes during learning, and the resulting policies can generalize poorly when downstream conditions differ.

GenDa addresses the changing meaning of skills through a relabeling mechanism. By revising skill labels, it mitigates this non-stationarity and improves the efficiency of pretraining data use. The method also introduces a Complementary Information Bottleneck, which encourages the policy to emphasize ego-centric features—features centered on the agent—and become more robust to distribution shifts.

These components address different parts of the same goal: learning reusable skills efficiently and retaining their usefulness beyond pretraining conditions. Across the reported experiments, GenDa improves sample efficiency and generality, supporting more scalable unsupervised reinforcement learning. The findings suggest that skill learning benefits from treating both evolving skill semantics and downstream robustness as explicit design problems within a unified framework.
summary.tldr: GenDa combines skill relabeling with an information bottleneck to improve unsupervised skill learning efficiency and generalization.

title: Learning Generalizable Skill Policy with Data-Efficient Unsupervised RL

abstract: A central challenge in large-scale decision-making under incomplete information is estimating reliable probabilities. Recent approaches use Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate explanatory factors and coarse-grained probability estimates, which are then refined by a Naïve Bayes model over factor combinations. However, sparse factor spaces often yield ”unknown” predictions, while expanding factors increases noise and spurious correlations, weakening conditional independence and degrading reliability. To address these limitations, we propose Anchor, an aggregated Bayesian inference framework over a hierarchical factor space. It constructs dense factor hierarchies through iterative generation and clustering, maps contexts via hierarchical retrieval and refinement, and augments Naïve Bayes with a Causal Bayesian Network to model latent factor dependencies. Experiments show that Anchor markedly reduces ”unknown” predictions and produces more reliable probability estimates than direct LLM baselines, achieving state-of-the-art performance while significantly reducing time and token overhead.

paragraphs: Estimating probabilities from incomplete information requires both useful explanatory factors and a reliable way to combine them. Existing approaches ask language models to propose factors and rough probabilities, then refine these with Naïve Bayes. Too few factors leave cases unresolved, but simply adding more introduces noise and correlations that undermine the independence assumptions behind that refinement.

ANCHOR organizes explanatory factors into a hierarchy through repeated generation and clustering. It matches a context to this hierarchy using retrieval and refinement, allowing probability inference to draw on a denser, structured factor space. It also supplements Naïve Bayes with a Causal Bayesian Network that represents otherwise hidden dependencies between factors. Together, these components address both missing coverage and unreliable combinations of correlated evidence.

The reported experiments show fewer unknown predictions and more reliable probability estimates than direct language-model baselines. ANCHOR also achieves leading performance while reducing time and token overhead. These findings support hierarchical organization and explicit dependency modeling as complementary ways to improve probability inference.
summary.tldr: ANCHOR organizes explanatory factors hierarchically and models their dependencies to improve language-model-based probability estimates.

title: ANCHOR: Abductive Network Construction with Hierarchical Orchestration for Reliable Probability Inference in Large Language Models

abstract: Safety-critical scenarios are central to evaluating autonomous driving systems, yet their rarity in naturalistic logs makes simulation-based stress testing indispensable. Most scenario generation methods treat surrounding agents as adversaries, but they either (i) induce failures without explicitly modeling vehicle-road physical limits, yielding visually extreme yet physically unsolvable crashes, or (ii) enforce physical feasibility or policy feasibility in isolation, which can over-focus on aggressive maneuvers or remain tied to a controller-dependent capability boundary. We propose ScenePilot, a feasibility-guided, boundary-driven framework that targets the boundary band: scenarios that are physically solvable in principle yet still cause the deployed autonomy stack to fail. We formulate generation as constrained multi-objective reinforcement learning, combining an RSS-derived physical-feasibility score $\sigma$ with an online-learned AV-risk predictor $\Phi$, and introduce step-level feasibility-aware shielding to keep exploration near the feasibility boundary while avoiding infeasible artifacts. Experiments on SafeBench with multiple planners show that ScenePilot yields substantially higher collision rates (+6.2 percentage points) while preserving physical validity, and that adversarial fine-tuning on these boundary-band scenarios consistently reduces downstream crash rates. The code is available at https://github.com/QiyuRuan/ScenePilot.

The framework formulates scenario generation as constrained multi-objective reinforcement learning. It combines an RSS-derived physical-feasibility score with an autonomous-vehicle risk predictor learned online. A feasibility-aware shield acts at individual steps to keep exploration near the physical boundary while avoiding infeasible artifacts. These components jointly direct the generator toward challenging, physically valid situations.

They also find that adversarial fine-tuning on these scenarios consistently reduces downstream crash rates. The results support using physically solvable failures both to expose weaknesses in deployed planners and to generate training cases that improve performance in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: ScenePilot generates physically solvable driving scenarios that expose planner failures and support training that reduces subsequent crashes.

title: ScenePilot: Controllable Boundary-Driven Critical Scenario Generation for Autonomous Driving

abstract: We introduce WildCat, a high-accuracy, low-cost approach to compressing the attention mechanism in neural networks. While attention is a staple of modern network architectures, it is also notoriously expensive to deploy due to resource requirements that scale quadratically with the input sequence length $n$. WildCat avoids these quadratic costs by only attending over a small weighted coreset. Crucially, we select the coreset using a fast but spectrally-accurate subsampling algorithm – randomly pivoted Cholesky – and weight the elements optimally to minimise reconstruction error. Remarkably, given bounded inputs, WildCat approximates exact attention with super-polynomial $O(n^{-\sqrt{\log(\log(n))}})$ error decay while running in near-linear $O(n^{1+o(1)})$ time. In contrast, prior practical approximations either lack error guarantees or require quadratic runtime to guarantee such high fidelity. We couple this advance with a GPU-optimised PyTorch implementation and a suite of benchmark experiments demonstrating the benefits of WildCat for image generation, image classification, and language model KV cache compression.

These experiments demonstrate benefits across several applications, complementing the theoretical account of how accuracy and computation scale under the stated assumption.
summary.tldr: WildCat approximates attention with a small weighted coreset, achieving near-linear runtime and strong error guarantees for bounded inputs.

title: WildCat: Near-Linear Attention in Theory and Practice

abstract: AI has the potential to transform cybersecurity by enabling systems that can autonomously detect, analyze, and remediate software vulnerabilities. However, existing cybersecurity evaluations of AI systems are limited in scale or scope, and fail to capture the end-to-end lifecycle of real-world software vulnerability discovery and remediation. To address this gap, we propose CyberGym-E2E, a large-scale and realistic end-to-end cybersecurity benchmark that comprehensively evaluates AI agents’ abilities across the full lifecycle of vulnerability discovery, PoC generation, and patch generation. CyberGym-E2E is comprehensive and scalable, as we build an automated, agent-enhanced pipeline for transforming open-source vulnerability data into realistic evaluation environments. Currently, the benchmark consists of 920 real-world vulnerabilities across 139 different open-source projects.

paragraphs: Cybersecurity agents may need to discover a software vulnerability, demonstrate that it exists, and produce a repair. Evaluating only one of these activities gives an incomplete view of the overall workflow. CyberGym-E2E addresses this evaluation gap with a benchmark designed to cover the full sequence of vulnerability discovery, proof-of-concept generation, and patch generation.

The benchmark draws on real vulnerabilities in open-source software. An automated pipeline, enhanced by agents, transforms existing vulnerability data into realistic evaluation environments. This construction method is central to the contribution: it provides a way to build a broad evaluation collection from existing records while retaining a connection to actual software problems.

The reported collection includes 920 vulnerabilities across 139 open-source projects. Its breadth and coverage of connected stages make it an infrastructure contribution for assessing end-to-end cybersecurity capabilities. The abstract presents the benchmark and its construction, rather than comparative agent scores; its stated result is a scalable evaluation resource spanning both finding vulnerabilities and generating their fixes.
summary.tldr: CyberGym-E2E evaluates vulnerability discovery, proof-of-concept generation, and patch generation using 920 real vulnerabilities across 139 projects.

title: CyberGym-E2E: Scalable Real-World Benchmark for AI Agents’ End-to-End Cybersecurity Capabilities

abstract: Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes from blurry monocular videos is challenging because motion-induced blur entangles object motion and geometry, hindering geometric consistency. We present Kinematics-GS, a kinematics-aware framework that models blur as motion-aligned deformation and introduces a kinematic prior to reparameterize Gaussian shapes along motion trajectories, thereby mitigating degenerate shape collapse without auxiliary motion supervision. To stabilize optimization, we decompose scenes into dynamic and static components using temporal deformation variance and employ a coarse-to-fine deformation strategy to capture both global motion and fine-grained details. We also introduce a challenging real-world dataset of deformable and elastic objects exhibiting non-rigid motion with spatially non-uniform motion blur that obscures geometric cues. Extensive experiments on real-world benchmarks with realistic motion blur demonstrate that Kinematics-GS outperforms prior methods by a clear margin in monocular dynamic scene reconstruction, highlighting its effectiveness in handling complex and non-rigid motion scenarios.

To stabilize optimization, we decompose scenes into dynamic and static components using temporal deformation variance and employ a coarse-to-fine deformation strategy to capture both global motion and fine-grained details. We also introduce a challenging real-world dataset of deformable and elastic objects exhibiting non-rigid motion with spatially non-uniform motion blur that obscures geometric cues. paragraphs: Kinematics-GS reconstructs moving 3D scenes from blurry video recorded by a single camera. Motion blur entangles an object’s movement with its apparent geometry, making consistent reconstruction difficult. The method treats blur as deformation aligned with motion and uses a kinematic prior to parameterize Gaussian shapes along motion trajectories.

This coupling helps mitigate degenerate collapse of the reconstructed shapes without requiring auxiliary motion supervision. To stabilize learning further, the framework separates dynamic and static scene components according to how their deformation varies over time. A coarse-to-fine strategy then captures broad motion before refining smaller details, coordinating reconstruction across different levels of movement.

The authors also introduce a real-world dataset featuring deformable and elastic objects. Its non-rigid motion creates blur that varies spatially and hides geometric cues. Experiments on real-world benchmarks with realistic blur show a clear improvement over prior reconstruction methods. The findings support using motion structure to guide Gaussian geometry in difficult monocular scenes, including complex non-rigid movement.
summary.tldr: Kinematics-GS uses motion-aligned Gaussian deformation to improve reconstruction of blurry, non-rigid scenes from single-camera video.

title: Kinematics-Driven Gaussian Shape Deformation for Blurry Monocular Dynamic Scenes

abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning successfully enhances the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet it incurs substantial computational overhead for inference. Existing CoT compression methods often suffer from a critical loss of logical fidelity at high compression ratios, resulting in significant performance degradation. To achieve high-fidelity, fast reasoning, we propose a novel EXTreme-RAtio Chain-of-Thought Compression framework, termed Extra-CoT, which aggressively reduces the token budget while preserving answer accuracy. To generate reliable, high-fidelity supervision, we first train a dedicated semantically-preserved compressor on mathematical CoT data with fine-grained annotations. An LLM is then fine-tuned on these compressed pairs via a mixed-ratio supervised fine-tuning (SFT), teaching it to follow a spectrum of compression budgets and providing a stable initialization for reinforcement learning (RL). We further propose Constrained and Hierarchical Ratio Policy Optimization (CHRPO) to explicitly incentivize question-solving ability under lower budgets by a hierarchical reward. Experiments on three mathematical reasoning benchmarks show the superiority of Extra-CoT. For example, on MATH-500 using Qwen3-1.7B, Extra-CoT achieves over 73% token reduction with an accuracy improvement of 0.6%, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods. Our source codes are released in the Supplementaries.

paragraphs: Long chains of reasoning improve language-model performance but increase inference computation. Compressing them aggressively can remove logical content and damage accuracy. Extra-CoT addresses this problem with a training pipeline designed to preserve the meaning of reasoning traces while substantially reducing their token budgets.

The pipeline first trains a dedicated compressor on mathematical reasoning data with fine-grained annotations. title: Towards Efficient Large Language Reasoning Models via Extreme-Ratio Chain-of-Thought Compression

abstract: Exploring causal relationships in stochastic time series is a challenging yet crucial task with a vast range of applications, including finance, economics, neuroscience, and climate science. Many algorithms for Causal Discovery (CD) have been proposed; however, they often exhibit a high sensitivity to noise, resulting in spurious causal inferences on real data. In this paper, we observe that the frequency spectra of many real-world time series follow a power-law distribution, notably due to an inherent self-organizing behavior. Leveraging this insight, we build a robust CD method based on the extraction of power-law spectral features that amplify genuine causal signals. Our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives on both synthetic benchmarks and real-world datasets with known causal structures, demonstrating its robustness and practical relevance.

paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships in time series is difficult because noise can make unrelated variation look like meaningful influence. This paper addresses that problem through the frequency structure of the data. The authors observe that many real-world time series have power-law spectra, a pattern they connect notably to self-organizing behavior.

Their method extracts spectral features based on this power-law structure to amplify genuine causal signals. The key choice is to use the way variation is distributed across frequencies as information for causal discovery. This brings a recurring property of real-world stochastic signals into the design of the inference method, with robustness to noise as the motivating objective.

The authors report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art alternatives on synthetic benchmarks and real-world datasets with known causal structures. Those known structures allow inferred relationships to be checked against a reference, giving the comparisons a direct basis for assessing causal recovery. The findings support the practical value of power-law spectral features in the evaluated settings, connecting a statistical regularity in time series with more reliable causal inference.
summary.tldr: Power-law spectral features improve reported causal discovery performance on noisy synthetic and real-world time series.

title: Robust Causal Discovery in Real-World Time Series with Power-Laws

abstract: State-of-the-art large language models require specialized hardware and substantial energy to operate. Consequently, cloud-based services that provide access to these models have become very popular. In these services, the price users pay depends on the number of tokens a model uses to generate an output–they pay a fixed price per token. In this work, we show that this pricing mechanism creates a financial incentive for providers to strategize and misreport the (number of) tokens a model used to generate an output, and users cannot prove, or even know, whether a provider is overcharging them. However, we also show that, if an unfaithful provider is obliged to be transparent about the generative process used by the model, misreporting optimally without raising suspicion is hard. Nevertheless, as a proof-of-concept, we develop an efficient heuristic algorithm that allows providers to significantly overcharge users without raising suspicion. Crucially, the cost of running the algorithm is lower than the additional revenue from overcharging users, highlighting the vulnerability of users under the current pay-per-token pricing mechanism. Further, we show that, to eliminate the financial incentive to strategize, a pricing mechanism must price tokens linearly on their character count. While this makes a provider’s profit margin vary across tokens, we introduce a simple prescription that allows a provider to maintain their average profit margin when transitioning to an incentive-compatible pricing mechanism. To complement our theoretical results, we conduct experiments with large language models from the $\texttt{Llama}$, $\texttt{Gemma}$ and $\texttt{Ministral}$ families, and prompts from a popular benchmarking platform.

paragraphs: Charging a fixed amount per token gives a language-model provider a financial reason to misreport how many tokens an output used. This paper analyzes that incentive and the difficulty users face in detecting or proving overcharging. It studies a vulnerability of the pricing mechanism rather than presenting evidence that particular providers engage in it.

Requiring transparency about the generation process makes optimal, unsuspected misreporting computationally difficult. However, the authors construct an efficient proof-of-concept heuristic that can still substantially overcharge without raising suspicion. Its computational cost is lower than the extra revenue, showing that transparency alone does not remove the incentive within the studied setting.

The authors also give a prescription for preserving a provider’s average profit margin during that transition, despite variation in margins across tokens. Experiments with Llama, Gemma, and Ministral models complement the theory, connecting the pricing analysis to practical language-model tokenization.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies incentives for token-count misreporting and derives character-proportional token pricing as necessary to remove them in its framework.

title: Is Your LLM Overcharging You? Tokenization, Transparency, and Incentives

abstract: Existing approaches for multimodal variational autoencoders (VAEs) face a trade-off between generative quality and coherence—i.e., they struggle to generate realistic and diverse samples that, at the same time, are semantically consistent across modalities. A recent work shows that using a simple approximation to Hölder pooling as an aggregation method improves coherence over the SOTA MMVAE+, despite assuming a single shared representation across all modalities. Yet, it slightly compromises sample diversity. Inspired by this insight, we propose Hölder++, a novel multimodal VAE that improves the generative quality-coherence trade-off through: (i) the first implementation of Hölder pooling without any approximation for multimodal VAEs; (ii) an extended architecture that models distinct shared and private (i.e., modality-specific) representations (Hölder+); and (iii) hierarchical inference that further enhances the disentanglement between the shared and private representations (Hölder++). Our experiments corroborate that Hölder++ consistently improves the generative quality-coherence trade-off, yields more structured latent spaces, and learns shared representations that are informative for downstream tasks.

A recent work shows that using a simple approximation to Hölder pooling as an aggregation method improves coherence over the SOTA MMVAE+, despite assuming a single shared representation across all modalities. Yet, it slightly compromises sample diversity. Inspired by this insight, we propose Hölder++, a novel multimodal VAE that improves the generative quality-coherence trade-off through: (i) the first implementation of Hölder pooling without any approximation for multimodal VAEs; (ii) an extended architecture that models distinct shared and private (i.e., modality-specific) representations (Hölder+); and (iii) hierarchical inference that further enhances the disentanglement between the shared and private representations (Hölder++). Our experiments corroborate that Hölder++ consistently improves the generative quality-coherence trade-off, yields more structured latent spaces, and learns shared representations that are informative for downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Multimodal variational autoencoders must generate samples that are realistic and diverse while keeping their meaning consistent across modalities. Improving this consistency can reduce diversity. Earlier work used an approximation to Hölder pooling to improve coherence, but relied on one shared representation and slightly compromised sample diversity.

This paper develops the approach in three steps. It first implements Hölder pooling without approximation. It then introduces Hölder+, an architecture with separate shared and modality-specific representations, allowing common information and information particular to one modality to be represented distinctly. Hölder++ adds hierarchical inference to improve separation between those shared and private components.

Experiments show that Hölder++ consistently improves the balance between generation quality and cross-modal coherence. The model also produces more structured latent spaces and shared representations useful for downstream tasks. The contribution therefore concerns both generated outputs and the organization of internal representations: the proposed pooling and inference design improves their reported balance without treating all information as a single shared representation.
summary.tldr: Hölder++ combines exact Hölder pooling, shared and private representations, and hierarchical inference to improve multimodal generation quality and coherence.

title: Hölder++: Improving the Quality-Coherence Trade-off in Multimodal VAEs

abstract: Constant-stepsize stochastic approximation is widely used in learning for computational efficiency. For a fixed stepsize, the iterates typically admit a stationary distribution that is rarely tractable. Prior work shows that as the stepsize $\alpha \downarrow 0$, the centered-and-scaled steady state converges weakly to a Gaussian limit. However, for fixed $\alpha$, this weak convergence offers no usable error bound for approximating the steady-state by its Gaussian limit. This paper provides explicit, non-asymptotic error bounds for fixed $\alpha$. We study (i) stochastic gradient descent on smooth strongly convex objectives, (ii) linear SA, and (iii) contractive nonlinear SA, and we treat both i.i.d. and Markovian noise models to ensure broad applicability. Our main results first give dimension- and stepsize-dependent, explicit bounds in Wasserstein distance between the centered-scaled steady state and its Gaussian limit, with errors that vanish as $\alpha \downarrow 0$. We further derive sharp tail control, comparing the steady-state tail probability to Gaussian tails with an explicit error term that decays in both the deviation level and $\alpha$. Our analysis combines steady-state Stein’s method with moment bounds on the SA iterations, and uses Poisson equation techniques to manage temporal dependence in the Markovian noise setting. We adapt the same toolkit to SGD with general convex objectives and suggest non-Gaussian limiting behavior, which is validated in numerical experiments.

However, for fixed $\alpha$, this weak convergence offers no usable error bound for approximating the steady-state by its Gaussian limit. This paper provides explicit, non-asymptotic error bounds for fixed $\alpha$. paragraphs: With a constant learning step size, stochastic approximation typically settles into a stationary distribution of iterates. Earlier Gaussian-limit results describe what happens as the step size approaches zero, but do not give a usable approximation error for a fixed step size. This paper supplies explicit bounds for that practical setting.

The analysis covers stochastic gradient descent on smooth strongly convex objectives, linear stochastic approximation, and contractive nonlinear updates. It considers both independent noise and temporally dependent Markovian noise. The main results bound the Wasserstein distance between the centered, scaled stationary distribution and its Gaussian limit, explicitly tracking dimension and step size. The bounds vanish as the step size decreases.

The authors also compare stationary tail probabilities with Gaussian tails, with an error term that decreases with deviation level and step size. Their toolkit combines Stein’s method, moment bounds, and Poisson equations for temporal dependence. Extending the analysis to general convex objectives suggests non-Gaussian limiting behavior, supported by numerical experiments rather than asserted as a universal Gaussian approximation.
summary.tldr: The paper quantifies Gaussian approximation errors and tail behavior for stationary stochastic approximation at fixed step sizes.

title: Steady-State Behavior of Constant-Stepsize Stochastic Approximation: Gaussian Approximation and Tail Bounds

abstract: Real-world data contains aleatoric uncertainty – irreducible noise arising from imperfect measurements or from incomplete knowledge about the data generation process. Mean-variance estimation networks can learn this type of uncertainty but require ad-hoc regularization strategies to avoid overfitting and are unable to predict epistemic uncertainty (model uncertainty). Conversely, Bayesian neural networks predict epistemic uncertainty but are notoriously difficult to train due to the approximate nature of Bayesian inference. We propose to cooperatively train a variance estimation network with a Bayesian neural network and empirically demonstrate that the resulting model disentangles aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties while improving the mean estimation. We demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of this method across a diverse range of datasets, including a time-dependent heteroscedastic regression dataset we created where the aleatoric uncertainty is known. The proposed method is straightforward to implement, robust, and adaptable to various model architectures. Code is available at https://github.com/bessagroup/VeBNN.

paragraphs: An uncertain prediction can reflect noise in the data or uncertainty in the model itself. The paper distinguishes these as aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Networks that estimate a mean and variance can capture data noise, but may overfit and require additional regularization. Bayesian neural networks address model uncertainty, although approximate Bayesian inference makes them difficult to train.

The proposed method trains a variance-estimation network cooperatively with a Bayesian neural network. This brings the two uncertainty estimates into a shared training approach. The authors empirically find that the resulting model separates the two sources of uncertainty while also improving its estimate of the mean prediction.

Evaluation covers diverse datasets, including a newly created regression dataset whose noise varies over time and whose aleatoric uncertainty is known. That known uncertainty provides a direct reference for evaluating the noise estimate. The reported results support the method's effectiveness and scalability, and the authors describe it as robust, straightforward to implement, and compatible with different model architectures.
summary.tldr: Cooperatively training variance estimation and Bayesian networks empirically separates data noise from model uncertainty while improving mean predictions.

title: Cooperative Variance Estimation and Bayesian Neural Networks for Disentangling Aleatoric and Epistemic Uncertainties

abstract: Despite the remarkable success of Vision Transformers (ViTs) across a wide range of vision tasks, recent studies have revealed that they remain vulnerable to adversarial examples, much like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). A common empirical defense strategy is adversarial training, yet the theoretical underpinnings of its robustness in ViTs remain largely unexplored. In this work, we present the first theoretical analysis of adversarial training under simplified ViT architectures. We show that, when trained under a signal-to-noise ratio that satisfies a certain condition and within a moderate perturbation budget, adversarial training enables ViTs to achieve nearly zero robust training loss and robust generalization error under certain regimes. Remarkably, this leads to strong generalization even in the presence of overfitting, a phenomenon known as benign overfitting, previously only observed in CNNs (with adversarial training). Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets further validate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers can perform well on ordinary images while remaining vulnerable to adversarial examples. Adversarial training is a common defense, but its theoretical basis for these models has been less developed. This paper studies simplified Vision Transformer architectures to explain when fitting adversarially perturbed training examples can also support reliable performance on unseen examples.

The central result is conditional: under a specified signal-to-noise requirement, a moderate perturbation budget, and particular regimes, adversarial training yields nearly zero robust training loss and robust generalization error. This permits benign overfitting, where fitting the training data very closely coexists with strong generalization. The analysis extends this phenomenon to adversarially trained Vision Transformers, beyond its earlier observation in adversarially trained convolutional networks.

Experiments with synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical findings. The contribution is an explanation of how overfitting and robustness can coexist under the studied conditions. Its guarantees concern simplified architectures and the stated regimes, so the result should be read as a conditional account of robust learning rather than a guarantee for every Vision Transformer.
summary.tldr: Under specified signal, perturbation, and model conditions, adversarially trained Vision Transformers can overfit while still generalizing robustly.

title: Benign Overfitting in Adversarial Training for Vision Transformers

abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have exhibited remarkable efficacy in various image restoration tasks. However, existing approaches typically operate within the high-dimensional pixel space, resulting in high computational overhead. While methods based on latent DMs seek to alleviate this issue by utilizing the compressed latent space of a variational autoencoder, they require repeated encoder-decoder inference. This introduces significant additional computational burdens, often resulting in runtime performance that is even inferior to that of their pixel-space counterparts. To mitigate the computational inefficiency, this work proposes projecting data into lower-dimensional subspaces using dynamic resolution DMs to accelerate the inference process. We first fine-tune pre-trained DMs for dynamic resolution priors and adapt DPS and DAPS, which are two widely used pixel-space methods for general image restoration tasks, into the proposed framework, yielding methods we refer to as SubDPS and SubDAPS, respectively. Given the favorable inference speed and reconstruction fidelity of SubDAPS, we introduce an enhanced variant termed SubDAPS++ to further boost both reconstruction efficiency and quality. Empirical evaluations across diverse image datasets and various restoration tasks demonstrate that the proposed methods outperform recent DM-based approaches in the majority of experimental scenarios. The code is available at https://github.com/StarNextDay/SubDAPS.git.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based image restoration can be computationally expensive when it operates directly over all image pixels. Compressed latent representations offer another approach, but repeated encoding and decoding can add enough overhead to undermine their runtime advantage. This paper investigates reducing the dimensionality of restoration through diffusion models that support dynamic image resolution.

The authors fine-tune pretrained diffusion models to provide dynamic-resolution priors, then adapt two existing restoration methods, DPS and DAPS, to this framework. The resulting methods are called SubDPS and SubDAPS. Their shared idea is to project data into lower-dimensional subspaces so that restoration inference can use a less expensive representation.

Because SubDAPS offers a favorable combination of reconstruction fidelity and inference speed, the authors develop SubDAPS++ to improve both further. Evaluations span multiple image datasets and restoration tasks, with the proposed methods outperforming recent diffusion approaches in most tested scenarios. The findings support dynamic resolution as a useful way to balance restoration quality and computational cost; the reported advantage is broad across the experiments, rather than universal.
summary.tldr: Dynamic-resolution diffusion methods accelerate image restoration while improving reconstruction results in most reported experimental settings.

title: Image Restoration via Diffusion Models with Dynamic Resolution

abstract: Long video understanding faces a critical dilemma: cloud-based Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) offer superior reasoning but suffer from prohibitive bandwidth costs and latency, while edge-based solutions sacrifice perception accuracy for speed. Current collaborative approaches attempt to bridge this gap via similarity-based filtering, yet they treat complex queries as flat semantic vectors. We identify this as a fundamental flaw leading to "Semantic Submergence," where dominant visual features drown out subtle but logically critical cues. To solve this, we introduce SCOPE (Semantic Cloud-Orchestrated Perception at Edge). Shifting the paradigm to "Think in Cloud, Look at Edges," SCOPE utilizes a cloud LMM to decompose complex queries into a structured Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). This "observation plan" guides the edge to retrieve evidence based on logical necessity rather than mere statistical similarity. Experiments on Video-MME and LongVideoBench demonstrate that SCOPE redefines the Pareto frontier, matching cloud-level accuracy with significantly lower transmission costs and outperforming state-of-the-art baselines on complex reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: Long-video reasoning creates a tension between powerful cloud models and the cost of sending video to them. Existing collaborative systems often select evidence using similarity to a single representation of the query. The paper argues that this can bury subtle but logically essential cues beneath dominant visual features, a problem it calls Semantic Submergence.

SCOPE uses a cloud multimodal model to decompose a complex query into a directed acyclic graph. This structured observation plan tells edge devices which evidence is needed and how the observations relate. Retrieval is therefore guided by logical requirements in the question, rather than only by broad statistical similarity between the query and video content.

On Video-MME and LongVideoBench, the paper reports cloud-level accuracy with significantly lower transmission costs, along with improvements over state-of-the-art baselines on complex reasoning tasks. The findings support assigning planning to the cloud and evidence retrieval to the edge. Explicit query structure helps determine which video information must be transmitted to support the reasoning.
summary.tldr: SCOPE converts complex video queries into cloud-generated observation plans, enabling edge retrieval that preserves accuracy with lower transmission costs.

title: Think in Cloud, Look at Edges: Semantic-Driven Query Decomposition for Efficient Video Reasoning

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing across diverse domains, yet their application in theoretical physics remains inadequate. While current models show competence in mathematical reasoning and code generation, we identify critical gaps in physical intuition, constraint satisfaction, and reliable reasoning that cannot be addressed through prompting alone. Physics demands approximation judgment, symmetry exploitation, and physical grounding that require AI agents specifically trained on physics reasoning patterns and equipped with physics-aware verification tools. We argue that LLM would require such domain-specialized training and tooling to be useful in real-world for physics research. We envision physics-specialized AI agents that seamlessly handle multimodal data, propose physically consistent hypotheses, and autonomously verify theoretical results. Realizing this vision requires developing physics-specific training datasets, reward signals that capture physical reasoning quality, and verification frameworks encoding fundamental principles. We call for collaborative efforts between physics and AI communities to build the specialized infrastructure necessary for AI-driven scientific discovery.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that current language models remain inadequate for theoretical physics research despite their mathematical and coding abilities. The authors identify shortcomings in physical intuition, satisfaction of constraints, and dependable reasoning. Their claim is that prompting alone cannot close these gaps because useful physics work requires specialized forms of judgment.

The paper emphasizes deciding when approximations are appropriate, exploiting symmetries, and grounding reasoning in physical principles. It proposes agents trained specifically on physics reasoning patterns and supported by verification tools that understand physical requirements. Training and verification serve complementary roles: producing plausible reasoning is only part of the task when theoretical results also need physical consistency.

The authors envision agents that handle multiple data modalities, propose physically consistent hypotheses, and verify theoretical results autonomously. They identify physics-specific datasets, rewards that reflect reasoning quality, and verification frameworks encoding fundamental principles as necessary infrastructure for that vision. This is a research agenda calling for collaboration between physicists and AI researchers, with specialized capabilities and checking mechanisms developed together.
summary.tldr: The authors argue that useful physics research agents require specialized training and verification tools grounded in physical principles.

abstract: In recent years the L1,Infinity norm has been proposed for joint regularization. In essence, this type of regularization aims at extending the L1 framework for learning sparse models to a setting where the goal is to learn a set of jointly sparse models. In this paper we derive a simple and effective projected gradient method for optimization of L1,Infinity regularized problems. The main challenge in developing such a method resides on being able to compute efficient projections to the L1,Infinity ball. We present an algorithm that works in O(n log n) time and O(n) memory where n is the number of parameters. We test our algorithm in a multi-task image annotation problem. Our results show that L1,Infinity leads to better performance than both L2 and L1 regularization and that it is is effective in discovering jointly sparse solutions.

We present an algorithm that works in O(n log n) time and O(n) memory where n is the number of parameters. We test our algorithm in a multi-task image annotation problem. paragraphs: Learning several related models creates an opportunity to encourage sparsity jointly. Instead of merely making each model use few parameters, joint regularization encourages a coordinated sparse solution across the collection. This paper develops an optimization method for the L1,Infinity norm, which extends the sparse modeling role of L1 regularization to this shared setting.

The proposed method uses projected gradient optimization. Its central computational requirement is an efficient way to project parameter values onto an L1,Infinity ball, bringing an update back into the permitted region. The paper supplies an algorithm for this operation that takes O(n log n) time and O(n) memory, where n counts the parameters. This addresses the main obstacle to using the projected gradient approach.

The authors evaluate the method on multi-task image annotation. In that experiment, L1,Infinity regularization performs better than both L2 and L1 regularization and discovers jointly sparse solutions. These findings support the practical value of coordinating sparsity across related prediction tasks, alongside the contribution of an efficient optimization building block.
summary.tldr: An efficient projection algorithm makes joint sparse regularization practical and improves performance in a multi-task image annotation experiment.

title: An efficient projection for l1,infinity regularization

abstract: Random projections have been applied in many machine learning algorithms. However, whether margin is preserved after random projection is non-trivial and not well studied. In this paper we analyse margin distortion after random projection, and give the conditions of margin preservation for binary classification problems. We also extend our analysis to margin for multiclass problems, and provide theoretical bounds on multiclass margin on the projected data.
originalAbstract: Random projections have been applied in many machine learning algorithms. However, whether margin is preserved after random projection is non-trivial and not well studied. We also extend our analysis to margin for multiclass problems, and provide theoretical bounds on multiclass margin on the projected data.

paragraphs: Random projection changes the representation of data, raising a classification question: what happens to the margin separating classes? A useful representation should preserve the separation relevant to prediction. This paper examines that question directly by analyzing how a random projection can distort classification margins.

For binary classification, the authors give conditions under which the margin is preserved. This is a conditional result: using a random projection alone does not establish that class separation survives. The analysis identifies circumstances in which preservation can be supported theoretically, making the margin an explicit object of study when assessing the projected data.

The authors then extend their analysis to multiclass problems and derive theoretical bounds on margins after projection. This extends the question beyond separation between two classes to settings involving several possible labels. Together, the binary conditions and multiclass bounds provide a theoretical basis for reasoning about classification after random projection, with the central contribution being control of margin distortion rather than an unconditional preservation claim.
summary.tldr: The paper gives conditions for preserving binary classification margins under random projection and theoretical bounds for multiclass margins.

title: Is margin preserved after random projection?
